comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I have been an immigration practitioner specializing in higher education since 1989. My political views are pragmatic and over the many years I have worked with members of Congress on both sides of the aisle, as well as their members of staff, to find common ground and a bipartisan approach to matters that impact international education. Besides simply being completely arbitrary and capricious, the proposal to institute a $70,000 fee on F-1 Optional Practical Training (OPT), and a subsequent $30,000 for a STEM OPT extension, is perhaps one of the stupidest and poorly thought out public policy decisions in recent memory, even by this current administration’s ineptitude. Here is why:
•Article 1, Section 8, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution declares that only Congress shall have the power to lay and collect taxes. This proposed OPT fee is ultimately a tax, not a fee. Indeed, there is already a fee made payable to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for OPT. Thus, the fee proposal is indeed a tax and inherently unconstitutional.
•A $70,000 fee is an impossible financial burden on F-1 visa holders as well as their host institutions who sponsor their F-1 visas. There is simply no basis for such a fee other than to arbitrarily disincentivize international students and their sponsoring institutions from obtaining OPT.
•The proposed OPT fee provides chronic and unresolved lack of direction and instruction on how the fee shall actually be implemented by all parties, including by the federal government.
•For a public institution such as where I work, a federal OPT fee essentially places a federal charge and administrative burden on the logistics and business practices of a state entity. This becomes a state’s rights issue.
•Facts? There is a consistent theme of “fraud” running throughout the administration’s justification for such an OPT fee. Where is the data? Where are the facts? If and when fraud is found, those responsible should absolutely face the repercussions. But to arbitrarily make up a narrative of “fraud” without quantifiable data and facts belittles the government’s credibility and justification for the OPT fee proposal. At my institution, great care is placed on the advising and guidance that is provided to our F-1 students so that they adhere to all tenets of F-1 OPT regulations. As someone who has worked in this field for nearly 40-years I can absolutely guarantee you that it is standard professional practice amongst our profession to uphold the highest standards and adherence to federal F-1 immigration regulations. Frankly, the implication that international students and their institutional F-1 sponsors are abetting OPT fraud is despicable and offensive.
•Current government systems, databases and DHS officers already monitor and oversee OPT participation and are less burdensome alternatives to an OPT fee. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), through the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) contains complete and thorough information on OPT participation, OPT employers, OPT unemployment, etc. Why not use existing government tools to monitor and oversee OPT rather than institute an arbitrary fee on OPT participation? Furthermore, the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) unit of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) already have dedicated and knowledgeable regional field representatives who work with the F-1 and J-1 populations and their institutional sponsors to oversee and advise on pertinent regulatory matters. Utilize these government officers to monitor any perceived OPT fraud and questionable practices by F-1 students, OPT employers or F-1 institutional sponsors. These SEVP field representatives are not currently and adequately utilized to assist in the government’s oversight of OPT, despite already having the resources and personnel to do so. This is a poor example of the mantra of better government efficiency (i.e. DOGE).
•The OPT fee will do exceptional harm to the U.S. workforce and scientific research. It is a completely false and politically disingenuous narrative that OPT takes away employment from the domestic workforce. There is overwhelmingly positive data and facts that prove the benefits of OPT on the U.S. economy and related industries, especially in the areas of scientific research, technology and business development. Ignoring the reality of the economic and scientific benefits of OPT shows a capricious disregards for facts and proven data regarding OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is an unconstitutional tax and an impossible financial burden.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Elizabeth Peterson
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees because their consequences would extend far beyond international students. The policy could undermine the financial stability of American universities, reduce educational resources available to domestic students, and threaten employment in college communities.

The Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report documented approximately 1.18 million international students in American higher education during the 2024-2025 academic year. Importantly, 59% attended public institutions.

International education is therefore not merely a concern for wealthy private universities. It is closely connected to the financial health of public higher education institutions serving American students.

The proposed fee would require universities to pay $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation. Consider an institution with 500 students seeking initial OPT annually. Supporting all 500 would require $35 million in fees, before accounting for subsequent OPT recommendations.

For many institutions, this would represent an extraordinary financial obligation. Universities could respond by limiting OPT recommendations, reallocating existing budgets, or seeking additional revenue.

Each response carries potential consequences for American students.

First, international students contribute tuition revenue that supports university operations. Although the extent of cross-subsidization varies across institutions, reduced international enrollment can place pressure on budgets supporting academic departments, instructional facilities, student services, and financial assistance.

If universities lose this revenue, domestic students may face higher tuition, reduced course offerings, larger classes, or diminished access to academic resources.

Second, universities employ American faculty, administrators, laboratory technicians, teaching assistants, maintenance workers, and student-service personnel. Financial pressures caused by reduced enrollment could lead institutions to freeze hiring, eliminate positions, or reduce academic programs.

Third, international graduate students contribute to research and teaching. Their participation can support laboratories, faculty research projects, and instructional activities that also benefit domestic students. Reduced international enrollment may therefore affect research productivity, course availability, and undergraduate research opportunities.

Fourth, universities are major economic anchors for their surrounding communities. International students rent apartments, purchase groceries, visit restaurants, use transportation, and support local businesses.

NAFSA estimated that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 American jobs during the 2024-2025 academic year.

In fall 2025, declining international enrollment was associated with an estimated $1.1 billion reduction in economic contributions and nearly 23,000 fewer supported jobs.

These findings illustrate that international student enrollment supports American employment outside university campuses as well.

Fifth, the proposed fee structure could exacerbate inequality between universities. Wealthy institutions may be better positioned to absorb extraordinary fees, while smaller universities, regional public institutions, and financially constrained schools may have little practical ability to do so.

The result could be a system in which access to practical training depends increasingly on institutional financial resources rather than academic qualifications or compliance.

DHS should also examine the potential effects on university competitiveness. If students increasingly choose universities in other countries because post-graduation training in the United States becomes financially uncertain, American institutions could lose tuition revenue, research talent, and international standing.

These risks deserve rigorous economic analysis.

For example, DHS should evaluate scenarios involving 10%, 20%, and 30% declines in new international enrollment and estimate the resulting effects on institutional revenue, domestic tuition, university employment, financial aid, and local economic activity. These figures should be treated as hypothetical stress scenarios, not assumed forecasts.

Protecting American workers and taxpayers is a legitimate policy objective. However, the Department must also consider whether its proposed measures would impose substantial costs on those same Americans.

A policy that reduces university employment, weakens public institutions, limits educational resources, and damages college-town economies may undermine the very interests it claims to protect.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and conduct a comprehensive assessment of their effects on American universities, domestic students, employees, taxpayers, and local communities before considering any alternative.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees would harm universities, students, and local economies.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to express concerns regarding ICEB-2026-0100 that proposes new fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). I write as a US Citizen physician-in-training at an accredited medical school in the US.
Section IV.A: "Preventing fraud and protecting students" raises concerns about fraud and inadequate oversight in the OPT program. However, it is unclear why this justifies the need for a 70,000 fee for the initial OPT and 30,000 for subsequent OPT request. Simple administrative restructuring would allow for more oversight of the program (i.e. employer audits). Further, this section describes instances of fraud in which international students were engaged in OPT and “working for highly suspect employers.” Yet the ability to pay a substantial fee does not establish that an employer is legitimate or that a training opportunity meets the program’s requirements. The fee could exclude students pursuing legitimate opportunities simply because they or their institutions lack the resources to pay. DHS should explain why targeted employer verification, audits, and enforcement against documented misconduct would not address these concerns more effectively and with less harm to legitimate participants. Additionally, regarding abusive labor arrangements: the proposed fees could in fact increase the level of dependence students have on their employers given the latter's financing and would facilitate more such abusive labor arrangements.
Section IV.B: "Effects on American students and workers" suggests that international students participating in OPT diminish opportunities for American workers. I am concerned that this framing overlooks the ways international graduates contribute to research, innovation, and the creation of opportunities for others. As a US Citizen involved in STEM fields, I have personally observed how international students serve as an essential component of the United States’s current scientific infrastructure, bringing invaluable knowledge, work ethic, and cultural benefits to education, medicine, science, technology, and other academic fields. The United States cannot be an international powerhouse in academic and intellectual pursuits if it does not function as a sink for the worlds best and brightest. As an example, the OPT program is often used by researchers studying rare diseases and cures, the benefits of which accrue directly to American citizens. Adding exorbitant fees to the OPT program would destroy the pipeline of international talent. An October 2026 study from the Institute for Progress estimated that the program would reduce international student enrollment by 40-80%, having a ripple effect of significantly reducing the US scientific and technical workforce, in addition to decreasing annual GDP by an estimated $362 billion after 10 years.
Second, Section IV.B implies that opportunities are being taken away from American-borne students by international students. I and others in my social circles have never felt unique difficulty in obtaining post-graduate employment related to the presence of international students. In contrast, research shows that such students have been instrumental in the formation and leadership of companies that provide hundreds of thousands of jobs in the United States. For example, a recent June 2026 study from the National Foundation for American Policy estimates that 24% of founders of ‘unicorn’ startups (worth more than a billion dollars) were once international students in the US. I hence strongly believe that the OPT program actually results in the creation of more opportunities for American citizens.
Thirdly, international students serve as an essential part of the financial ecosystem for expanding higher education to American students. These students do not qualify for federal financial assistance to attend post-secondary education in the US. As a result, most of these students pay higher prices to attend these institutions. This tuition revenue is an important part of university finances, and is part of what gets recycled into merit and need-based aid for American born students. The Institute for Progress analysis estimates that the proposed fees could result in approximately 46,000 fewer domestic enrollments in bachelor’s and master’s programs each year. As an American student who benefited from financial aid, I am particularly concerned about policies that could reduce educational access for others. DHS should evaluate these potential consequences before adopting a measure intended to protect American students and workers.
In closing, the diversity and rigor of the American educational system are unmatched anywhere in the world, and the proposed rule threatens that. Imposing prohibitive fees on the OPT program risks weakening our universities, limiting opportunities for American students, and losing contributions that could improve the lives of American patients and workers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees are excessively high, do not prevent fraud, and may harm legitimate students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a graduate student studying engineering in Oregon and concerned US citizen. I am writing to oppose the proposed rule on Optional Practical Training Fees. We want to have the best skilled workers in the United States, and imposing restrictive fees will ensure that they go to the competitors of the United States. The rule claims to be protecting American workers, when in fact, it would do the opposite. For example, the rule cites that "workers in computer occupations jumped from an average of 1.98 percent in 2019 to 3.02 percent in 2025." While they attribute this to foreign workers, this can be attributed to the investment in AI by many companies. In fact, here is an example of one of many articles that shows that companies are laying off workers due to investments in AI: https://www.forbes.com/sites/karadennison/2026/06/17/companies-are-firing-workers-to-fund-ai-that-isnt-working-yet/. Here are some reasons why the proposed rule should be rescinded:

1. The fees do not fund the enforcement DHS says it lacks (Sec. IV.A, IV.C). The rule justifies itself by citing understaffed oversight: roughly 60 SEVP field representatives for 6,186 schools, and compliance resources “not scaled” to the program. Yet the fees would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and the rule concedes ICE has no authority to retain them. DHS states it “cannot operate OPT” without these fees, but the fees add nothing to its capacity to operate it. That DHS lacks authority to retain the funds also raises serious doubt that INA 214(a) authorizes a charge of this size, which is unrelated to any cost of service.
2. The fee does not target the fraud described (Sec. IV.A, V.A). Every fraud example in the rule involves employers: shell companies, staged worksites, phantom employees. The fee is charged to schools and is explicitly “not tied to a specific employer.” A student whose fee is paid may still work for a fraudulent employer. Worse, DHS’s own low-participation scenario predicts schools will pay mainly for STEM students, the population where the cited HSI worksite findings occurred. The rule concentrates participation where the fraud was found.
3. The fee selects for wealth, not merit (Sec. IV.C, VI). DHS says the fee will limit OPT to “the most promising students,” but it also expressly allows schools to pass the cost to students or employers. A fee paid by students screens for family wealth. “Pay-to-stay” schemes already involve paying for fraudulent employment; a larger payment does not deter them.
4. The rule uses inconsistent figures for the same year (Sec. IV.B vs. VII.A.3). Section IV.B cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024 to argue STEM OPT is “nearly double” the H-1B cap. The economic analysis uses 95,384 as its high-end 2024 STEM OPT figure. The larger number also appears to be a count of everyone currently participating, compared against an annual cap on new H-1B visas. Using DHS’s own 95,384 figure, the 2016 projection of about 92,000 participants by year 10 was accurate, not “far surpassed.”
5. The H-1B rationale does not apply to cap-exempt employers. Universities, nonprofit research organizations, and government research organizations are not subject to the H-1B cap, so OPT employment there cannot circumvent it. The fee applies anyway, burdening university research with no connection to the stated goal.
6. Benefits are unquantified while costs are $4.1 billion per year (Sec. VII.A). DHS criticizes the 2016 rule for not quantifying effects on U.S. workers, then quantifies no benefits of its own: no jobs, wages, or fraud reduction. The opportunity-cost method assumes lost OPT is worth no more than the unpaid fee, which builds the conclusion into the premise. It also omits lost tuition and income-tax revenue while counting FICA gains as a benefit.

7. The statutory findings contradict each other (Sec. VII.D, VII.F). The UMRA section states the rule “would not result in” a $100 million expenditure, then states it “exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold.” The Federalism section finds no substantial direct costs to states, yet the RFA analysis treats all 1,044 public institutions as state-run. State universities would pay a large share of the fees, and DHS admits it consulted no state governments.
8. DHS rejected targeted alternatives without adequate reasoning (Sec. IV.C). Extending STEM OPT safeguards (training plans, employer site visits, E-Verify, reporting) to all OPT would target employer fraud directly. DHS rejected these as resource-intensive, but the fee provides no resources either.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. At minimum, it should reissue the rule with a corrected economic analysis and a 60-day comment period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, arguing the fees will drive skilled workers to competitors.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I’m writing to voice my strong opposition to the proposed fees for the OPT program. While I get that the bureau is trying to cover admin costs, putting a new financial burden on this program is totally counterproductive. It directly hurts local communities, small businesses, and our overall economic stability. Instead of just looking at this from one angle, the agency needs to think about the ripple effects this fee will have on different parts of daily life.

From a Main Street perspective, local small businesses and startups depend a lot on the specialized skills that international grads bring to high-demand tech and operational roles. Unlike massive corporations, small employers can’t easily absorb or subsidize extra regulatory costs for their talent pipeline. Forcing these candidates to pay steep fees just to get entry-level experience hurts the exact small businesses trying to grow in today's tough econ climate. Plus, when you raise the cost of entering the workforce for highly trained people, those costs eventually hit the general public. Industries like healthcare, tech, and advanced supply chain logistics need a smooth transition of grads into practical roles. Making the process pricier restricts the talent pool, drives up overhead, and ultimately hikes prices for everyday consumers.

Looking at this from a public safety and gov efficiency standpoint, imposing higher fees doesn’t guarantee better service or smoother processing. Honestly, creating new payment structures and paperwork hurdles usually just complicates agency workflows, increases errors, and diverts ICE personnel away from core enforcement and public safety priorities. The agency should focus on streamlining its current digital setup instead of adding financial friction to an existing admin process. Finally, we have to consider the immediate neighborhood and community angle. International students and grads live in our towns, rent local apts, shop at neighborhood stores, and pay local sales taxes. They’re active contributors to our local economies. Putting an unnecessary financial barrier on their ability to work legally during their training period just cuts their disposable income, which means less money gets spent directly in our local neighborhoods.

The OPT program has successfully worked as a bridge for talent and innovation for years without these extra fees. I urge ICE to withdraw this proposal and look for internal efficiency solutions that don't penalize workforce participation or burden local economies. Thanks for your time and for considering these different impacts.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm small businesses, consumers, and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment in my individual capacity on the Optional Practical Training Fees proposal, DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I oppose the proposed rule and request that DHS withdraw it.

1. Transition and reliance interests

Sections V.C and VI describe a 60-day transition that DHS says accounts for reliance interests. Under proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(3), a STEM OPT recommendation from a designated school official (DSO) dated on or after the effective date could trigger a $70,000 charge to the school if the initial fee was never paid for that student. This would reach students who already received initial post-completion OPT authorization and began degree-related training under the existing rules. By the time the fee applies, those students may have accepted jobs, begun supervised training, and worked with their employers to prepare Form I-983.

The current filing windows show why advance notice alone leaves some students exposed. Under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C), a student may file for the STEM extension up to 90 days before the current employment authorization expires and must file within 60 days of the DSO entering the recommendation in SEVIS. For a student whose authorization expires more than 150 days after the effective date, a recommendation entered before the effective date would already be too old when the filing window opens. Please assess this group's reliance interests separately. If DHS proceeds, it should amend § 214.13(i)(3) to exempt otherwise eligible STEM OPT extensions for students whose initial post-completion OPT was authorized before the effective date, regardless of the date of the extension recommendation.

2. School prepayment and interrupted training

Under Section V.A, school payment is a prerequisite for the DSO to enter the recommendation. A school might decline to pay, pass the charge on to the student or employer, or need more time to approve payment than the filing window allows. If the recommendation is delayed past the filing deadline, a student who otherwise meets the eligibility requirements could have to stop training when the current authorization expires.

Section VII.A's low-participation scenario assumes schools would pay for the STEM-eligible group and attributes lost participation to non-STEM students. Please add scenarios in which schools decline to pay for STEM extensions, pass through the charge, or delay payment. Estimate how many students already on initial OPT would miss the extension filing window or have to interrupt their training under each scenario.

3. Evidence for the fee levels and targeted alternatives

Sections IV and V.A cite fraud prevention and reference H-1B payments in selecting the initial fee. Please disclose the number of confirmed fraud cases and the corresponding number of participants for initial OPT and STEM OPT separately. Explain the basis for expecting $70,000 and $30,000 to reduce fraud and estimate how the proposed amounts and lower amounts would affect both fraudulent and compliant participation.

DHS recognizes existing STEM OPT safeguards, including Form I-983, E-Verify, reporting, and employer site visits. Please compare the cost and likely effectiveness of the proposed fees with audits and site visits targeted at employers or schools flagged by existing reporting or compliance records. Evaluate that alternative specifically for STEM extensions, where these safeguards already apply.

4. Statutory authority for the charge

Section III.A relies in part on INA § 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1), which addresses the terms and conditions of nonimmigrant admission. Section V.A cites 31 U.S.C. § 3302 for depositing the receipts in the U.S. Treasury. I question whether the cited authority extends to requiring a school to pay $70,000 or $30,000 as a condition of making an OPT recommendation. Please identify the statutory text that authorizes DHS to impose this charge on schools and explain how that authority supports the proposed amounts.

Please address these objections and alternatives in any final rule and make the supporting data and methodology available in the public docket. If DHS relies on materially new data or analysis, please provide an opportunity to comment before finalizing the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, citing reliance interests and requesting DHS to withdraw it.

I am a DSO at a 4-year institution, and I oppose the proposed rule. Permitting international students to engage in OPT (without unreasonable fees) strengthens the United States economy as well as its reputation abroad. When international students have successful work experiences in the U.S., they are able to return to their home countries and show that an education and work experience in the U.S. is of extreme value, encouraging more students to study and do OPT here. Rather than weaken the U.S., allowing international individuals to legally study and work on OPT makes our country stronger financially and as a global influence.

Additionally, the proposed $70,000 fee is not commensurate to the OPT application and does not reflect the actual cost to the government to process a student's application. Additionally, charging universities the fee does not make sense as they are not the ones applying for OPT. If the government's goal is to prevent fraudulent employers, universities or students should not be the ones being charged, if there is a fee at all. The government should instead seek to find and punish these fraudulent employers.

While this fee is framed as preventing bad actors from abusing the OPT system, it will largely just prevent good-faith students from engaging in valuable work experience and keeps the U.S. from strengthening our economy, research, and global influence.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Regarding Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Protecting the wages and job prospects of American workers, especially recent graduates, is a legitimate goal. I oppose the proposed OPT fees because the proposal does not show that they would serve that goal. Keeping OPT with no new fee is better for American workers than a rule whose benefits DHS has not measured, and I ask DHS to withdraw it. This comment addresses Section IV.B (Protecting American Workers) and Section VII.A (regulatory impact analysis).
The proposal does not measure the benefit it claims. Table 1 lists monetized benefits as Not Estimated and lists effects on wages and effects on growth as N/A. A rule that DHS estimates would move about $12.8 billion a year and impose about $4.1 billion a year in costs should rest on at least a rough estimate of how many jobs or how much wage growth American workers would gain. Without one, neither the public nor the agency can judge whether the rule helps the workers it names.
The evidence cited is not about OPT. Section IV.B relies on a proclamation concerning the H-1B program, on unemployment rates for recent computer science graduates, and on a study of the computer science labor market in 2001. None of these isolates the effect of OPT participants on wages or hiring. Unemployment among recent graduates may have many causes, including changes within the technology sector, and the proposal does not try to separate them.
A flat fee does not target low pay. DHS says the aim is to prevent a labor market oversaturated with low-paid foreign workers. The fee is the same whether a graduate is paid well above the market wage or below it. If underpayment is the concern, the direct tools are a wage floor or the attestation that pay match that of similar American workers, which already applies to STEM OPT under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C).
The payroll tax concern belongs to Congress. Section IV.B describes the FICA exemption as an incentive to hire F-1 students. That exemption is set by statute at 26 U.S.C. 3121(b)(19). If it distorts hiring, Congress can amend it, and DHS can recommend that. A $70,000 charge is many times larger than the 7.65 percent employer share on an entry-level salary and is not a tailored response.
The proposal may also cost American jobs. Section VI assumes that employers will replace OPT participants with American workers. Some will. Others, particularly firms that operate in several countries, can move the work and the team abroad, and the American jobs connected to that team move with it. Graduates who are turned away may start companies in other countries instead of here. The analysis in Section VII.A does not consider either outcome.
I recommend that DHS leave OPT without the proposed fee and, if it believes OPT harms American workers, do the following.
1. Publish data specific to OPT on wages, occupations, and employers, and estimate the effect on American workers before choosing a remedy.
2. Extend the wage and non-displacement attestations from STEM OPT to all OPT and enforce them.
3. Refer the payroll tax question to Congress.
American workers are better served by rules that address underpayment and displacement directly than by a fee that makes no distinction between good and bad employers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees lack justification and asks DHS to withdraw the rule.

To the Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my strong concerns regarding the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). I am a graduate student at the Yale School of the Environment, pursuing a Master of Environmental Management. Through my academic experience as a graduate student, I have seen the important contributions that international students make to U.S. universities and the broader research and professional communities. The proposed OPT fees would undermine these contributions, restrict opportunities for highly qualified international students and graduates, and weaken the ability of U.S. institutions to attract and retain talent.

[Section V.A: Establishing a Fee for Initial and Any Subsequent OPT; proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)]
The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee would create an extraordinary financial barrier for universities seeking to support international students' transition from academic study to professional employment. Although the fees would be formally imposed on educational institutions rather than individual students, the financial burden would ultimately affect students through universities' decisions about which students to support, the allocation of institutional resources, and potential reductions in employment opportunities. A fee of this magnitude could discourage universities from recommending international students for OPT altogether, regardless of their qualifications or the value of their potential contributions.

This is particularly concerning for graduate students pursuing specialized fields of study that require advanced technical, analytical, and research skills. My graduate education has focused on understanding complex challenges related to environmental resources and energy affordability and security. Addressing these challenges requires interdisciplinary research and collaboration across academic institutions, government agencies, nonprofit organizations, and the private sector. Restricting access to OPT would limit the ability of international graduates to contribute their expertise to these efforts.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and reject the establishment of the $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. The ability of U.S. universities to attract and retain highly qualified global talent is central to the country’s economic, technological, and scientific leadership. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Opposition to Proposed Rule – Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees
DHS Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100
RIN: 1653-AB01

To the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, ICEB-2026-0100, concerning the imposition of extraordinarily high fees on international students participating in Optional Practical Training (OPT).

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

As someone who recognizes the importance of education, professional development, and equal opportunities, I believe this proposal would create serious financial, educational, and economic hardships for international students while undermining the United States' position as a global leader in higher education, research, science, and innovation.

1. The proposed fees are excessively high and unfair.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee are unreasonable and disproportionate. International students already make substantial financial investments in tuition, living expenses, health insurance, and other educational costs.

Many students finance their education through family savings, personal loans, and other financial arrangements. Requiring such enormous additional payments would make it practically impossible for many qualified graduates to participate in OPT.

Students should not be financially punished for pursuing legitimate educational and professional opportunities in the United States.

2. The proposal would negatively affect U.S. employers and the economy.

OPT allows U.S. employers to recruit graduates who have received education and training from American universities. These graduates contribute valuable knowledge, technical skills, research capabilities, and professional expertise.

Imposing such high fees would discourage employers from hiring international graduates, particularly small businesses, startups, research institutions, and organizations with limited financial resources.

Rather than strengthening the American workforce, this proposal could reduce access to qualified talent and negatively affect innovation, productivity, and economic growth.

3. The proposal would harm American universities and higher education.

International students make important contributions to American universities through tuition payments, research activities, academic collaboration, and participation in campus communities.

The proposed rule could make the United States a less attractive destination for talented international students. Students may increasingly choose other countries that offer more accessible educational and professional opportunities.

This would hurt universities, research programs, local communities, and the broader American education system.

4. The proposal would negatively affect STEM education, research, and innovation.

International graduates contribute significantly to fields such as science, technology, engineering, mathematics, healthcare, and other specialized professions.

Many students pursue advanced degrees in the United States with the expectation that they will have an opportunity to apply their knowledge through practical training.

Restricting these opportunities through excessive fees could result in the loss of talented graduates to other countries. This would weaken the United States' ability to attract and retain highly educated professionals and maintain its global competitiveness.

5. The proposed rule places an unfair burden on students who have already invested in their education.

International students make major educational and financial decisions based on the existing immigration and educational framework.

Students commit years of hard work, significant financial resources, and personal sacrifices to earn degrees from American institutions.

Introducing extraordinarily high financial barriers to OPT would create uncertainty and undermine their ability to plan their educational and professional futures.

The government should carefully consider the consequences for students who have already made substantial investments in their American education.

6. Fraud prevention should not come at the expense of legitimate students.

I understand that DHS has a responsibility to protect the integrity of the immigration system and prevent fraud.

However, addressing fraud should involve targeted oversight, stronger compliance measures, effective enforcement, and appropriate penalties for violations.

Imposing fees of $70,000 and $30,000 on the OPT process is an unnecessarily broad approach that could penalize legitimate students and employers who follow the rules.

The government should pursue measures that address actual misconduct without creating unreasonable financial barriers for the entire international student population.

My Recommendation

I respectfully request that DHS:

Withdraw the proposed rule ICEB-2026

Title: Optional Practical Training Fees
Subject: Strong Support for Proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees Rule
I am writing as a parent to express my strongest support for the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to introduce a targeted fee structure for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. I am watching with deep concern as the un-tariffed exploitation of visa programs actively distorts entry-level job markets and displaces highly qualified domestic graduates, including my own daughter.
My daughter is on the verge of completing her higher education in the medical and healthcare field. Despite her intensive clinical qualifications and readiness to serve our communities, her job prospects have been severely diminished. She is entering an entry-level market where domestic talent must compete with an artificially incentivized pool of cheaper, tax-exempt foreign labor.
Under the current system, employers utilizing OPT are exempt from paying FICA (Social Security and Medicare) taxes, providing a built-in financial subsidy to choose foreign graduates over qualified American citizens and permanent residents. In the corporate healthcare and medical research sectors, where administrative and staffing costs are heavily scrutinized, this financial loophole creates an immense incentive to bypass local graduates. This structural distortion drives down entry-level clinical and research wages, leaving domestic students to carry the burden of domestic tuition while being structurally locked out of employment upon graduation.
This unfair playing field is part of a broader, systemic preference for non-domestic labor that has recently drawn urgent scrutiny from federal watchdogs. A prominent example occurred recently at Rochester General Hospital in New York, where public scrutiny and a subsequent inquiry by the U.S. Department of Labor's Inspector General highlighted a residency cohort where a reported 80 out of 82 incoming slots went to international medical graduates, leaving only two positions for applicants from U.S. colleges. The Department of Labor’s Inspector General formally demanded the hospital "show us the numbers" to investigate potential visa abuse and ensure American applicants are getting a fair shot.
When major hospital systems and medical corporations skew their hiring so drastically away from domestic applicants, it sends a message to American students that their hard work and investments are secondary to corporate staffing strategies. While the medical field faces complex staffing needs, our regulatory frameworks must not subsidize or incentivize the systematic exclusion of domestic graduates in favor of lower-cost visa options.
By implementing the proposed $70,000 employer fee for initial OPT participation and the $30,000 fee for STEM extensions, DHS will neutralize this artificial economic distortion. These fees will compel healthcare networks, research corporations, and medical institutions to prioritize domestic talent first. It will ensure that visa programs are utilized strictly for their original, intended purpose—filling genuine, highly specialized talent shortages—rather than sourcing cheap, tax-exempt entry-level labor.
This rule is a necessary and long-overdue step to restore fairness, protect young American medical and healthcare professionals, and ensure that our nation's medical infrastructure remains accessible to the domestic talent trained to sustain it. I urge DHS to finalize and implement this proposed rule without delay.

Thank you,
Nagendra
(Northern California)

comments.commentText:
As an American citizen who works with international students, I strongly oppose the proposed DHS rule on Optional Practical Training “Duration of Status” (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), published October 8, 2026

This proposed policy places an absurdly large fee on the OPT process which will create additional administrative burden and systemic strain for both an already overloaded federal bureaucracy as well as the colleges and universities that are required to collect and submit the “fee”, and ultimately result in unnecessary complications and negative results that affect far more people, both international and domestic, than fixing or resolving the issues it purports to address. The changes proposed would unjustly affect a significant number of students functioning within a system that has worked for decades, in order to give the appearance of fighting the specter and suggestion of rampant fraud that simply does not exist to the extent that DHS represents.

Rampant fraud in the OPT program is an overstatement by DHS. The proposed rule cites very few actual statistics and the ones that are linked reference events from over 5 years ago. Their implications and estimations try to prey on the fear of jobs being taken away from Americans and harm being done to the economy by the OPT program when that is not the case, as clearly stated in this article from Forbes: https://www.forbes.com/sites/stuartanderson/2026/02/22/new-research-finds-reducing-immigration-does-not-help-us-workers/

The inflated fee DHS has proposed raises several questions:

They suggest there may be issues with up to 10,000 students working for “highly suspect employers”. Putting aside the fact that DHS did not provide substantive evidence to corroborate that estimate, that number only constitutes ~3% of OPT participants. Why then apply an exorbitant fee for the other 97% that are following procedures and working for legitimate employers? The rule does not provide substantive evidence how implementing a fee of this size would be a deterrence to the issues of fraudulent employment as opposed to simply a deterrence to students applying for OPT.

The fees collected under this new rule do not seem to go to DHS or SEVP or HSI or USCIS but to some unspecified part of the Treasury. How does this specifically help combat the so-called “rampant fraud” occurring? Why not direct the funds from these fees to HSI or SEVP to assist with investigating and shutting down fraudulent employers? Or, why can’t DHS use some of the billions of dollars allocated to ICE through the 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill” and the 2026 Secure America Act to address this purportedly serious issue? Or, raise and revise the existing SEVP fees to help counter this as they did back in 2019?

Logistically, DHS does not address the difficulty of paying the proposed fee. There is no significant guidance on how colleges and universities are to pay the fee. The time and cost associated with additional processes, recordkeeping and payment processing would be significant for my institution and involve employees from 3 different departments at the college, in addition to staff members from our central financial services, not to mention the additional approvals required for each transaction of such a significant amount. Why are colleges and universities being tasked with the burden of collecting this fee for the government to the detriment of their educational missions?

The proposed rule is a heavy-handed solution in search of a problem. Instead of combatting the exaggerated perception of rampant fraud in Optional Practical Training, it instead creates unreasonable barriers for international students seeking to put the skills and knowledge they have gained through their degrees to use for a short, finite amount of time. It will reduce government efficiency and diminish international contributions to the economy as well as dry up funding for USCIS as applications will fall far short of the wildly overestimated benchmarks proposed.

This rule is another misguided attempt to unnecessarily meddle in a functioning system at the cost of the prestige, appeal and competitiveness of US higher education to international students and will only further deter students hoping to participate in the education and research opportunities and experiences in the United States particularly when combined with the other unwelcoming immigration policies and executive orders over the past 9 months.

In addition to losing out on the innovation and research breakthroughs, and overall educational benefits from having international students and scholars participate in our universities and colleges, we also lose the BILLIONS of dollars in spending in local economies that they bring. Driving these students away hurts small businesses, larger companies, and those in between at a time when the economy could use more stability, not less uncertainty.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and address documented abuse through targeted oversight. Legitimate OPT is a bridge between U.S. education and practical training. A price barrier of this size would screen for ability to pay, not whether a student, school, or employer complies with the law.

Section V.A would require a school to pay before its designated school official can recommend an otherwise eligible F-1 student. The fee applies even when the school has no identified fraudulent conduct, and DHS acknowledges that schools may pass it to students, other students, or employers (section VI). Schools with fewer resources may decline to recommend qualified students. Students with modest means could lose opportunities even when their training is directly related to their degree. The proposal contains no showing that a $70,000 fee distinguishes a legitimate placement from a fraudulent one better than verification and enforcement would.

The near-term effects reach beyond the student. DHS acknowledges in section VII.A.5.b that reduced OPT participation could mean lost earnings and training, employer productivity losses when replacements are unavailable, and reduced international enrollment and university revenue. Its low-participation scenario assumes non-STEM OPT is no longer recommended. DHS estimates up to $8.07 billion annually in post-transition opportunity costs in that scenario, while warning that its fee-based proxy cannot precisely measure the true loss. Those are not projected GDP losses; they are a reason to take the risk seriously and improve the analysis before imposing the rule.

The proposal would also distort educational choices. Under section VII.A.5.d, a student who uses pre-completion and then post-completion OPT could trigger $100,000 in fees, compared with $70,000 for post-completion OPT alone. DHS expects pre-completion participation to decline. That would deny some students practical experience during their studies for a reason unrelated to the training's quality.

Longer term, a less credible path from a U.S. degree to practical experience may make American universities less attractive, weaken their finances, and reduce the pool of graduates available to U.S. employers and research teams. The Institute of International Education counted 294,253 international students on OPT in 2024/25. The National Science Board reports that 46% of U.S. science and engineering workers with doctoral degrees were foreign born in 2023. These figures do not prove that every OPT participant produces a net economic benefit, but they show why DHS must analyze consequences for talent, research, and competitiveness rather than assume workers are interchangeable.

I recognize DHS's stated concerns about fraud, program integrity, and opportunities for U.S. workers (section IV.C). Fraud should be investigated and punished, and OPT training should be genuinely related to a student's field. But a fee collected from every compliant school does not directly inspect a placement or prove that a U.S. worker was displaced. DHS itself considered site visits, training plans, and reporting requirements (section IV.C). The notice rejects those approaches in part because they require government resources, yet the fee revenue would go to the Treasury and is not earmarked for OPT enforcement. That choice needs a much stronger explanation.

Before any final rule, DHS should publish evidence on the frequency and sources of OPT abuse; explain how the proposed fee amounts were derived and how they would prevent abuse; estimate how many students, schools, and employers would leave the program; assess tuition, research, labor-market, and regional effects; and compare the fee with targeted audits, employer verification, training plans, and enforcement against repeat violators. It should also analyze who would ultimately pay the fee and whether smaller institutions and lower-income students would bear disproportionate costs. The rule should not be finalized without a demonstrated net benefit and a serious assessment of less restrictive alternatives.

Please withdraw this fee proposal and pursue evidence-based oversight that preserves access to legitimate training while protecting workers and enforcing the law.

Sources: DHS NPRM, 91 FR 64566, sections IV.C, V.A, VI, VII.A.5; IIE Open Doors 2025, International Students (opendoorsdata.org/annual-release/international-students/); National Science Board, The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026 (ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsbsep20261/executive-summary).
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create unfair financial barriers and harm students.

After reading the proposed rule to add Optional Practical Training fees, I noticed some issues with the proposed rule that I would like to point out. Requiring schools to pay the fees, regardless of whether they can pass off the cost to the students or employers, adds an extra burden on schools in a time when institutions are already doing more with less when it comes to resources. Even schools with a small number of students applying for OPT would make payments of over $1 million each application cycle, which in not feasible. If the fees are passed off to students or employers, schools would have to create a payment process to make it possible, using time and resources that could be used on other processes that benefit the schools.

With the proposed fees being deposited into the Treasury, how can schools be sure the money is going toward Optional Practical Training rather than other government priorities? If the government is concerned with fraud, I would suggest a discussion with people who are directly working with students participating in Optional Practical Training in schools and with employers. Charging more money to apply for Optional Practical Training authorization will not change any allegations of fraud. A conversation to figure out the methods of alleged fraud and how to prevent it would make more of difference than charging fees.

Many international students choose to study in the United States for the added benefit of Optional Practical Training. Other countries have taken notice and have started to add practical training to the options for international students, which has made the international education market more competitive. Adding the proposed fees will have more of a chilling effect and decrease the total number of international students studying in the United States moving forward. The students who are already here will be at a disadvantage since they came with the understanding that Optional Practical Training would be an option for them, but if the proposed fees are implemented, practical training may be out of reach due to financial constraints. When international students are admitted to universities, they must show financial proof of funding for one year of study. They can plan ahead for the rest of their program of study and the current application fees for Optional Practical Training charged by USCIS, but they could not foresee the additional fees proposed in this rule. The fact that these fees cost more than one year of study in many schools is also an additional financial burden that may keep students away and send them home at the end of their program of study.

The decrease in the total number of international students and international students participating in Optional Practical Training does not only affect the students themselves. The loss of revenue impacts local communities and their economies. International students spend money on rent, utilities, food, vehicles, and other necessities when living in the United States in addition to their tuition costs. With less international students, the rental market in college towns is greatly impacted, which affects local landlords.

Bringing international students to the United States is not only beneficial for them, but for domestic students as well. In an increasingly global world, American students need to be prepared to work in diverse environments. Upon graduation, American students can say they have worked with diverse groups of people in their classes, in university clubs, and athletics. In offering Optional Practical Training, international students can also learn about American work culture and take those ideas home with them when they return at the end of their practical training experience.

With a decrease in international student numbers comes a decrease in the number of staff needed to monitor their immigration records, negatively impacting American workers in the field of international education. The field has already been hit with a wave of layoffs and firings as reactions to other government policies which have had a chilling effect on international student numbers. This proposed rule is yet another blow to the field and leaves international student advisors wondering if the field will continue to be a viable career path moving forward.

In conclusion, the proposed rule to add exorbitant fees to Optional Practical Training will have multiple negative consequences, not only impacting international students, but American workers and the U.S. economy. The money collected from the fees is not guaranteed to be put toward improving the Optional Practical Training program and the idea of collecting these fees will have a chilling effect on the number of international students due to the uncertainty of planning to study in the United States. Please reconsider the proposed fees and find other solutions that do not add unnecessary burdens to schools and international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I am an international doctoral student in music composition at Yale University. I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT, including the STEM extension . My qualifications to comment are direct: I am a current F-1 student, I work in a conservatory-adjacent research environment, and my field—music performance and scholarship—depends on the very post-completion practical training that this rule would price out of reach.

The fee is untethered to any demonstrated cost or fraud risk in my field. DHS justifies the fee by citing fraud and abuse in OPT, including “visa mill” schemes and employer clusters . Whatever the merits of those concerns in other sectors, they bear no relationship to the supervised, conservatory-based training that defines music doctoral work at Yale. A $70,000 charge imposed uniformly on a doctoral musician’s first year of OPT is not a fraud-deterrence measure; it is a prohibitive tax on entry into a profession that already offers modest compensation. The rule’s own logic—that schools will exercise “greater oversight and selectivity” when a fee is attached —collapses in a field where the “oversight” is already intensive and the “selectivity” is measured in auditions, not SEVIS entries.

The rule would devastate the pipeline into American musical institutions. Doctoral musicians in the United States do not enter OPT to displace American workers in a saturated labor market; they enter it to fulfill the final supervised phase of training that leads to positions in American orchestras, universities, and arts organizations. The American cultural sector relies on an international talent pool precisely because domestic supply in specialized areas—historical performance, composition, certain instruments—is thin. If the first year of post-degree employment carries a $70,000 price tag, no arts organization and no university will pay it, and no young musician will. The result is not “protection” of American workers; it is the removal of a talent stream that American cultural institutions have built over generations.

The fee is legally vulnerable and administratively incoherent. The APLU has documented that DHS lacks clear statutory authority for a fee of this magnitude and that its cost assumptions are flawed for public and nonprofit institutions . More fundamentally, the rule treats OPT as a commodity that can be priced at $70,000 without any showing that the value of OPT to a student or institution approaches that figure. For a doctoral musician, the first year of OPT is not a lucrative employment benefit; it is a continuation of professional formation at stipend-level pay. The fee’s benchmark to the vacated H-1B payment is arbitrary and has been flagged as such by institutional commenters .

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. If the Department believes specific fraud risks require targeted enforcement, it should pursue evidence-based enforcement against bad actors rather than imposing a blanket fee that will close the door on doctoral musicians, artists, and scholars whose work enriches American cultural life and whose training American institutions have invested in for years. The public comment record already contains substantial opposition from higher education and international educators; I add my voice as a doctoral student who would be directly and irreparably harmed by this rule.

Respectfully submitted.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are prohibitive and would devastate the academic pipeline.

Researchers develop models, maintain experimental datasets, and acquire technical knowledge over several years. Losing trained researchers because universities cannot afford OPT fees would disrupt ongoing projects, delay scientific discoveries, and waste investments already made in graduate education and professional training.

Many arrive through competitive international scholarships and make significant contributions to research and higher education.

Impact on American competitiveness and innovation

My research involves challenges directly relevant to American communities, including water availability, agricultural productivity, environmental resilience, and climate-related risks. International researchers contribute to these areas alongside American scientists through collaborative projects, scientific publications, and the development of innovative technologies.

Creating prohibitively expensive barriers to OPT would make it harder for American universities to recruit and retain talented researchers. It could encourage graduates trained in the United States to pursue their careers in countries offering more accessible research opportunities. Existing STEM OPT requirements already include employer verification, formal training plans, reporting obligations, and compliance monitoring. Strengthening targeted oversight and enforcement would be a more appropriate approach than imposing financial barriers on all participants.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee provisions and instead consider evidence-based measures that preserve program integrity without underm

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

I am writing to oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees and urge DHS to withdraw the proposal. I earned a master’s degree at a U.S. university and participated in both OPT and STEM OPT. Practical training allowed me to apply what I learned in graduate school, learn from experienced colleagues, and develop professional skills through work directly related to my degree. I am concerned that the proposed fees would make that opportunity unavailable to many future graduates.

The proposed fees would put practical training out of reach for many eligible graduates. Under proposed 8 CFR §§ 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i)(1)–(2), a school would have to pay $70,000 before recommending a student for initial OPT and $30,000 before a qualifying subsequent recommendation. Schools with limited budgets could respond by restricting or ending OPT recommendations. If schools seek to recover the cost from students or employers, access to training could depend on a student’s personal finances or an employer’s ability to absorb the fee. A graduate could meet the eligibility requirements and receive an offer directly related to their degree, yet still lose the opportunity because the school cannot pay. DHS should assess how institutions with different financial resources would respond before making school payment a condition of participation.

DHS should address fraud and protect U.S. workers through targeted enforcement. I urge DHS to compare the proposed fees with enforcement focused on specific signs of abuse, such as discrepancies between a STEM OPT training plan and the work actually performed. DHS can use existing tools, including Form I-983 and employer site visits, to verify that training is genuine and that employers comply with requirements on compensation and the non-displacement of U.S. workers. DHS should explain what evidence supports the proposed fee amounts and compare their expected effects and costs with those of targeted enforcement.

The proposed transition provision would disrupt plans already underway. Under proposed § 214.13(i)(3), a student who began OPT under the existing rules could trigger the $70,000 school payment requirement when seeking a STEM OPT extension after the transition date. By then, that student may have completed a U.S. degree, accepted a job, and started training that both the student and employer expected to continue. If DHS adopts any new fee, it should exempt students already enrolled in a U.S. degree program or already participating in OPT or STEM OPT when the rule takes effect. That exemption should cover eligible STEM OPT extensions tied to the same degree.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue targeted measures that address documented fraud and protect U.S. workers while preserving access to legitimate practical training.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

**1. The fee levels would functionally end OPT for all but a handful of students.**

The proposal requires SEVP-certified schools to pay $70,000 for a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including the 24-month STEM OPT extension — against a current cost of roughly $500 per student, an increase of approximately 13,900%. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and then post-completion OPT would cost their school $100,000. No plausible university budget absorbs this. The result is not a "fee" — it is a de facto elimination of the program for ordinary students, which no statute authorizes DHS to do through a fee rule.

**2. DHS's own proposal concedes the burden falls on students and employers.**

The proposal expressly states that schools may pass the cost on to the F-1 students, to all students, or to employers, and sets no limits on how a school collects or sources the money. In practice this means the fee becomes either a $70,000 surcharge on young graduates who already invest hundreds of thousands of dollars in U.S. tuition and living expenses, or a hiring tax on the American employers who recruit them. Neither outcome is consistent with the rule's stated worker-protection rationale.

**3. The rule harms the U.S. technology sector and American competitiveness.**

OPT and STEM OPT are the principal lawful path by which U.S. employers — including the data-platform and AI teams I work with daily — bring international graduates of American universities onto their engineering staffs. These are graduates of U.S. institutions, trained in U.S. labs and classrooms, who build the data infrastructure and AI systems American companies depend on. A $70,000 entry fee will not redirect these graduates to American employers; it will redirect them to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries competing for the same talent — while American companies lose access to the pipeline and American universities lose the enrollment that sustains STEM programs and research. This proposal punishes rule-following students and the employers who hire them, not fraud. Fraud and program-integrity concerns should be addressed through targeted enforcement and the existing compliance framework, not a blanket fee that makes the program unusable.

**4. The agency's own estimates confirm the rule's disproportionate scale.**

DHS estimates 2,478 affected schools and $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion in annual fees. A rule imposing tens of billions of dollars in annual costs on higher education — with fees deposited into the general Treasury rather than tied to program administration costs — demands far more than a 30-day comment period and a cost-benefit analysis that treats a 13,900% fee increase as routine. The proposed alternative of charging the $70,000 fee again each time a student advances to a higher degree level would compound the harm and should be rejected outright.

**5. Request.**

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. At a minimum, DHS should (a) reject the alternative of re-charging the initial fee at each degree level, (b) set any fee at a level tied to the actual administrative cost of processing OPT recommendations, and (c) provide a comment period commensurate with the rule's multi-billion-dollar annual impact before any re-proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Apoorve Tyagi
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations.

I am an international MBA student at the Yale School of Management, with a professional background in data science, technology, and business operations. Before pursuing my MBA, I worked at companies including Uber and Zomato, and during my graduate studies, I completed a summer internship with Uber in New York. These experiences have reinforced my belief in the value of combining academic education with practical professional training.

1. The proposed fees would discourage legitimate participation rather than specifically targeting fraud.
I recognise the importance of maintaining immigration programme integrity and protecting American workers. However, imposing a substantial financial barrier on all OPT participants does not distinguish between legitimate students and those attempting to misuse the programme.

Under Section V.A of the proposed rule, universities would be responsible for paying these fees before recommending students for OPT. DHS acknowledges that institutions may pass these costs on to students or employers. Consequently, access to practical training could become dependent on financial resources rather than academic qualifications, professional merit, or regulatory compliance.

2. The proposal could undermine American economic competitiveness.
International students invest substantial financial resources in American higher education, contribute to university communities, and bring diverse professional perspectives to American businesses.

My own experience working in technology has shown me how companies benefit from individuals with different educational and professional backgrounds. OPT provides an opportunity for international graduates to apply skills developed through American education in American workplaces.

A $70,000 fee could make hiring international graduates economically impractical for many employers, particularly startups and smaller businesses. This risks discouraging talented students from studying in the United States and weakening the country's ability to attract globally competitive talent.

3. The economic analysis does not sufficiently establish the consequences of the proposed fees.
In Section VII.A.3, DHS acknowledges that it cannot confidently predict how much OPT participation would decline. Section VII.A.5 further acknowledges the difficulty of quantifying the opportunity costs experienced by students, universities, and employers.

These uncertainties are especially significant given the magnitude of the proposed fees. Before implementing such a consequential policy, DHS should conduct a more comprehensive assessment of its effects on international student enrolment, employer hiring, university finances, and the broader American economy.

4. The proposal fails to adequately protect students who made educational commitments under existing rules.
Students currently enrolled in American universities made significant financial and professional commitments based on the regulatory framework available when they enrolled. The proposed 60-day transition period does not adequately address these reliance interests.

For students pursuing expensive graduate degrees, an unexpected $70,000 financial barrier could fundamentally change their ability to access practical training after graduation.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and instead pursue targeted anti-fraud measures, including stronger employer verification, risk-based institutional audits, and more effective enforcement against demonstrable violations.

Protecting the integrity of OPT and preserving opportunities for legitimate international students are not mutually exclusive objectives. A carefully designed regulatory approach can achieve both without undermining the competitiveness of American higher education and the American economy.

Thank you for considering my comments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I oppose this proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I am an F-1 student in the M.S. Computer Science program at Northeastern University in Seattle, expecting to graduate in September 2027 with a 4.0 GPA. I previously earned an M.A. in Business/Marketing, and I have worked as a software engineering intern at AWS and HireBeat and as a Junior QA Engineer co-op at MasterControl. My plan after graduation is post-completion OPT followed by the 24-month STEM OPT extension, working as a software development engineer in a job directly related to my degree, and then seeking H-1B sponsorship and, in time, a green card through my employer.

For me, this fee is not $70,000 or $30,000 in isolation. It is $70,000 for my first OPT recommendation plus $30,000 for my STEM extension: $100,000 for one student, one degree, one training path. My school is the legal payer, but the proposal itself says schools may pass the fee on to students, and a school that cannot pay or will not risk $100,000 per student will simply recommend fewer students, or none. That would make OPT effectively unavailable to me, even though I have done everything the program asks: studied full time, kept a 4.0, and taken degree-related internships.

OPT is not optional for me in any real sense. It is the supervised, degree-related work experience my program is designed to lead into, and the only lawful way for me to do that work after graduation. Without it, the training the United States has already invested in through my degree is cut off at graduation, and the employer pipeline from OPT to H-1B to PERM that my whole plan depends on breaks at its first step.

The fee also fails on its own terms. A lawful fee must be tied to the cost of a service. The current Form I-765 adjudication fee is about $500; this proposal is roughly 140 times that, and the proposal contains no cost analysis linking $70,000 or $30,000 to any government cost. The proposal admits the amounts are meant to deter, stating that passing the fee on "would further discourage misuse of OPT," and concedes the money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, not to the fraud enforcement the rule claims to serve. A charge designed to deter behavior and raise general revenue is a tax, and only Congress can impose it. DHS's own estimate is $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion, across 2,478 institutions. An exaction of that scale needs clear congressional authorization, which the general "time and conditions" language of INA section 214(a) has never provided.

The proposal is also arbitrary in its amounts and its targeting. It gives no reasoned basis for why $70,000 and $30,000 are the right figures rather than any others, and it values a lost year of skilled work at exactly the amount of the fee it invented. DHS's own evidence shows fraud concentrated among a small minority: its 2026 probe identified roughly 10,000 suspect participants out of about 194,554 OPT employment authorizations in 2024, around 5 percent. This fee punishes the other roughly 95 percent across every field, and treats compliant universities identically to bad actors. Targeted tools such as site visits, training plans, and employer verification were considered and rejected as too administratively burdensome. Convenience is not a reasoned basis for a blanket punitive fee. Compounding makes it worse: a student who uses pre-completion OPT and then post-completion OPT triggers $70,000 plus $30,000, although any fraud risk is per person, not per recommendation.

Finally, the chilling effect is already happening. New international student enrollment fell 17 percent from fall 2024 to fall 2025, a loss estimated at more than $1.1 billion in revenue and about 23,000 fewer jobs. International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 355,736 American jobs in 2024-25. Skilled immigration complements rather than displaces U.S. workers: research cited by ITIF found H-1B immigration raised native non-STEM workers' incomes by about 15 percent in computer systems design. Driving away U.S.-trained graduates harms, rather than helps, the domestic workers DHS claims to protect. STEM OPT already requires formal training plans, employer reporting, and site visits; extending verification to post-completion OPT would target fraud directly, at its actual source.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

Respectfully submitted,
Anonymous
F-1 M.S. Computer Science student, Northeastern University, Seattle
Expected graduation: September 2027
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and asks DHS to withdraw it due to the high $100,000 fee.
