I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule, Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. A fee of $70,000 for an initial OPT authorization and $30,000 for a subsequent authorization is disproportionate and would make practical training inaccessible to many eligible students.

As a student, OPT would allow me to apply the skills I developed in my field in a workplace and lean practical skills while contributing productively to the organization and to the American society in general. This provides a path for professional development for students like me and increases the pool of quality workforce available to American firms. The proposed fee would make everyone involved much more hesitant to utilize or recommend this option and will cause disproportionate damage to the students who worked hard to obtain their degrees, and also significantly damage businesses and industries who rely on entry level employees for basic but important work and cause slowdown in career opportunities within such organizations. It will also cause immense harm to the wider economy and businesses and services that cater to students which will lose customers due to such changes in policy, causing negative knock on effects down the line

I requires you to please withdraw the proposal. At a minimum, DHS should explain how these amounts were calculated, assess the effects on students and schools, and consider a substantially lower fee that reflects documented administrative costs rather than creating a barrier to training which can be commented on by the public.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are disproportionately high and asks DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Melissa Heid
comments.commentText:
As the Principle Designated School Official at Santa Clara University (SCU) I am submitting these comments in opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule establishing $70,000 and $30,000 fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations.

The OPT Fees would make OPT essentially unattainable
We currently have 264 students with pending or active OPT and 322 students with pending or active STEM OPT. If we had to pay $70,000 for the OPTers and $100,000 (the $70,000 initial fee as well as the $30,000 subsequent fee) for those with STEM Extensions, the cost would be $50,680,000! 50 million dollars cannot be absorbed into operating expenses without significant increases in tuition, which is not realistic in an already competitive higher education environment so the fee would have to be passed along to the student. From our 2026 International Student Belonging and Success Survey, only 26% of respondents who indicated that their plans were to work in the U.S. on OPT had job offers prior to program completion. With the current job market we see a sizable number of students volunteering for at least some portion of OPT. Without a high paying job lined up, I see it unlikely that students would risk the $70,000 fee even if they could afford it. Further, unless the student was from an affluent family, having just completed an undergraduate degree costing over $250,000 in tuition alone or graduate degree costing between $50,000 to $100,000 or more in tuition, the additional expense is unfathomable.

Without a realistic possibility of OPT, students will not enroll
OPT is a highly sought after benefit of the F-1 student visa. This is clear from both large scale national/international research as well as surveys conducted at SCU. From our 2026 New International Student Survey 40% of graduate respondents and 18% of undergraduate respondents indicate the primary reason for choosing SCU is employment opportunities after graduation. From our 2026 International Student Belonging and Success Survey, 68% indicated that their future plans were to work temporarily in the U.S. on OPT. According to Emerging Futures 8, Voice of the International Student, IDP’s survey of more than 7,900 international students from 134 countries and regions, conducted summer 2025, 66% of respondents would go elsewhere or consider going elsewhere if post-graduation work opportunities were not available.

According to the Institute of International Education (IIE)’s Fall 2025 International Student Enrollment Snapshot Survey, 76% of institutions responded OPT was an important recruiting tool for international students. In addition, 92% responded that without OPT, many international students would likely choose to study in other countries. If students cannot realistically participate in OPT and being candid that a $70,000 initial fee will essentially make OPT unfeasible, we could expect declines of 60% or more based on the research referenced above. This would have a catastrophic impact on our international student enrollment, but also be a noticeable impact on overall enrollment, and in turn, have substantial financial and planning implications.

The impacts would have a domino effect
If the OPT fees go into effect, the impacts will be felt beyond enrollment. According to NAFSA, 139,351 international students contribute $6.3 billion and support 52,049 jobs in California and 4,136 international students contribute $177 million and support 1,139 jobs in the 17th District where SCU is located. The OPT fees would lead to significantly fewer international students and thus less money going into the economy. As enrollment drops, DSOs, faculty, and other university staff would be expected to lose jobs. On campus housing and apartments in college towns with historically high international student numbers would be vacant.

Aside from the economic benefits that international students bring in general, SCU benefits directly from F-1 alumni on OPT. From our Summer 2026 OPT Employment Snapshot, Santa Clara University was one of the top employers of SCU alumni on post-completion OPT, employing over 20 students.

DHS needs to consider alternatives
The proposed rule does not demonstrate why the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts are required. Further, DHS did not articulate why alternative less burdensome options would not be effective.
DHS can address fraud concerns without an exorbitant fee. SEVIS frameworks exist to identify potential fraud. For example, SEVIS has an unemployment day counter, but I have never seen action when a student exceeds the allowed 90 or 150 days of unemployment. Additionally, DHS could use SEVIS data to look for patterns of fraud and address them directly with students, employers, or other parties rather than initiate excessive fees.

In closing, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and to seek a path where OPT can be preserved and even improved.

Thank you,
MH
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessively high and would make the program unattainable for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Strong Opposition to Proposed Fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT)

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to impose new or increased fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program.

As a recent graduate with a Master of Science in Computer Science from a USA University, I am currently utilizing my OPT to work as a Software Development Engineer at Amazon. The OPT program has been instrumental to my professional growth, allowing me to apply the advanced software architecture and programming principles I studied during my graduate degree to real-world, large-scale engineering challenges.

More importantly, my employment through OPT directly benefits the United States. In my role at Amazon, I contribute to building and optimizing software applications that drive technological innovation, helping to maintain U.S. leadership in the highly competitive global tech industry. Like thousands of other STEM OPT participants, I am a tax-paying resident who actively contributes to the local economy, supports American businesses, and helps fill critical talent shortages in the U.S. technology sector.

International students already shoulder immense financial burdens to study in the U.S., including steep international tuition rates, SEVIS fees, and visa application costs, all without access to federal financial aid. Imposing an additional fee for OPT creates an unnecessary and punitive financial hurdle during the vulnerable transition from academia to the workforce. It also sends a discouraging message to prospective international talent, potentially pushing highly skilled individuals toward competing nations like Canada or the UK, which offer more welcoming post-graduation pathways.

The OPT program is a mutually beneficial initiative that strengthens the U.S. economy while providing essential training for students. I strongly urge the agency to reconsider and withdraw the proposal to impose fees on OPT applications.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong opposition to the proposed fees for the OPT program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. These excessive fees would harm American businesses, universities, and technological competitiveness by making it harder to retain talented graduates educated in the United States.

American universities invest years in training scientists and engineers. Making practical training prohibitively expensive risks sending their expertise to competing countries. In fields such as quantum computing, semiconductors, and advanced manufacturing, losing specialized talent can delay research, product development, and investment.

These consequences would also affect American workers. Businesses depend on teams with complementary skills; losing one specialist can reduce opportunities for the entire team. Startups and university laboratories would be particularly vulnerable because they have limited resources to absorb additional costs. Schools that cover the fees could face pressure to reduce funding for teaching, research, or student support.

Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate goals, but ability to pay a large fee does not establish compliance. DHS should use targeted audits, employment verification, and enforcement against violations.

I urge DHS to withdraw this fee proposal and preserve affordable, legitimate practical training that supports American innovation, economic growth, and jobs.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm competitiveness, universities, and businesses, and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Natalie Holzwarth

Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am Natalie Holzwarth and have been a faculty member of the Physics Department of Wake Forest University since 1983, officially retiring in 2025, but remaining an active participant in physics research and teaching.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Throughout my career I have observed that talent for engaging in physics research is distributed world wide and have personally enjoyed working with several very impressive international students. The proposed increase in OPT fees will discourage international students from pursuing training and postgraduate study in the USA and deprive US students from having international colleagues.

The presence of international students and graduates in science efforts within the USA has not only contributed to important advances but, through collaboration, has also strengthened the contributions US students and graduates.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Natalie Holzwarth

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lansing Horan
comments.commentText:
These proposed changes to the Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee structure seem overly ambitious -- too dramatic of a change, incorporated too suddenly, and further, it is unclear if this is in the best interests of the United States. If changes are to be made to "combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers" (which are laudable goals), it would be far better for such changes to be implemented with more discretion and at a slower pace -- if changes are to be made at all, that is.

In practice, when a typical graduate student receives a PhD, he/she is often interested in post-doctoral positions. Such "post-doc" positions are very typically the "next step" in career development for those individuals interested to remain in academia or other such research employment options. This is the case both for U.S. citizens and for international students. Much of academia (and the broader research employment network) is structured on a post-doc being a rather typical progression after graduation with a PhD.

I do not see much benefit, other than some potential monetary gains in the short-term, behind a sudden, very-steep additional fee of 70,000 USD for international students to complete a post-doc in the U.S. If the United States chooses to admit a foreign national to obtain an advanced degree -- which requires the investment of hundreds of thousands of dollars, through several years of time and effort by various accomplished individuals -- it would seem reasonable to *not* unduly discourage these same individuals from remaining in the U.S. and conducting further research, post graduation, on an inherently limited basis (which is what a post-doc already is). When a foreign national graduates from a U.S. institution, they contribute to the greater scientific output of the U.S. at-large.

In the course of obtaining a PhD, individuals receive significant training, knowledge, and skills, making them particularly useful and productive towards niche research endeavors. Why should the U.S. invest sizeable resources in providing foreign nationals with such advanced training, only to then, via charging such a lofty fee for OTP, render it impractical for them to stay-on afterwards and further contribute to U.S. scientific output? If anything, the United States should continue to admit the best foreign national candidates to permit their study at our world-renowned institutions, and perhaps encourage their stay in the U.S. afterwards, rather than take the fruits of their PhD (which we provided) elsewhere.

Discussions can and should be had regarding federal funding for advanced education, the steepening cost of college education, any fraud or inefficiencies in this system, and how to admit the best U.S. citizens alongside foreign nationals in a way that makes sense for U.S. national interests. There is doubtless a balance to be found somewhere in the middle against these various competing factors, and more. This is a complicated system to optimize -- which only makes me more skeptical of the merit of implementing an additional +70,000 USD fee on OTP (at least as it pertains to foreign nationals interested in U.S. post-doctoral positions), which would be a rather sudden and harsh cost to pay.

If indeed the U.S. national interests are to, effectively, heavily discourage foreign nationals from attending U.S. institutions and making their contributions to our research output, then perhaps this sudden and dramatic change makes sense. Otherwise, I would urge caution, further study, and greater discussions, to ensure that the U.S. academic posture is well-calibrated to our goals.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is too drastic and harms international students and post-doc research.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Many years ago, I was an international student from a country where it was not possible to pursue exciting cutting edge research: due to severe economic, political, and social restrictions for me personally, and due to lack of resources for the field in general. I was able to build a successful career in the US and I feel like I have positively contributed to the US economy, higher education, and world-class quality of research. Over the last 25 years, I have interacted with hundreds of international students and postdocs, some of whom have proceeded to become stars in their field. We must give these talented students an opportunity to give back to American academia, research, and economy. In fact we should be giving Green Cards with a PhD to encourage these people to stay!

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international standing and influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Nadia Zakamska

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Comments in Response to Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule and urge that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety.

DHS specifically requests input on this particular portion of the proposed rule: "DHS has also considered, as an alternative to the approach described above, having the one-time initial fee of $70,000 apply again to any initial period of OPT following the F-1 student's change to a higher educational level (e.g., to a post-bachelor's degree OPT and again to the student's master's degree OPT)." (p. 64578). I strongly oppose this alternative and urge DHS to consider withdrawing this proposal altogether.

The rationale presented in this proposed rule for a higher initial OPT fee amount is that "when nonimmigrant students initially apply for employment authorization, they may not have been vetted by the U.S. Government since their initial application for an F-1 visa and subsequent admission into the country." (p. 64576). Continuing the same logic, students who are applying for a change of education level have likely been in the US for a while and have already undergone at least one round of the exorbitant fee and the vetting process supposedly associated with it, if not multiple rounds of verification. There is no obvious reasoning for why a student's motivations and intents would suddenly undergo drastic changes or be classified as fraud simply for pursuing training opportunities at a higher level of education. With Curricular Practical Training severely restricted for now, there are no other pathways for students to gain hands-on training and professional experience in their fields of choice. This is particularly true for non-STEM majors, who do no benefit from the STEM extension provision as their STEM-major peers do; for many non-STEM students, 12 months of training is often inadequate for it to translate into serious careers back home, particularly if their field of work requires a fixed number of hours to obtain licensing. Pursuing specialized studies and the training that supplements it is often their only option to gain experience in their industries. There is no evidence that a change of education level poses a threat to national security or to the US labor market, and students should not be penalized with a repeat initial $70,000 fee for pursuing higher education.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the proposed rule and urges that it be withdrawn in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 graduate student completing a Master of Science in Supply Chain Management at a public university in Arizona, graduating in December 2026. I filed my application for post-completion Optional Practical Training (Form I-765) in early October 2026, paid the required filing fee, and my case remains pending. Since then I have applied to more than 400 positions in supply chain and procurement, and I hold a verbal job offer that depends on receiving my Employment Authorization Document. I write to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees.

A $70,000 charge per student bears no visible relation to the cost of what it pays for: a school official's recommendation entered into SEVIS. It is many times the filing fee I already paid to USCIS, and it would exceed several months of a new graduate's salary. DHS acknowledges schools may pass the cost to students, to all students, or to employers. In practice, few students could pay $70,000 on top of tuition already spent, and few schools could absorb it for every international student. Schools would instead restrict or stop recommending OPT, ending the program in practice without repealing it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Arbitrary and Capricious Flaws in the Proposed OPT Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

I am writing to formally oppose the proposed rule to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee on the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. As a Master’s graduate from the University of California, San Diego, currently employed as a Software Development Engineer at Amazon, I urge the withdrawal of this rule due to its severe logical flaws, factual inaccuracies, and arbitrary nature under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Specifically, the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) contains three major loopholes:

1. Contradictory Funding Logic (The "Miscellaneous Receipt" Flaw)
The NPRM claims that the fees are necessary because DHS lacks the compliance resources to scale its anti-fraud efforts. However, in Section IV.C, the NPRM admits that ICE has no legal authority to retain these funds, stating that the fees "would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt." It is inherently arbitrary and capricious to justify a massive fee by claiming a lack of agency resources, while simultaneously acknowledging that not a single dollar of the collected fee will actually go toward funding ICE's investigative or administrative operations. This transforms the proposed "fee" into an unauthorized, punitive tax.

2. Factually Incorrect Justification for the $70,000 Amount
The NPRM attempts to justify the exorbitant $70,000 initial fee by claiming it was "selected... comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" to deter employers from bypassing H-1B costs. This is factually incorrect. The statutory fees for an H-1B petition—including the base fee, Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee, ACWIA fee, and even Premium Processing—total approximately $5,000 to $7,000, which is only 10% of the proposed OPT fee. Imposing a $70,000 fee is not "leveling the playing field"; it is establishing an insurmountable financial barrier designed to implicitly terminate the OPT program without congressional approval.

3. Blanket Punishment Instead of Targeted Enforcement
The NPRM cites specific examples of fraud, such as "shell companies" and fake IT service networks. Instead of implementing targeted enforcement mechanisms against these bad actors—such as requiring stricter employer vetting, mandatory E-Verify participation, or verifying employer tax records—the rule imposes a blanket $70,000 penalty on all students and educational institutions. Legitimate graduates working for highly vetted, compliant, and globally recognized companies like Amazon should not be financially penalized for the agency's failure to police fraudulent shell companies.

The proposed fees do not evaluate a student's educational merit or a training program's legitimacy; they only evaluate wealth. This rule is fundamentally flawed, lacks sound legal and factual basis, and will devastate the pipeline of highly skilled talent that sustains U.S. technological leadership. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this arbitrary proposal immediately.

Thank you for your time.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and urges its withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I work in the construction industry that benefits directly from the foreign student workers who bring their talent to help the American industry maintain its edge over other nations.
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

These changes would inhibit our industry for having access to talented workers who bring their perspectives to the field of construction.

The OPT fee will generally prohibit international students from coming to the US because it is less viable to pursue careers in the US. This will lead to highly talented students (undergraduates and graduates) choosing to pursue their educations in other countries and regions which are more welcoming to international scholars. These include Canada, the UK, China, and Australia.

The OPT fee will be a strong deterrent for international scholars wishing to pursue research and industry careers in the US. Talented PhD graduates are likely to leave and pursue postdoctoral research and or industry positions in other countries. Cutting edge industries which rely on PhD graduates, such as quantum computing and AI development will be severely impacted, leading to the US losing its competitive edge in these industries.
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Zeming Liu
comments.commentText:
We are individual legal scholars and educators writing in opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026), Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (OPT fees rule). In our capacity as law school teachers and scholars, we have witnessed how international students become competent professionals and indispensable talents in the U.S. economy. In our individual capacity, we urge U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) NOT to proceed with the proposed rule, as it would hurt U.S. employers and the broader U.S. economy, as well as the graduates impacted, their U.S. citizen family members and U.S. higher education institutions.

The proposed OPT fees of $70,000-$100,000 would heavily burden universities, rendering OPT effectively infeasible on a national scale.

The proposed OPT fees would hurt U.S. higher education institutions, both financially and in research and development. Many international students are drawn to the practical training element built into the current F visa program. If OPT is virtually eliminated, prospective students may seek degrees in other nations, which could lead to drastic decrease in the number of international students enrolled in U.S. higher education and significantly diminished tuition income. This would not only lead to decreased financial support for American students and revenue for universities and colleges, it would also mean the loss of talent for long-term research and development in the United States.

The proposed OPT fees would also hurt U.S. employers. Keeping the costs of OPT applications low enables talents graduating from U.S. higher education to contribute directly to the U.S. economy for 12 months (and up to 36 months for STEM graduates), usually at relatively low costs to employers. In our personal capacity as educators of international students, we have seen individuals work under OPT authorization for a wide array of U.S. entities, including U.S. universities, U.S. law firms and legal aid organizations, U.S. companies, U.S. think tanks, among others. Losing access to such affordable talents on an aggregate scale would lead to sizable financial losses as well as immeasurable human capital losses for all kinds of U.S. businesses and organizations.

Consequently, the proposed OPT fees also will hurt the U.S. economy in the long run. The proposed rule would indirectly result in the “reverse brain drain,” where the U.S. has expended resources to educate and train foreign talents but then just lose them immediately to other countries.

Kathleen Rubenstein
Ruth Bader Ginsburg Academic Fellow
Columbia Law School

Zeming Liu
Research Fellow
Columbia Law School

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. The $70,000 initial fee is about 135 to 150 times the $470-$520 fee students already pay USCIS to apply for OPT, and a STEM graduate using OPT plus the STEM extension would trigger $100,000.
(1) It is a tax, not a fee. DHS does not tie the amounts to any cost of processing an OPT recommendation; it says it picked $70,000 to match the H-1B fee. DHS also says a main purpose is to discourage OPT use, and receipts would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, not to ICE. A charge meant to deter conduct and raise general revenue is a tax, and only Congress can tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. U.S., 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). INA 214(a) says nothing about fees. A federal court struck down the $100,000 H-1B fee on exactly this ground in June 2026, the First Circuit refused to stay that ruling, and a second court blocked the fee in September. Pegging the OPT fee to it invites the same result.
(2) It does not fit the fraud problem. DHS's evidence is a few prosecutions, a news report, and a figure sourced to a YouTube video, against 194,554 OPT participants in 2024. A $70,000 charge screens by ability to pay, not legitimacy, and because the money goes to the general Treasury it funds no investigators or site visits. Congress's own anti-fraud fee for H-1B and L petitions is set by statute and dedicated to fraud detection.
(3) DHS's analysis is incomplete. DHS projects $8.4-$16.5 billion a year in fees and costs ranging from $32 million to $8.2 billion, yet says it "cannot confidently predict" the drop in participation, the rule's central effect. Studies of a $100,000 charge (what a STEM student would face here) project 35% fewer international graduate applicants (Economic Innovation Group), 80% of students reconsidering staying (Institute for Progress), and up to $4 billion a year in lost university revenue (Clemens). DHS also ignores reliance interests of students who enrolled and paid tuition under current rules (DHS v. Regents, 2020).
(4) Americans would pay. DHS admits schools may pass costs to "all students." International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-25 (NAFSA). 56% of affected schools are small entities, and DHS estimates 98 would pay fees above 20% of revenue. Startups and small employers could not compete for U.S.-trained graduates.
[Personal statement: 2-4 sentences on who you are and how this rule would affect you, your school, or your employer.]
I ask DHS to withdraw the fees; target fraud directly through employer verification, E-Verify, SEVIS data and site visits for high-risk employers; tie any fee to published costs; exempt currently enrolled students; reject re-charging $70,000 at each degree level; and extend comment to at least 60 days, as E.O. 12866 recommends for significant rules.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed rule is an illegal tax, disproportionate, and urges DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The United States of America attract the brightest and hardest working individuals from across the world. Many of these individuals choose to study in the country and remain for a training program following their graduate degrees. This makes America stronger and stimulates innovation. These proposed rule changes, not only create burdens on the individuals, but also decreases the competitiveness of the United States and harms US businesses who benefit. I am a PhD candidate in Water Resources and I know many individuals who have come to study in the United States specially because they knew they could get practical experience via Optional Practical Training. We risk losing this intelligent hard working international students to China or to Europe and our companies risk losing well trained workers who can stay for short periods. I see no personal competition, in fact working with individuals on STEM OPT has taught me very much and lead to new pathways for my research.

Apart from my personal reasons, this rule change has many many issues. DHS should withdraw this proposed rule. The fee does not address the problems DHS identifies, and the agency’s own analysis contains errors and contradictions that undermine its conclusions.

The fee is mismatched to the problem. The fraud described in Section IV.A is employer fraud: shell companies, residential addresses listed as worksites, students who never reported to work. Yet the fee falls on schools, and Section V.A states it is not tied to any employer. Paying $70,000 to a school does nothing to verify that a job is real. Targeted measures DHS already uses for STEM OPT, such as Form I-983 training plans, E-Verify, and employer site visits, address employer fraud directly. DHS dismissed extending them as too resource-intensive (Section IV.C).

The fee provides no new resources. DHS points to understaffed oversight as a core reason for the rule. But under Section IV.C, fee revenue goes to the general Treasury, and ICE cannot retain it. The rule claims DHS cannot run OPT without these fees, yet the fees do not fund DHS’s operation of OPT at all.

The fee would favor wealth over merit. The rule claims schools will recommend only “the most promising students,” but it also permits schools to pass the fee on to students. Students who can personally cover $70,000 to $100,000 are not necessarily the strongest; they are the wealthiest. Students in fraudulent schemes are already paying for fake employment letters, so a higher price is unlikely to stop them.

The rule harms university research without serving its own goals. One stated purpose is preventing OPT from being used to circumvent the H-1B cap. Universities and nonprofit research institutions are cap-exempt, so OPT employment there circumvents nothing. Yet the fee still applies, raising costs for academic research and early-career researchers. The rule also expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT to avoid paying twice (Section VII.A.5.d). Pre-completion OPT is the form most closely tied to a student’s program of study.

The economic analysis is internally inconsistent.

Section IV.B cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024. Section VII.A.3 uses 95,384 as its high estimate for the same year.
The paperwork analysis (Section VII.E) estimates 226,200 responses at 5 minutes each. Its own footnote cites 289,938, and the cost analysis assumes a full hour of staff time per application.
The UMRA section says the rule both does not reach and does exceed the $100 million threshold.
The Federalism section finds no substantial costs to states, even though DHS classifies all 1,044 affected public institutions as state-run.

Costs are quantified; benefits are not. DHS estimates $4.1 billion in annual costs but quantifies none of the claimed benefits to U.S. workers or fraud reduction. That is the same shortcoming DHS criticizes in the 2016 STEM OPT rule.

A rule with these defects should not be finalized. DHS should withdraw it, or at minimum correct the analysis and reopen comment for 60 days.

Re: ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

Dear DHS and ICE Officials,

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. These excessive financial barriers would harm American universities, businesses, and economic competitiveness without effectively addressing immigration fraud.

1. Unreasonable financial burden

A $70,000 fee is beyond the financial capacity of most international graduates. Even if formally imposed on universities, these costs would inevitably affect students and employers. OPT should provide legitimate practical training opportunities, not become a privilege reserved for wealthy individuals.

2. Damage to American universities

International students contribute billions of dollars to the U.S. economy through tuition, living expenses, and research. Making OPT financially inaccessible would discourage talented students from choosing American universities, benefiting competing countries instead.

3. Harm to American businesses

OPT allows U.S. employers to recruit graduates trained at American institutions. These fees would particularly harm startups, small businesses, and research organizations that cannot afford extraordinary immigration-related expenses. The result could be fewer innovations, reduced competitiveness, and the loss of skilled talent.

4. Ineffective fraud prevention

I support stronger enforcement against immigration fraud. However, imposing enormous fees on legitimate students and universities does not directly prevent fraud. Targeted audits, employer verification, and stronger compliance monitoring would be more effective and proportionate.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. The United States should encourage talented international graduates to contribute to its economy rather than push them toward competing countries.

Immigration enforcement should focus on actual misconduct, not impose unreasonable financial penalties on law-abiding students and educational institutions.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international student studying in the United States on an F-1 visa, and I strongly oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions.
Start with the scale. The current federal filing fee for an OPT work permit application is $470. This proposal would attach a $70,000 charge to the school's recommendation alone, roughly 150 times the existing fee and more than the entire first-year salary of many entry-level jobs. A fee bears no relationship to the actual cost of processing a recommendation, and no relationship to any service provided. It is not a user fee. It is a price on participation itself.
The Department justifies these fees partly as a tool against fraud. But a blanket fee is not an anti-fraud measure. Fraud is committed by a small number of bad actors, and a fee does not screen them out; if anything, well-funded fraudulent schemes are the ones best able to pay. The people a $70,000 fee actually screens out are ordinary, compliant students and the schools that follow the rules, complete SEVIS reporting, and verify employers and training plans. Punishing the compliant majority for the conduct of a few is not program integrity. Targeted enforcement against the institutions and employers that abuse the program already exists, and it addresses fraud directly without ending the program for everyone else.
The practical effect of this rule would be to end OPT for all but a small, wealthy minority. Most universities, especially public ones, cannot absorb $70,000 per student, and the Department acknowledges schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Students who cannot pay will lose access to the practical training that has been part of the F-1 program for more than three decades. Employers, faced with a five-figure charge tied to one candidate, will simply hire a different one. The rule would divide otherwise equally eligible graduates into two classes: those who can buy access to work experience, and those who cannot.
The damage would extend well beyond the students affected. In a recent survey of 734 international students, 87 percent planned to use OPT, but 80 percent said they would be less likely to stay and work in the United States if this fee were adopted, and 69 percent said they would not have enrolled in a U.S. program at all had it been in effect. The United States educates much of the world's top STEM talent and then, under this proposal, would charge it out of the country, while Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia actively recruit the same graduates. Fewer than 200,000 students participate in OPT in a year; they are not a threat to the American workforce. They are part of its research labs, hospitals, and technology sector, and this rule treats them as a revenue source instead.
Finally, I ask the Department to respect reliance interests. Students choose schools, sign leases, turn down opportunities in other countries, and plan their lives around the rules in place when they enroll and when their schools recommend them for OPT. At a minimum, no fee should apply to any recommendation issued before a final rule takes effect, and no $30,000 fee should be imposed on a STEM OPT extension for a student already in post-completion OPT.
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. If the Department's concern is program integrity, the answer is targeted oversight of bad actors, not a fee that prices legitimate students out of a program that has served the United States well for over 30 years.
Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are exorbitant and will effectively end the program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Elizabeth Madden
comments.commentText:
I am in total opposition to this rule and urge a complete withdrawal of it.

Imposing the $70,000 fee would result in many US schools whose international students would be shut out of OPT due to the expense and the logistics of the fee. Small schools, such as those in rural or disadvantaged areas, cannot afford additional staff time to facilitate such a fee, and the international students who are seeking training cannot afford the expense of such a fee. Only the wealthy could afford it. It is an unnecessary burden.

The fee will not pay for investigating the fraud that DHS is claiming. Because the fees will be deposited into a general Treasury account, and not earmarked for DHS’s purported fraud investigation, there will be no way of knowing how or whether the OPT vulnerabilities are actually being investigated. There will also be no way of knowing how much has been collected.

Further, the fee is a blunt instrument that is unlikely to deter or reveal the fraud that DHS is claiming. Fraudulent schools can simply pass on the fee burden to the student or employer, and DHS’s lack of plan for using the fee to pay for investigators, site visits, or data systems means that no new fraudulent activity is likely to be revealed.

OPT and the STEM OPT extension are significant training opportunities for international students interested in pursuing degrees in the US. As an advisor at a US university, I often have conversations with first year students regarding their plan for complementing their academic studies with practical training experiences. The fee will deter international students from enrolling in US degree programs and will significantly reduce their participation in OPT training. Obtaining US training is a significant factor in international students’ interest in coming to the US for higher education. Limiting the opportunity to only those who can afford the $70,000 fee will cause international students and their families to choose higher education in other countries.

American students also lose when international students choose to study in other countries. With fewer international students enrolling here, there will be fewer programs and courses available to American students.

Since the 1950s US higher education has been a critical source of US achievements in research and development. With their interest and talents in STEM fields, international students are an important part of those achievements. Imposing this $70,000 OPT fee will discourage the best and the brightest international students from enrolling in US universities, and they will gladly take their talents to universities in other countries.

In closing, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is an unnecessary burden that harms international students and schools.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am sharing comments regarding the OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees." I strongly oppose the rule and find the fees exorbitant and burdensome. I am writing as an international education expert with 27 years of direct experience advising and working with F- 1 students.

First, this is not a fee. It is a tax. Fees are payments to offset costs of providing a good/service. Taxes are compulsory payments that fund provision of public goods. The rule claims this is a fee, so then why does it go to the Treasury instead of DHS/SEVP? If it is a fee, then it should have gone through the normal fee change process.

This tax is an administrative burden to higher educational institutions. There is no way a university can pay this tax for their students without adding it to the student’s bill. Our university prides itself on providing a group of promising undergraduate students full scholarships for their education. Finding another $100,000 for each of them would be impossible. To hire entry level employees for any position, no company or educational institution would be willing to pay this. Only students who come from incredibly wealthy families might consider it but then the tax is being paid by those who can afford it, not necessarily based on the merit of those applications. From a university perspective, many on OPT working at universities are postdocs. These are temporary training positions by definition and the exact type of position for those on OPT. Nationwide they typically make just over $60,000. This tax is 110% of their salary. I cannot imagine a university willing to pay this additional tax to employ this group of talented recent graduates.

The Administrative Procedures Act indicates that the government must provide evidence that the proposed change is the least burdensome way to make a change. There is no provided evidence that there is systematic fraud with OPT, only a few anecdotes presented in the proposed rule. From my own experience, again, 27 years, I have seen countless students partake in OPT. They are gaining valuable skills that enhance what they learned in the classroom. Some take these experiences back to their home country after they have finished their experiences here. Many times I have also seen them fill positions in less desirable, rural places in the U.S. to gain experience, places U.S. graduates may not want to live.

I support appropriate oversight and think it already exists. As a school official, at every school I have worked at we have had detailed instructions on how to apply for OPT and obligations while on OPT. We have workshops both digital and in-person. We continue to communicate with those on OPT after graduation through communications and messaging. If DHS/SEVP thinks more needs to be done, perhaps they could create a course students would have to complete before accessing the portal, much like university’s do before they recommend an OPT application.

At my current institution 53% of our students use OPT. At my previous institution 59% used OPT. Both institutions are Research 1 universities - one public and one private. The usage is high and provides post-academic real-world applications of what is learned in the classroom. Just because these students are using this post-completion option does not mean these students will stay in the U.S. According to https://optobservatory.org/, “From 2006-2022, change of status request rates varied significantly by degree level. Bachelor's graduates saw a steady decline from 10% to just 4%, with rates remaining consistently low since 2014. Master's graduates saw change of status rates rise from 16% in 2006 to peak at 32% in 2016, then decline to 20% by 2022. Doctorate graduates consistently had the highest change of status rates throughout the period, peaking at 39% in 2008 and exceeding one-third in most years from 2007 to 2020, before declining to 25% in 2022.” The top job candidates rise to the top and find those longer term opportunities.

I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. It is flawed in its premises and will harm higher education even more.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, calling them exorbitant, burdensome, and effectively a tax.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket Number: ICEB-2026-0100
Federal Register Document Number: 2026-20660

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees.

International students choose the United States for its world-class education, research opportunities, and professional growth. OPT, particularly the 24-month STEM OPT extension, provides eligible graduates an opportunity to apply their academic knowledge to real-world challenges while contributing to the U.S. workforce.

Although the proposed fees are formally payable by educational institutions, the financial burden could ultimately be passed on to students or employers, making OPT opportunities inaccessible to many qualified graduates. These substantial costs could also discourage universities from supporting eligible students.

As a professional working in the technology sector, I have personally witnessed the tremendous potential of students and recent graduates who bring fresh ideas, innovative thinking, and diverse perspectives to solve real-world problems. Their contributions help organizations innovate, develop better solutions, and address complex technological challenges. OPT provides an important pathway for this emerging talent to contribute to American companies and the broader economy.

Introducing such high fees could discourage talented STEM graduates from pursuing opportunities in the United States, resulting in a loss of skilled talent to other countries. This would not only affect international students but could also impact U.S. employers, innovation, research, and America's global competitiveness.

While I recognize the importance of preventing fraud and maintaining the integrity of the OPT program, such objectives should be achieved through targeted compliance measures and stronger oversight rather than disproportionately high fees that could penalize legitimate students and educational institutions.

I respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security:

a. Withdraw or substantially reduce the proposed OPT fees.
b. Evaluate the financial burden these fees could place on international students and universities.
c. Consider alternative fraud-prevention and compliance measures.
d. Preserve legitimate OPT and STEM OPT opportunities for qualified international graduates.

International students represent an investment in American education, innovation, and economic growth. Providing them with reasonable opportunities to gain practical experience benefits both the graduates and the United States.

Based on my firsthand experience in the technology industry, I believe the contributions and potential of emerging talent should be recognized and encouraged, not discouraged by excessive financial barriers.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and adopt an approach that protects the integrity of the OPT program while preserving opportunities for legitimate international graduates.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed high OPT fees because they harm students, employers, and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an early-career software engineer with a U.S. master's degree in computer science, on post-completion OPT at a technology company in the San Francisco Bay Area, paid at market rate. I ask DHS to withdraw this rule, or at minimum to fix the transition provision described in point 1.

1. The rule penalizes students already on OPT, and its transition text is internally inconsistent (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3); Sec. V.C, VI).

Under 214.13(i)(2), the $30,000 fee applies only to a student who "has previously paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000." A student whose initial OPT began before the effective date never paid that fee, so the STEM extension would cost $70,000. A student who starts OPT after the effective date would pay $30,000 for the identical extension. The RIA confirms this reading: its Year 1 model assumes STEM OPT participants pay $70,000. DHS gives no reason for charging more to the students with the strongest reliance interests.

Those interests are concrete. Students on initial OPT accepted jobs, signed leases, and declined other options in reliance on the 24-month extension under the 2016 rule; employers invested in I-983 training plans. Calling these interests "outweighed" in one sentence is not the weighing required by DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020).

My own STEM OPT recommendation will likely be dated after the proposed effective date. My school would owe $70,000, likely passed to me or my employer, for work I already perform lawfully. No fraud is involved.

Request: exempt from all fees any STEM extension for a student whose initial OPT EAD was approved before the effective date.

2. The fee is a revenue measure, not a condition of admission (Sec. IV.C).

DHS states that the fee is not based on processing cost, will be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, will not fund ICE or SEVP, and was set to be "comparable" to H-1B fees. DHS projects $12.8 billion in annual transfers. A charge unrelated to the cost of any service and paid into the general fund is a tax. INA 214(a) authority over the "time and conditions" of admission is not taxing power (see National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). A federal court vacated the $100,000 H-1B payment on this ground (California v. Mullin, D. Mass. June 8, 2026).

3. The fee cannot address the fraud DHS describes (Sec. IV.A, IV.C).

DHS cites about 10,000 students tied to suspect employers. In 2024, 194,554 students were on OPT and 165,524 on STEM OPT. The fee falls on all of them. It is also paid before the DSO recommendation and, in DHS's words, "would not be tied to a specific employer." The fraud described occurs at the employer and worksite; a fee paid before an employer is known cannot screen for it, and because the money goes to the Treasury it adds no investigative capacity. Nothing in the rule links payment to merit, so the real filter is who can pay $70,000. DHS set aside targeted tools (site visits, training plans for all OPT, employer verification) mainly because they take resources, which is not a reasoned basis for choosing a measure that does not reach the problem (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983)).

Requests: (1) withdraw the rule; (2) if not, adopt the exemption in point 1; (3) limit any fee to documented processing cost; (4) refund the fee in full when employment does not begin.
comments.reason: Commenter asks DHS to withdraw the rule and argues it unfairly penalizes students on OPT.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-01000 – Comment on Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees
Submitted by: Individual International Graduate Student

I am an international graduate student pursuing a Master’s degree in Mechanical Engineering, specializing in Energy Conversion and I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT fee, including STEM OPT extensions.

I came to the United States to pursue advanced education and develop the technical knowledge necessary to contribute to engineering and energy related industries. Throughout my graduate studies, I have worked as a Graduate Research Assistant, contributing to research involving energy conversion technologies, combined heat and power systems, waste heat recovery and thermal management. My current research also includes techno-economic analysis of alternative power generation and cooling technologies for data centers, an area increasingly important to the U.S. energy infrastructure.

My academic experience has extended beyond classroom education. I actively participate in engineering research, system modeling and technical analysis, and the development of practical engineering solutions that address real industrial challenges. I intend to apply this knowledge in the U.S. workforce after graduation, particularly in energy systems to give something back in return for the opportunity to pursue a higher degree.

Optional Practical Training is an important bridge between academia and professional engineering experience. It allows me to apply my knowledge in real industrial environments, develop further specialized skills, and contribute to projects that require advanced technical education. For students in engineering and STEM fields, this experience is particularly important for transitioning from university research into professional practice, continuing to develop relevant skills, and keeping up with the industry’s progress.

I am concerned that the proposed fees could make access to OPT dependent not on a student’s qualifications, academic achievements, or compliance with immigration requirements, but on whether their university can afford or is willing to pay $70,000 for an initial recommendation and another $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation. Although the institution is responsible for paying these fees, the financial burden could ultimately be transferred to students, employers, or other university programs. Institutions with limited financial resources may also choose not to recommend otherwise qualified students. This creates significant uncertainty for students who have invested years of education and substantial financial resources in obtaining a U.S. degree. Even after completing their studies and meeting all other requirements, and securing employment, they can lose the opportunity to gain experience due to a financial decision made by their institution.

The proposed fees could also have broader consequences for the United States. Universities may become less attractive to international students who also consider post-graduation employment opportunities when deciding where to pursue a degree. Reduced international enrollment could affect university funding, graduate research programs, and availability of qualified researchers, which subsequently could reduce the pool of specialized graduates for employers in industries like energy, engineering and manufacturing.

I understand the objectives of DHS, however, imposing substantial fees for every individual OPT recommendation does not necessarily distinguish legitimate students from fraudulent participants. A student who completed a qualifying degree, maintained legal status, and obtained a genuine employment opportunity should not face reduced opportunities if the university cannot afford such a substantial financial expense. The proposed fee should be reconsidered or alternative measures to strengthen the program should be explored. The fees should not make the program inaccessible and discouraging to both students and universities but rather be proportionate to actual administrative work.

I have invested significant time and resources in my U.S. education with the intention of applying my engineering research and knowledge and contributing to the U.S. workforce. I believe that practical training is an important part of realizing the value of that education and reinvesting the skills and knowledge I have gained into industries that can directly benefit from it. The consequences of this proposal extend beyond international graduates. They affect universities, employers, and long-term competitiveness of the U.S. technical workforce, research and technological progress.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses concern that the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees will harm international engineering students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
"Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I am a physics PhD student at Yale University on an F-1 visa. I use computer simulations to study how proteins fold. After graduation, I want to do computational work in industry. I plan to start with a summer internship during my PhD so I can get experience working on an industry team before I apply for full-time jobs.

My physics PhD does not require an internship. My university currently approves Curricular Practical Training only when the training is required of every student in the program, so I expect to need pre-completion Optional Practical Training (OPT) for the summer. If the proposed rule takes effect before my first OPT recommendation, my university would have to pay $70,000 to recommend me for that internship. After graduation, it would have to pay $30,000 to recommend me for post-completion OPT and another $30,000 if I sought a 24-month STEM extension. That comes to $130,000 for the three recommendations, on top of the application fees I would pay USCIS. [Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), Section V.A]

The summer internship would use part of my 12 months of regular OPT. If I skipped it and used all 12 months after graduation, my university would save $30,000 and I would have the same total training time available. DHS says it expects schools to encourage students to make exactly that choice. For me, it would mean applying for my first full-time industry job without the experience I had hoped to gain that summer. [Section VII.A.5.d(3)]

DHS says a school may pass the cost on to a student or employer, or decline to recommend the student. I could not pay $70,000 to take a summer internship. If a university has funds for only some recommendations, two students who both meet the OPT requirements could have different opportunities simply because one has an employer willing to cover the fee. [Section VI]

DHS describes employers that listed residential addresses as worksites for hundreds of students. Investigators went to those addresses and found no employees there. That example gives DHS a concrete reason to check a particular employer’s records and speak to the people listed as supervisors. For STEM OPT, employers already have to participate in E-Verify, sign a training plan, and attest that the student will receive terms comparable to those of similarly situated U.S. workers and will not replace a U.S. worker. DHS can visit the worksite to check whether the employer is following the plan. Collecting a fee from my university would tell DHS little about the work I actually do, and the revenue would go to the Treasury with no funds earmarked for those checks. [Sections III.D.2, IV.A, IV.B, and IV.C]

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and focus enforcement on employers where it has found evidence of fraud. If DHS adopts the fees, I ask it to exempt students already enrolled on the effective date. Those of us partway through a degree should be able to finish it and pursue related training under the fee structure in place when we enrolled. I also ask DHS to exempt pre-completion OPT for internships and the 24-month STEM extension from the fees. [Section V.C and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)]"
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees are excessively high and will restrict access to internships and jobs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
"Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am an international PhD student in computer science at Yale university. I conduct research with my advisor and other graduate students, and I am considering both academic and industry research positions after graduation. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 fee for each subsequent recommendation. However, I do support enforcing wage protections and investigating fraudulent placements. The following are my comments to the proposed rule and why I think this rule should not be enforced:

1. DHS should use workforce data that identify OPT participants. [Section IV.B] DHS reports that the “foreign share” of workers in computer and math occupations rose from 17.7% in 2000 to 26.1% in 2019. Its source, Table 4 of the American Immigration Council’s 2022 report, measures the foreign-born share. That includes naturalized U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, neither of whom needs OPT to work. The 8.4-percentage-point increase tells us neither how much the OPT share changed nor whether OPT displaced U.S. workers. Please correct the description and use OPT-specific evidence to assess effects on wages and employment in my field.

2. Investigate fraudulent placements directly. [Sections IV.A–C, V.A, V.C] DHS reports that only about 20% of the 1.4 million F-1 students in higher education participated in OPT in 2024. No fraud rate is given by DHS. The cases DHS cites warrant investigation, but they do not establish how common fraud is. An applicant for initial OPT does not yet need to have a job offer. A designated school official cannot verify an employer who has not been identified, and paying $70,000 gives the official no new information. Once employment is reported, DHS should audit a random sample to estimate the violation rate and investigate employers that report implausible numbers of trainees.

3. Address payroll taxes through tax policy. [Section IV.B] The FICA exemption under 26 U.S.C. § 3121(b)(19) does not apply to every OPT worker. As IRS Publication 519 explains, students who become U.S. residents for tax purposes generally pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on ordinary private-sector employment. On $80,000 in annual wages, an employer saves $6,120 when the full exemption applies and nothing when both taxes are due. The proposed initial fee is $70,000 either way. If equal payroll-tax treatment is the goal, DHS should work with Treasury and recommend that Congress address off-campus practical training directly in the tax code.

4. Justify the fee amounts independently of H-1B. [Sections IV.B–C, V.A] Lawful OPT does not confer H-1B status or exempt an employer from later petition requirements. Comparing active participants in a multiyear STEM OPT program with an annual H-1B cap does not measure the amount of misuse. Nor does the comparison explain why DHS chose $70,000. Under DHS’s own example, twelve months of OPT after graduation would cost $70,000, while splitting the same twelve months before and after graduation would cost $100,000. What additional cost or risk justifies the extra $30,000 for the same amount of training?

5. Consider how research careers are funded. [Sections IV.C, V.A, V.C] DHS compares the fee to one or two years of educational costs. A university lab could have funding for a postdoctoral salary but not for a separate OPT fee. If Yale cannot pay this fee, the lab may decline to recruit a qualified graduate like me. Passing the charge along instead favors students with personal wealth or a well-funded sponsor. A U.S.-trained researcher like me may then accept a position abroad, and the research may move with the researcher rather than becoming a potential startup in the U.S. that creates jobs for other U.S. workers.

6. Count the costs beyond DHS. [Sections IV.C, V.C, VII.A–B] A fee that is easy to collect is not necessarily the least costly way to protect workers. An international applicant comparing funded PhD offers may choose a university abroad where postdoctoral training is financially feasible. The loss to a U.S. lab would begin years before an OPT application: the student’s doctoral research, collaborations, and potential contributions as a mentor would develop elsewhere. Please compare the fees with targeted enforcement on fraud prevented, effects on U.S. workers, and legitimate research opportunities lost.

I urge DHS to withdraw both fees. Should DHS pursue a revised fee, it should publish the evidence supporting each amount and seek further public comment. At a minimum, students already enrolled on the effective date should be exempt from new fees for OPT associated with their current degree, including any eligible STEM extension. [Sections V.A, V.C]"

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international Ph.D. candidate at Yale University, where my research focuses on Slavic studies. I am in F-1 status and plan to pursue a research career in the United States after I graduate. I write as someone the rule would directly affect, and I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

1. Fees of $70,000 and $30,000 [proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2); 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii)]
Under the proposal, a school cannot enter an OPT recommendation in SEVIS, and USCIS cannot grant an EAD, until the school has paid the fee. For me, a post-completion OPT recommendation would cost $70,000. A STEM OPT extension would add $30,000, for a combined $100,000 per graduate. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass this cost on to students or employers. Doctoral trainees live on stipends and cannot absorb it. Universities and labs funded by fixed-term federal grants cannot easily absorb it either, and it is not an allowable expense on most of those grants.
In practice, a fee of this size would make me a liability on a hiring budget. I would be forced to choose between giving up the research I have trained for years to do and leaving the country.

2. Impact on my field, lab, and career [8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)–(11)]
OPT is the bridge between a doctorate and a postdoctoral appointment, a faculty position, or an industry R&D role. Many of these positions are filled before an H-1B petition can be filed. A cost that large in the OPT recommendation would effectively close that bridge for many of the international scientists who train here. {ADD A SPECIFIC EXAMPLE: e.g., labmates who moved from PhD to postdoc through OPT, a collaboration or dataset that depends on continuity, a field where international researchers are a large share of the workforce.} Losing trained graduates at the moment they become independent researchers wastes the public and institutional investment in their training. It also breaks up the research teams that depend on them.

3. Competitiveness of U.S. universities [Section VI, “Reliance interests”]
DHS states that schools should be able to attract foreign students without relying on OPT. That does not match how prospective graduate students decide. They compare the U.S. with Canada, the U.K., Germany, Australia, and China, many of which are expanding post-study work options. If the U.S. adds a six-figure charge to post-study work, the strongest applicants will go elsewhere, and U.S. departments will lose them at the recruitment stage. DHS’s own figures show about 194,000 OPT participants and 165,000 STEM OPT participants in 2024. Those are people who currently study, work, and pay taxes here. The effects on recruitment are not meaningfully analyzed.

4. Weaknesses in DHS’s justification [Section IV; Section VII, Regulatory Impact Analysis]
DHS justifies the fee as a way to combat fraud by shell employers and “visa mills.” I share the goal of stopping fraud. But a flat fee on every student recommendation, including Yale doctoral students working in funded labs, is not targeted at fraud. DHS itself describes the fee as a deterrent, and the fees would be deposited in the general Treasury rather than used to fund oversight. The Regulatory Impact Analysis reports no monetized benefits, while estimating annualized costs of roughly $4.1 billion and transfers of roughly $12.8 billion. DHS also acknowledges a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. DHS considered less costly alternatives, such as extending site visits, training plans, and reporting requirements to OPT, and dismissed them largely on the ground that a fee is faster. Speed is not a reason to adopt a measure whose costs so far exceed its documented benefits. A 30-day comment period for an economically significant rule of this size is also too short for universities, employers, and students to assess its effects.

5. Broader effects on the U.S. [Section VII]
The international scientists trained at U.S. universities have contributed to public health research, biotechnology, clinical advances, semiconductor and AI research, and many startups and employers. Discouraging them from staying lowers the supply of researchers here, weakens the U.S. research pipeline, and gives competitor countries the benefit of talent trained at U.S. expense.

6. Request
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. If DHS believes OPT fraud needs to be addressed, it should do so through targeted measures. Examples are strengthening employer verification, enforcing against specific fraudulent employers and sham schools, and focusing site visits on high-risk employers. These measures would address fraud without imposing a $70,000–$100,000 charge on legitimate students. At a minimum, DHS should exempt students in accredited degree programs at established universities and extend the comment period so that affected parties can assess the rule fully.

Thank you for considering my comment.
