comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule published under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which would impose a $70,000 fee on a student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and a $30,000 fee on each subsequent recommendation.

I am a graduate student at Yale University in MBB department working on gene regulation research. I also serve as a teaching assistant for MB&B 3000, an undergraduate course in molecular biophysics and biochemistry. I am submitting this comment because the proposed fees would directly affect my research community, and the students I teach.

$70,000 fee for a student’s first OPT recommendation
A $70,000 fee is larger than the annual stipend of most U.S. PhD students and many postdoctoral researchers. For any students, OPT is the bridge between completing a degree and beginning a research or industry career in the United States. Because the fee applies to pre-completion OPT as well, it would also eliminate internships and practical training that students undertake during their programs, which are often essential for gaining industry experience and securing jobs after graduation. A fee of this size would effectively end OPT for all but the wealthiest students, regardless of their talent or the value of their work.

$30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension
The STEM OPT extension exists because Congress and DHS have recognized that STEM graduates contribute disproportionately to U.S. innovation. Imposing an additional $30,000 for each later recommendation penalizes exactly the fields that the extension was designed to support. In our biological research field, a two-year extension is often the period in which a researcher completes a project, publishes key results and becomes eligible for longer-term employment. Pricing this period out of reach would push trained scientists to Canada, the UK, Germany, etc., which are actively recruiting the same people.

Requirement that schools pay the fee before issuing an I-20 with an OPT recommendation
Requiring universities to pay up front makes schools the gatekeepers of a financial decision they cannot sustain at scale. At an institution with hundreds or thousands of international students, these fees would add up to tens of millions of dollars per year. Schools would face pressure to limit OPT recommendations, delay them, or deprioritize admitting international students at all. Students who have done everything required of them could be denied training opportunities simply because their institution cannot or will not front the cost.

DHS’s statement that schools may pass costs to “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers”
DHS itself acknowledges that these costs may be passed to all students. That means domestic students, including the U.S. undergraduates I teach, could see higher tuition or fees to subsidize a charge that has no connection to their education. Passing the cost to employers would discourage the very companies and labs that hire OPT participants, many of which are small startups and research groups that cannot absorb a $70,000 charge per hire. Every pathway DHS identifies for these costs harms students, universities, or U.S. employers.

Broader impact on research and teaching
International students and researchers make up a large share of the scientific workforce in U.S. labs and STEM classrooms. In my own lab, many members are international, and our work on gene regulation depends on collaboration with many of these talented individuals that would get affected by this change. If OPT becomes unaffordable, fewer international students will choose U.S. programs to begin with, reducing the talent pool that U.S. research, teaching, and industry rely on.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. The OPT program should remain accessible on the basis of a student’s academic standing and eligibility, not their ability or their school’s ability to pay fees of this magnitude.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am a postdoctoral associate at Yale University and an international researcher with over five years of postdoctoral experience in chemistry and physics. I develop computational methods that predict molecular and materials properties, work that feeds directly into U.S. drug discovery, energy and materials R&D. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw this rule.

1. The fee is a near-prohibitive barrier for STEM graduates [8 CFR 214.13(i)]. $70,000 for initial OPT plus $30,000 for STEM OPT is $100,000 per student. DHS calls this comparable to one or two years of tuition [Preamble IV.C], but most STEM PhD students pay no tuition: they are grant-funded and paid stipends smaller than this fee. No student, grant-funded lab or startup can absorb $100,000 per person. Surveys show 54% of current international students would not have chosen the U.S. without OPT, and 80% would reconsider staying under a $100,000 fee; EIG projects a 35% drop in international graduate applicants. This contradicts DHS's claim that schools can recruit without relying on OPT.

2. The H-1B fee shows what this rule will do. After the $100,000 H-1B fee of September 2025, DHS processed 87% fewer affected applications and collected the fee on only 85 petitions through mid-February 2026. It did not redirect hiring to Americans; it stopped the flow. New international enrollment fell 17% in fall 2025 and international PhD applications for fall 2026 fell about 21%. I am aware of no evidence that the H-1B fee raised wages or employment for U.S. workers. Research generally finds skilled immigrants complement U.S. workers; one study found a 1-point rise in a city's foreign tech worker share raised college-educated wages 7-8%.

3. Competitor countries are recruiting this talent, not raising hurdles. Germany gives its graduates an 18-month job-search permit for about EUR 100. The UK gives PhD graduates three years of post-study work for under GBP 5,000 including health coverage. Canada's post-graduation work permit costs about CAD 255. China launched a K visa in 2025 that admits young STEM graduates without employer sponsorship. Even countries that have tightened their rules charge a small fraction of $100,000. Every student this rule deters will be welcomed elsewhere, and their discoveries, patents and companies will strengthen our competitors.

4. Impact on my field and lab. In computational chemistry and physics, a large share of PhD students and postdocs are international. They write the codes, run the simulations and co-author the papers behind NSF-, DOE- and NIH-funded projects. About two-thirds of international PhD graduates use OPT to start their careers. The AI-for-science, materials and pharmaceutical companies that hire from my field rely on OPT to bring on new graduates; for an early-stage company, $100,000 per hire removes that option, and the training U.S. taxpayers funded leaves with the graduate.

5. Fraud should be targeted precisely, not punished collectively [Preamble IV.A; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)-(iii)]. DHS's own evidence points to a specific problem: shell employers. Its investigation flagged about 10,000 students tied to suspect employers, out of roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. A blanket fee does nothing to detect a fraudulent employer, its revenue goes to the Treasury rather than SEVP oversight, and it falls on the honest majority who follow the rules. DHS has precise tools: require E-Verify for all OPT employers as it already does for STEM OPT, extend training plans and site visits to all OPT, verify employers, and bar and prosecute fraudulent employers and the schools that enable them.

NAFSA projects up to 111,000 fewer international students this fall, costing about $3.4 billion and nearly 40,000 U.S. jobs. This rule would deepen that loss.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers instead of a blanket fee on all students.

Respectfully,
Postdoctoral Associate, Yale University

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment as a Designated School Official (DSO). I advise F-1 and J-1 students on federal regulations, including Optional Practical Training (OPT). These comments reflect my professional experience administering the F-1 program.

I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. DHS should instead integrate practical training into the academic experience, remove financial barriers, and give schools an appropriate role in authorizing eligible students.

1. The proposal makes schools fiscal intermediaries for an individual benefit

Under current regulations, F-1 students who meet eligibility requirements may apply for OPT. The DSO verifies eligibility (one completed academic year, valid F-1 status, timely filing) and provides the recommendation in SEVIS. USCIS makes the final determination on employment authorization.

The proposed rule would require schools to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one, including STEM OPT. This makes schools financially responsible for a benefit that belongs to the student. Students need not have an employer when they apply, so reliance on employers as a funding source does not reflect how OPT operates.

2. The proposal assigns schools responsibilities that belong to the government

Investigating employers. Identifying fraudulent employers is an enforcement responsibility of DHS, including HSI. DSOs lack the authority and information to do it.

Ranking programs. Faced with these fees, schools would have to decide which students or fields justify the expense. Nothing in the regulations or the DSO’s role supports ranking fields of study by perceived value.

Assuming others’ decisions. If schools limit recommendations based on perceived fraud risk or program value, they take on judgments that belong to federal agencies and invite claims of unequal treatment. The alternative is absorbing costs they have no obligation to pay.

Either outcome undermines the DSO’s role as a source of accurate, consistent guidance.

3. The fee is not tied to fraud prevention and restricts access to OPT

The fee applies regardless of risk. Every recommendation is charged whether or not there are indicators of fraud. It is a barrier to participation, not a measure against misconduct.

The revenue is not dedicated to enforcement. As I understand the proposal, it would go to the general Treasury, not to oversight or investigations.

It restricts a benefit through regulation. Congress has considered changes to practical training and has not enacted them. Fees that make participation financially impossible for most institutions achieve a similar result through rulemaking.

4. The proposal would undermine the international student experience

Tran and Soejatminah (2017) describe how work-integrated learning helps international students develop the skills and attributes employers seek. (Ly Thi Tran & Sri Soejatminah, “Integration of Work Experience and Learning for International Students: From Harmony to Inequality,” Journal of Studies in International Education, 21(3), 261-277.) Making OPT inaccessible would create inequality between students based on their institution’s finances rather than their qualifications.

5. Recommended alternative

Integrate practical training into the academic experience. Rather than treating OPT as an entirely separate process after completion of academic coursework, DHS should explore ways to incorporate practical training into the student's overall degree experience. Planning with academic departments, establishing appropriate learning objectives, and documenting relevant training expectations would provide schools with a legitimate academic basis for oversight. This would also encourage students to view practical training as an extension of their education rather than simply an employment benefit.

Eliminate the application fee. Remove the per-recommendation fee, and reconsider the separate employment authorization application fee for OPT, so that the cost of access does not determine who can use a benefit the regulations grant.

Make the DSO’s recommendation the operative authorization. Schools already verify eligibility and enter recommendations in SEVIS. Treating the recommendation as authorization, subject to DHS oversight and audit authority, would remove a duplicative adjudication step while DHS retains enforcement authority.

Target fraud directly, don't dance around the issue and have your agencies do their job, not the schools.

Conclusion

The proposed rule shifts substantial financial responsibility to schools, pressures DSOs into decisions outside their authority, and would make OPT inaccessible at many institutions regardless of student eligibility. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

OPT should remain an opportunity based on student eligibility and regulatory compliance, not on an institution's ability to pay an extraordinary fee.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed rule creates severe financial and administrative burdens for schools and urges DHS to withdraw it.

Raising its cost from roughly $500 to $70,000, an increase of more than 100-fold, would close that bridge for all but the wealthiest students. I ask DHS to explain how a fee of this size relates to the actual cost of processing an OPT recommendation.

[Proposed $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT, including the STEM OPT extension] The STEM OPT extension exists because the United States has recognized that it needs scientists and engineers. Charging $30,000 for that extension specifically penalizes the fields this country has said it wants to grow. Research projects take years, and trainees forced to leave after one year take their expertise with them before it can benefit American patients and institutions.

[Requirement that universities pay the fee before issuing an I-20 with an OPT recommendation] The proposed rule acknowledges that schools could pass these costs on to “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers.” This means the burden could fall on domestic students as well, at a time when the cost of medical and graduate education is already a serious barrier. As an advisor, I see how financial pressure shapes students’ decisions about whether to pursue medicine and research at all. Smaller institutions and those with fewer resources would be hit hardest, widening existing inequities in access to scientific training.

Talented students choose where to train based partly on the opportunities available after graduation. Other countries actively recruit the scientists this rule would push away, and when we lose them, we lose their discoveries, their companies, and their contributions to American public health. In medicine especially, international researchers and physician-scientists strengthen clinical research, drug development, and patient care across the country.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and preserve OPT as an accessible pathway for international students to contribute to American science, medicine, and innovation.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they would create a prohibitive barrier to practical training and risk harming students, universities, and American employers.

Students already enrolled in U.S. institutions made substantial educational and financial commitments under the existing framework. Although OPT does not guarantee employment, suddenly making participation financially inaccessible would undermine the reasonable expectations that informed those decisions. DHS should protect currently enrolled students and provide meaningful transition arrangements.

The proposal could also weaken the international competitiveness of American universities. Reduced international enrollment could diminish tuition revenue at some institutions, while the fees themselves could divert resources from teaching, research, and student support. Access to practical training could increasingly depend on an institution’s financial resources rather than a student’s qualifications.

American employers would also risk losing access to qualified graduates whom U.S. universities have already trained. DHS should evaluate the consequences for research, innovation, small businesses, and jobs that depend on complementary skills, rather than assume that excluding an international graduate necessarily creates an equivalent opportunity for a U.S. worker. Graduates who cannot pursue opportunities here may instead take their expertise to other countries, shifting the long-term benefits of their U.S. education abroad.

Finally, the proposal should demonstrate how these fees would effectively address fraud. Ability to pay is not evidence of compliance, and inability to pay is not evidence of misconduct. Targeted oversight, verification of genuine employment, and enforcement against actual violations would address those concerns more directly.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity without making legitimate practical training financially inaccessible.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences
comments.submitterName: University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences
comments.commentText:
Speaking on behalf of the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences as a representative of their Graduate School , we respectfully disagree with the proposed rule that would impose new Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. Below, we detail our concerns and the high potential for a negative impact of ICEB-2026-0100on the American economy and health system and the State of Arkansas.

1.OPT FEES WILL DECREASE THE ABILITY OF INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS TO UTILIZE OPT
The Institute For Progress’ SEVIS analysis, projects a 79% decline in OPT starts if universities must pay the full cost of a $100,000 OPT fee. The impact of this proposed rule is thus disproportionate and would essentially close down the OPT training pipeline.

2.INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS CONTRIBUTE GREATLY TO THE UNITED STATES ECONOMY
NAFSA reports international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs in 2024-25. In Arkansas, 6,409 international students contributed $153.8 million and supported 985 jobs. These contributions extend beyond universities. NAFSA also estimates declining international enrollment in Fall 2025 resulted in $1.1 billion in lost economic activity and nearly 23,000 fewer American jobs.

3.OPT SUPPORTS AMERICAN JOBS
The Economic Innovation Group reports greater access to international STEM graduates stimulated employment gains equivalent to ~450 additional American workers per 100,000 residents in areas with greater STEM OPT exposure, alongside an approximately 1% increase in local firms, without declines in average wages.

4.OPT IS HOW AMERICAN EMPLOYERS IDENTIFY THE BEST GRADUATES
Among international STEM graduates who stay to work in the United States, 82% do so through OPT before receiving an H-1B. OPT functions as a probationary period: an American employer observes a graduate’s performance before committing to sponsorship. A public academic health center in Arkansas cannot absorb such cost, and talent trained in Arkansas would leave the U.S. workforce before an employer can evaluate them.

5.THE RULE WOULD FALL HARDEST ON ARKANSAS AND THE MID-SOUTH
Arkansas has approximately 224 physicians per 100,000 residents, 72 fewer than the national average. In 2024, temporary visa holders earned about one-quarter of U.S. doctorates in the biological and biomedical sciences. OPT is the mechanism that allows Arkansas employers to retain roughly 90% of those students.

When UAMS trains a PhD scientist, federal research agencies, the State of Arkansas, and our faculty have already made a multi-year investment. Under the proposed rule, the return on that investment would go to competing nations.

6.FEES PROPOSED IN ICEB-2026-0100 UNDERMINE U.S. COMPETITIVENESS IN A GLOBAL MARKET
Arkansas has approximately 224 physicians per 100,000 residents, 72 fewer than the national average. Closing that gap depends not only on clinicians but on the biomedical scientists, pharmaceutical scientists, and health-data professionals who develop treatments, run clinical trials, and staff our laboratories. In 2024, temporary visa holders earned about one-quarter of U.S. doctorates in the biological and biomedical sciences. Roughly 90% of those with definite post-graduation plans committed to remaining in the United States. OPT is the mechanism that allows Arkansas employers to retain them.

International doctoral training is financed largely through research grants and institutional funds, not tuition. When UAMS trains a PhD scientist, federal research agencies, the State of Arkansas, and our faculty have already made a multi-year investment. Under the proposed rule, the return on that investment would go to competing nations. A public academic health center earns no tuition margin from which to pay a $70,000 fee; for each PhD graduate, the fee would be a direct loss.

7.FEES PROPOSED IN ICEB-2026-0100 WOULD UNDERMINE U.S. COMPETITIVENESS IN A GLOBAL MARKET
The requirement for universities to spend $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation would make participation financially unsustainable for essentially all institutions, with the direct impact of losing talented international students, and sending their current and future economic contributions to other countries.

In Conclusion:

The outcome from the proposed rule will be the undermining of the United States’ ability to attract and retain global talent. The most competitive applicants, with an array of options are more likely to choose competing universities in Canada, Australia, or Europe. If U.S. universities bear the fee, the resulting enrollment losses are estimated to cost U.S. universities $2.5 to $4.2 billion per year in net revenue.

To be clear, the proposed rule changes of ICEB-2026-0100 would create prohibitive barriers for international students to continue to train in the United States. We urge DHS to withdraw ICEB-2026-0100.

Thank you
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will drastically reduce participation and negatively impact the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:
As an F-1 student in the U.S., I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 subsequent fee (91 Fed. Reg. 64566) and urge DHS to withdraw this rule. OPT access was vital to my decision to study in the U.S.; 69% of F-1 students would not have enrolled—and 37% definitely would not have—under these fees (Institute for Progress, Oct. 6, 2026). 
1. Wealth Replaces Merit and Compliance
These fees tie training access to wealth rather than merit, qualifications, or compliance. Most entry-level jobs pay under $70,000/yr, so a 12-month fee exceeds a graduate's annual salary in nursing, teaching, research, pharmacy, and agriculture. DHS's claim that $70,000 is "on par" with 1–2 years of tuition (91 Fed. Reg. 64575) lacks data: public non-resident tuition is often $20,273–$25,938/yr ($70,000 is 86% of $81,090 4-year tuition), and campus OPT fees are ~$150. 
2. The "Pass-Through" Premise Fails
The rule charges 2,478 schools—including 1,044 public schools (42%) excluded from DHS's institutional analysis (91 Fed. Reg. 64593)—assuming they can pass the $8.4B–$16.5B/yr cost ($109.4B/10 yrs, 91 Fed. Reg. 64583–84) to students or employers (91 Fed. Reg. 64575). All 3 options fail: 
Schools Cannot Pay: State anti-donation clauses (Tex. Const. art. III, §§ 50–52; La. Const. art. VII, § 14), fee rules (UNC Policy Manual 1000.1.2.1[R]), and budgets bar using public funds for private fees. 
Students Cannot Pay Upfront: Students apply 90 days before to 60 days after graduation (8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)), usually before a job offer. Because payment precedes SEVIS recommendation (Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii)) and refunds end once an EAD issues (Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(1)–(2)), students risk $70,000 upfront with no offer or refund right, driving debt and employer dependence. Foreign-exchange caps (China's $50,000/yr limit) also block payments. 
Employers Cannot Pay: Most applicants lack an employer when applying. Even with offers, $70,000 payments exceed $50,000 state procurement limits, trigger foreign-gift reporting ($250,000 under 20 U.S.C. § 1011f; $50,000 under CHIPS Act § 10339B), and exceed Pay.gov's $24,999 card cap and $5,000 state p-card limits—far beyond DHS's 5-min to 1-hr burden estimate (91 Fed. Reg. 64585, 64598). 
3. No Statutory Authority and Flawed Fraud Deterrence
I support protecting U.S. workers and stopping fraud, but ability to pay does not prove compliance and lower participation is not proof of prevented fraud. Because fees go to the general Treasury (31 U.S.C. § 3302; 91 Fed. Reg. 64576) rather than ICE oversight, this is an unauthorized tax under INA § 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1) (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229 (2026)). DHS also benchmarked the fee to a vacated $100,000 H-1B fee under Proclamation 10973 (91 Fed. Reg. 64575; California v. Mullin, 833 F. Supp. 3d 50 (D. Mass. 2026); Global Nurse Force v. Trump (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2026)) and contradicted its Aug. 2026 H-1B rule exempting universities from a $103,265 fee (91 Fed. Reg. 54817, 54831). DHS should use targeted compliance and employer enforcement instead. 
4. Penalties on Pre-Completion OPT, Transfers, and Higher Degrees
The rule penalizes pre-completion OPT—capped at 20 hrs/wk (8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(A)) with zero cited fraud—charging $100,000 ($70,000 + $30,000) if a student does an internship before post-completion OPT (91 Fed. Reg. 64590), even after Aug. 18 & 24, 2026 SEVP CPT limits forced healthcare, pharmacy, and business students into pre-completion OPT. It also risks duplicate $70,000 transfer fees, and I oppose charging $70,000 again at each higher degree level ($140,000–$170,000 total, 91 Fed. Reg. 64577). 
5. Retroactive Impact and Harm to Critical Sectors
A 60-day effective date and 30-day comment window on a $12.8B/yr rule (91 Fed. Reg. 64579; E.O. 12866 § 6(a)(1)) harm students who committed to degrees years ago. Worse, under Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(3), current OPT holders seeking a STEM extension after the effective date owe $70,000, not $30,000 (91 Fed. Reg. 64583). F-1 students add $42.9B and 355,736 jobs (NAFSA & JB Int'l, Aug. 11, 2026), founded 25% of U.S. $1B+ startups (NFAP, June 2026), cross-subsidize domestic courses (Shih, 156 J. Pub. Econ. 170 (2017)), and staff labs, hospitals, and rural clinics, where curbing OPT risks 443,000 jobs over 10 yrs (Business Roundtable). 
Requested Actions: Please withdraw this rule. At a minimum, DHS must set far lower fees, grandfather all current F-1 students and active OPT holders (including STEM extensions), exempt pre-completion OPT, reject repeat fees for transfers or higher degrees, and refund fees whenever no EAD issues. 
Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Emmanuel Kobby
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing in opposition to the proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT. This proposal should not be finalized.

First, the fee would place an enormous burden on schools. Institutions would be required to pay tens of thousands of dollars for each student they recommend, and many schools — especially smaller ones — would respond by recommending fewer students or passing the cost on. That would restrict access to OPT based on a school's or a student's ability to pay, not on the student's merit or qualifications.

Second, the proposal would burden employers. Companies, startups, hospitals, and research institutions that hire OPT graduates would face higher costs and greater uncertainty when hiring international talent. The predictable result is that many employers, particularly small businesses and research labs, would simply avoid hiring these graduates altogether.

Finally, and most importantly, this fee would drive away the very people the United States should be working to keep. International graduates are among the most highly trained and brilliant minds in the world. If working in the United States after graduation becomes unaffordable, many will take their skills to other countries instead. That would mean a real reduction in the talent contributing to the American economy, to scientific research, to medicine, and to innovation — fields where the United States has long led precisely because it welcomed the best minds from around the world.

OPT is not just a benefit to international students; it is a benefit to the United States. For these reasons, I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal.

Respectfully submitted,
Emmanuel

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gregory Zilberg
comments.commentText:
I am a postdoctoral researcher at the Yale School of Medicine working on the molecular mechanisms underlying taste in mammals and birds. This comment refers to Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 regarding the proposed changes to cost for recommendations of F-1 visa holders to obtain Optional Practical Training (OPT) extension.

As a scientist working in biomedical research for over a decade, I have met many incredible international scientists who started their careers pursuing an education in the United States. These scientists are frequently as talented and competent as, if not necessarily moreso than, some of the American researchers I have worked alongside during that same period of time. Their skills are sufficiently niche and valuable that it naturally makes sense for American industry and academic labs to retain their labor beyond the period of time provided by their training visas. It therefore follows that regulations crafted with a clear intention to reduce the number of OPT participants is a direct attack on the productivity of our biomedical output. Long-term, this change will cripple the strength of our biomedical research system by discouraging international students from applying for OPT, and downstream, less likely to apply to our advanced educational programs to begin with.

In our current academic environment of government-imposed research austerity, the requirements for a successful academic career domestically and abroad have shifted towards a de facto need for post-baccalaureate or postdoctoral research experience. OPT, then, is a practically required element of advanced education for international students. Adding the undue burden of up to $100,000 in personal expenses to pursue institutional recommendations for an OPT or STEM OPT extension is very blatantly an attempt to discourage applications in the first place. While the regulations offer the institution to bear the cost of the recommendation, they suggest that they could shift the cost to "F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers". Often times, STEM OPT's employers are the same or another academic institution. The practical effect of this is that universities will refuse to put up $100,000 for each of their international students, and that will kill the OPT system for all but the wealthiest international students.

Frequently, the academic workers on OPT (and especially STEM OPT) will opt to continue working in the United States after their extended visa, requiring tedious additional efforts to obtain a J-1 or H1B visa that include necessary time away from work back in their home countries. This additional time results in a decrease in research productivity for their employers, and a reduced quality of life for the employee caused by the interruption in employment. The fact that so many OPT visaholders proceed with these costly and personally destabilizing bureacratic processes is proof of their desire to continue contributing to our nation's research efforts.

These regulations are justified as "strengthen[ing] the integrity of the immigration system, and protect[ing] U.S. workers". They accomplish neither of these claimed purposes.

The rationale proposed by DHS's SEVP in this docket involves a convoluted fantasy where F-1 visaholders are contracting the services of illicit shell companies en masse to stay in the United States without having to pursue relevant work. These reports are based entirely on the claims of an out-of-control agency that has provably attempted to cover up the deaths of both nonimmigrant residents and American citizens at the hands of their agents.

Even if ICE is to be believed that there exists such a problem, how is this solved by increasing the cost of OPT application fees? In effect, DHS is arguing that the reasonable way to fix a problem that they tenuously claim exists with 10,000 OPT participants *in total* is to financially destroy the prospects of applications for over 200,000 OPT participants *every year*. The suggestion that this fee is to cover processing OPT visas is ludicrous on its face - DHS's discretionary budget has ballooned from $46 billion to $65 billion dollars over the course of the two Trump administrations. In no way does attempting to rip more money away from productive nonimmigrant workers strengthen the integrity of a system that has grown one-and-a-half-fold in scale in the last decade.

The inability of academic institutions to host more students than they currently do is a direct result of austerity in government funding of scientific research. In the absence of more science funding, US workers are not being protected in any way by their coworkers being forced out of employment roles that require niche skilled labor. If DHS Secretary Mullin truly wanted to address the existing problems with academic labor, he would instead lobby his boss to propose substantially larger operating budgets for the NSF and NIH.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee will cripple biomedical research and harm the U.S. academic system.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to register my objections on behalf of myself as parent and the relevant student to the proposed changes to the OPT regime.

The student in question has been studying in the US for three years and is currently in the last year of their undergraduate degree.

The student had the opportunity to study in their home country but decided to take the opportunity to attend a world class college in the US using an F1 visa. Having won a merit scholarship I agreed to meet the remaining costs running to the best part of $100,000 per year.

At the time, the institution in question made clear that there was an entitlement to work both during and after the relevant degree in order to obtain additional practical experience over and above the knowledge learned as part of a student’s degree studies.

In my case, the student has worked hard throughout with significant success. As a result, the student has secured a paid internship generally requiring the student to work a day a week during term time at a leading company in their field.

This company looks to employ both US citizens and non-US citizens if they meet its requirements. To my knowledge, there is no difference in the pay dependent on whether the individual question is a US citizen.

Although the student is working for a high profile company, the sector is not particularly highly paid even at a relatively senior level and certainly by comparison with say a tech or finance business.

As a result, it is with respect completely unrealistic to look to impose a charge of $70,000 for a first time OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPTs.

This is particularly the case in relation to a pre-graduation OPT where the student will necessarily be working part time in relation to a field that is closely related to their degree. Even post completion of the degree the OPT is only for a limited duration and there is a deduction for previous time worked. So I respectfully submit the proposed charge is excessive even for a post-completion OPT approval.

In relation to this student and others who have already obtained a pre-graduation OPT, I appreciate that there is transitioning of the existing approval proposed. However, whilst I personally consider that $30,000 further charge is too high in any event, someone who has already obtained a pre-completion OPT should be treated subsequently as if they had effectively already paid the initial $70,000, with the result that any post completion OPT should be $30,000 consistent with the original transitioning of the first OPT.

As already mentioned, the figures that are proposed do not respectfully make sense in the context of the sort of hourly pay that most people would be paid even in relatively high profile, graduate roles.

This is particularly the case in the case of a pre-completion OPT given it is part time. This point is well illustrated in my view by the hourly rate that the student in my case is getting paid which is $17 per hour before tax. So a $70,000 charge for a pre-completion OPT for a student working a day a week in term time and likely only a few days per week even in vacations is completely disproportionate.

I could understand why it might be thought appropriate to charge a higher administration fee than is currently the case. For example, the fast track fee of $1,780 could be seen as more appropriate particularly for a post-completion OPT.

In addition, I respectfully see it is as unrealistic to think that the relevant educational institution will be willing to cooperate by administering these payments, particularly in relation to post-graduation OPTs.

In the long-term, there must also be a concern that US educational institutions end up with a lower standard of students or unfilled places if changes such as these are implemented. I am aware of this happening in other jurisdictions where this is happening (although I appreciate the need to ensure that only legitimate students are admitted and able to take advantage of schemes such as these).

Further, I respectfully note that, in my opinion, it would be more appropriate to introduce a major change such as this with more lead time. It seems particularly unfair in my view that the changes should apply to someone already in the US studying in circumstances in which options such as OPT were part of the “sell” when they applied in the first place. It would seem more appropriate in my respectful view for changes of this significant nature to be made (if made at all) in relation to those who are admitted subsequently as they would at least enter the US university system knowing of these restrictions.
comments.reason: The commenter objects to the proposed changes, highlighting financial burdens and impacts on the student's career plans.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Philipp Lojak
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student in year 3 of a PhD program in music history at Yale University, a private nonprofit institution. Like many humanities doctoral students, I expect my first post-degree position to be a modestly paid postdoctoral or teaching post at a university. I respectfully oppose the proposed fee and ask DHS to withdraw it.

1. The fee targets the wrong party. Every fraud example in Section IV.A involves employers: shell companies, staged worksites and “phantom employees” (91 FR 64570-64571). None involves a university. DHS should extend its existing STEM OPT employer safeguards to all OPT instead.
2. Universities have no cap to circumvent. They are H-1B cap-exempt (8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)). If a university pays $70,000 so its own graduate can hold a postdoc on campus, money moves from research funds to the Treasury and program integrity gains nothing.
3. The rule asks schools to choose “the most promising students” but gives no standard (64574-64575). In practice, schools will favor students whose employers can repay the fee. Students in the humanities and the arts (like me) will be cut first. That has nothing to do with fraud risk.
4. The fee has no cost basis. 31 U.S.C. 9701 and 8 U.S.C. 1372(e) require fees to reflect cost. DHS instead copied the H-1B payment (64575), which a federal court vacated in June 2026.
5. Current students are unprotected. I enrolled relying on the OPT rules then in force. DHS should grandfather every student enrolled on the effective date.

I ask DHS to quantify the fraud it expects to prevent, as Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 require. Any measure it adopts should act on employers, be cost-based, and exempt doctoral graduates and employment with cap-exempt institutions. Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee harms students, lacks a cost basis, and asks DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS states that they "[do] not need to define which OPT experiences provide genuine
educational value" and expects schools to recommend only "the most promising students." There are no regulations to DSO rank students by promise.

The rule creates a merit gate, hands it to more than 2,000 institutions, and
supplies no standard. The criterion that will fill that vacuum is money: a school deciding whom to fund will favor students who can repay the fee or whose employers will, which means the highest-paid industry placements. Students headed to research, nonprofits, public agencies, clinics or startups lose first. That selection has nothing to do with fraud risk and everything to do with wealth and field, and because every student the rule reaches is a foreign national, it falls entirely along national-origin lines, a consequence the proposal does not analyze. Any school-side measure must come with published eligibility standards, a written decision and an administrative appeal; a fee with none of those is arbitrary and should be withdrawn.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed rule is arbitrary and should be withdrawn because it creates wealth-based selection.

comments.commentText:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) proposed rule to establish a $70,000 fee for F-1 nonimmigrant students seeking initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT periods, including the STEM OPT extension.

Sincerely,
Brandon Tran
Department of Statistics an Data Science
Yale University

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed OPT fees. I agree that any abuse of OPT should be found and penalized, but I don’t think this fee does that. In practice, it will remove OPT as an option for most students.

Most schools will not pay this fee, and most students or hiring companies cannot afford it either. So most students will simply stop applying for OPT. A fee like this doesn’t separate honest applicants from dishonest ones. It only separates people who can pay from people who can’t. DHS’s own analysis even expects schools to stop recommending non-STEM students completely, and it expects small schools to be hit very hard.

There is already a system in place to vet OPT. The school has to recommend the student, and USCIS reviews every application, which is not a quick or automatic process. During OPT, students have to keep reporting their employer, their address, and any changes to their school, which updates SEVIS. There is also a limit on how long they can be unemployed. STEM OPT has even more requirements, like the training plan signed by the employer, E-Verify, and site visits. The fraud cases mentioned in the proposal were found through this existing system, which shows it works. If DHS needs more resources, this fee won’t help, because the money goes to the Treasury and not to oversight.

The proposal talks about fraud cases but says nothing about the large number of students who follow every rule. Compared to everyone on OPT, the suspected cases are a small part. It is not fair to punish all students for the actions of a few.

It is also not clear how this fee was calculated or why this amount is reasonable. The proposal says it was set to be similar to the H-1B fee, but there is no explanation of why this amount is needed to stop fraud.

I also don’t agree that international students are taking jobs from American workers. The US job market is based on merit, not nationality, and salary depends on a person’s experience. Companies hire the people with the skills they need. Hiring someone less qualified just because they cost less would hurt the company, because it would need more time and resources to fix that person’s mistakes. In fact, international students already have a harder time finding jobs, because their work authorization lasts only a limited time. So when a company hires an international student anyway, it means they saw real potential in that person to help the company reach its goals. STEM OPT employers also already have to attest that the student’s pay and working conditions are comparable to those of similar American workers. The job market is also different for each major. The unemployment numbers in the proposal are about computer science and computer engineering, but the fee applies to every major the same way. That doesn’t make sense.

The proposal also says students use OPT as a way to get an H-1B visa. But H-1B is not automatic. A company has to sponsor the student, pay the fees, and pay at least the required wage, and the student still has to be selected in the lottery like everyone else. Even after being selected, approval is not guaranteed. The employer has to file a full petition with supporting documents, and USCIS reviews and vets it before deciding. OPT does not let anyone skip any of these steps. If a company decides to sponsor someone, it means that person has been contributing to the company and the company wants to keep them. That is good for the company and for the US work environment. If a student follows all the rules and goes through the legal H-1B process, I don’t see what the problem is. Using a legal path the way it was designed is not abuse.

Finally, I know OPT is not guaranteed, and students don’t expect it to be. They know they have to qualify and be approved. But they chose their programs knowing the rules and costs of OPT, and planned their education and finances around them. This rule doesn’t just change the rules. It adds a cost so high that OPT becomes impossible for most students, even those who follow every rule. Some students are already on OPT and planning to apply for STEM OPT, which their degree makes them eligible for. The transition plan protects their current OPT but not their STEM extension, and the proposal does not address this group. If any fee is adopted, it should apply only to students who have not started their program yet.

For the reasons above, I disagree with this proposed rule. Thank you for taking the time to read my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. The proposal would require a school to pay $70,000 to SEVP before recommending an F-1 student for Optional Practical Training (OPT) for the first time, and $30,000 for each later OPT recommendation. The rule's goal is to stop fraud, and that goal is legitimate. The fee does not serve it. The main reasons are:

1. **The fee lacks statutory authority.** DHS grounds the fee in INA § 214(a), which governs the "time and conditions" of admission. The rule itself concedes that ICE lacks legal authority to keep the money, which is why it goes to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt (p. 64576). A charge of roughly $12.4 billion a year that is not tied to any service and is not kept by the agency is a revenue measure, and Congress has not authorized one.
2. **The fee is not tied to the fraud it targets.** DHS identified fraud at a specific set of employers. The rule charges every student and every school, including the large majority who have no connection to that fraud.
3. **The record does not support the rule's own conclusions.** The benefits are not quantified, the opportunity-cost estimate is a proxy the agency admits may be wrong in either direction, and several figures are used in ways that do not support the claims built on them.
4. **The fee is designed to reduce OPT participation broadly.** The rule says it would "effectively eliminate" students from OPT and may "shut down the program entirely" (pp. 64572, 64574). That is a policy choice Congress has not made.

I would like to write to object to the proposed rule. I work in higher education and have witnessed thousands of international students graduate and apply for OPT. The vast majority of student are getting legitimate work experience in their fields. They later return home to build their careers or immigrate to the US and become valuable members of American society. It seems like the real motive behind this rule is to decrease international student numbers in the US and to discontinue work authorization for them, as well as to decrease legal immigration.

The rule also has flaws:

-It proposes to combat fraud. While some fraud may exist, slapping an outrageous fee on the benefit only serves to effectively end the OPT program. If the government’s intent is to combat fraud, USCIS and SEVP could implement measures that increase oversight, require additional documentation, verify employers, etc. Such improvements to the process and oversight better align with the intention of the rule than an exorbitant fee. DHS says it needs the fee to operate OPT and focus on preventing fraud. However, it does not describe how the exorbitant fee will go to preventing fraud. Also, with such an expensive fee, few, if any students will be able to do OPT. It is not ethical for the government to propose a rule that claims to tighten oversight of a program, when the real motive is to end it.
-It proposes to strengthen the integrity of the immigration system. But the fees go to the general fund, not the Department of Homeland Security
-It proposes to protect US workers. The rule says that fees will ensure only highly qualified F-1 students will participate in OPT. What is meant by “highly qualified”? Remember, a student doesn’t need a job offer to apply for OPT. So a student who has the means may be able to apply for OPT without the student being “highly qualified”. Does highly qualified mean the one with the most monetary resources? The proposed rule has to expand on this meaning so the public can understand how this fee ensures that only the “highly qualified” can do OPT.
-The fee is exorbitant. OPT only provides one year of work authorization to help the student gain experience, and the training can be paid or unpaid. It’s not like the student is given years and years of authorization and makes a six figure salary. The government could look into other, more reasonable options, like expanded use of SEVIS or perhaps the use of the I-983 training plan for the initial 12 months of OPT. Another example of how this fee doesn’t make sense, is that it also applies to pre-completion OPT which is done while the student is still enrolled in their program.

Instead of this fee, DHS could look into other, more reasonable options. These can include requiring a job offer in order to apply for OPT, require an employer to be E-Verified, like for STEM OPT, or require the employment to paid, instead of allowing unpaid positions. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
RE: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01 — Optional Practical Training Fees

To Whom It May Concern:

I write to strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee on schools recommending F-1 students for Optional Practical Training. This rule would inflict severe harm on U.S. businesses, weaken our innovation ecosystem, and undermine the national interest it purports to serve.

1. The Proposed Fees Would Devastate Employer Access to Critical Talent

American employers — from Fortune 500 companies to startups — rely on OPT as a vital pipeline for recruiting highly skilled graduates from U.S. universities. Companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta employ thousands of OPT participants driving breakthroughs in AI, cybersecurity, and biomedical research. These workers represent the top of a global talent funnel the United States has spent decades building.

By making OPT prohibitively expensive, this rule would choke off that pipeline. Schools unable to absorb six-figure fees per student would stop recommending OPT, and employers would lose access to graduates they have already invested in recruiting. The result is not protection for American workers — it is a self-inflicted talent shortage in sectors where the U.S. already faces critical workforce gaps.

2. OPT Strengthens — Not Weakens — the American Workforce

Research consistently shows that OPT participants complement rather than displace domestic workers. A 2023 Niskanen Center study found that increased OPT participation led to higher innovation levels without depressing wages or employment for Americans. The National Foundation for American Policy similarly found no evidence that OPT participants take jobs from U.S. workers.

The relationship is additive: regions with more OPT participants show greater patenting and economic activity. International students contribute nearly $43 billion annually to the U.S. economy, supporting hundreds of thousands of American jobs. Curtailing OPT does not create more jobs for Americans; it destroys them.

3. The Fee Structure Is Arbitrary and Disproportionate

DHS justifies the fee by claiming it should "closely align" with H-1B fees to prevent circumvention. This rationale is fundamentally flawed. OPT and H-1B are not substitutes — they operate in sequence. OPT is a temporary educational training period; the H-1B is a longer-term employment visa. Treating them as interchangeable ignores their distinct statutory purposes and penalizes students for following the lawful pathway Congress and DHS established.

A combined fee of up to $100,000 per student is wildly disproportionate to any legitimate regulatory cost. DHS has not demonstrated that fraud is so pervasive as to justify such fees, nor has it shown how these fees — which it admits would not fund additional enforcement — would meaningfully address identified problems.

4. This Rule Surrenders America's Competitive Advantage

The U.S. is in a global race for talent. Canada, the UK, Australia, and Germany have all expanded post-graduation work pathways to attract the students America now proposes to drive away. Eighty-six percent of prospective international students consider post-graduation work opportunities a decisive factor in choosing a university.

If finalized, this rule tells the world's brightest minds: the United States does not want you. They will go elsewhere — taking their talent, innovations, and future companies with them. The foreign-born STEM workforce contributed an estimated $367 to $409 billion in labor value added in 2019 alone. Voluntarily ceding this advantage serves no rational national interest.

5. The Costs Will Fall on Employers and Students

DHS acknowledges that schools may pass fees onto students or employers. Employers will face yet another cost barrier — on top of H-1B fees, legal expenses, and processing delays — to hiring talented graduates of American universities. Small and mid-size employers will be disproportionately harmed and may stop hiring international graduates altogether, concentrating talent in a handful of large corporations and stifling the entrepreneurial ecosystem that drives American innovation.

Conclusion

The OPT program is not a "back door" into the American workforce. It is the front door — a decades-old pathway connecting the best graduates of American universities with the employers who need them. This rule would slam that door shut, harming U.S. businesses, U.S. workers, and the U.S. economy.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed fee, arguing it harms U.S. businesses and creates talent shortages.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Brenna Connell
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I support the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT, including STEM extensions, to be paid by the SEVP-certified school before it recommends the student.

OPT has allowed hundreds of thousands of foreign nationals to enter the U.S. workforce instead of leaving the country after completing their degrees. Because the authorization is tied to the school’s recommendation rather than an employer petition and has historically carried only nominal processing costs, it functions as a cheap pathway into the U.S. labor market. The proposed fees will help correct this abuse of the American workforce. Schools that previously faced no consequences for recommending large numbers of foreign students will now face a substantial cost—$70,000 for the first period and an additional $30,000 for a STEM extension. These costs, to be paid by the institutions rather than the students or a specific employer, disincentivise the current abuse of the OPT program and create a direct incentive for colleges and universities to only back those students whose presence truly justifies the fees.

The fee amounts are justified by the scale of the program and the need to reduce abuse and fraud within the OPT program and other related visas. DHS has documented concerns about compliance and oversight. Requiring schools to pay the fees before the recommendation is entered in SEVIS, and conditioning USCIS employment authorization on that payment, disincentivizes reckless recommendations, and ties the institution’s financial interests to program integrity. Fees paid to the Treasury further support funding for oversight capacity that has not kept pace with application volume.

This change protects American workers and wages. By making this form of temporary foreign labor substantially more expensive, the rule reduces the volume of OPT participants undercutting U.S. citizens in the same fields. Schools that cannot or will not absorb the fee will recommend fewer students; those that pass costs onward will face market pressure that further limits participation. Either outcome narrows the gap between the cost of employing an OPT worker and the cost of employing a domestic graduate, supporting wage growth and hiring of U.S. workers. This step follows earlier adjustments to other temporary foreign-worker programs and applies a consistent principle: access to the U.S. labor market should not be subsidized by artificially low administrative costs.

I ask DHS to finalize the rule as proposed.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a United States citizen and an American, born and raised in this country, and I strongly support the proposed $70,000 fee for F-1 Optional Practical Training (OPT). However, my position goes further: I support substantially restricting the OPT program or even eliminating it entirely.

My support is rooted in three concerns: protecting employment opportunities for American graduates, discouraging employers from using immigration programs to obtain cheaper labor, and addressing what I see as an increasingly troubling lack of civic responsibility and willingness to assimilate among many recent immigrants.

First, American graduates deserve a fair opportunity to compete for jobs in their own country. American students and their families invest substantial amounts of money, time, and effort in higher education. It is reasonable to question whether the OPT program, particularly in highly competitive industries such as technology, creates incentives for employers to favor foreign graduates over American graduates.

I believe the federal government should examine whether existing employment and payroll-tax arrangements give employers financial reasons to prefer OPT workers. American graduates should not be disadvantaged by incentives created through federal immigration policy.

Second, immigration programs should not become a mechanism for reducing labor costs at the expense of American workers. If employers genuinely need specialized international talent, they should be prepared to demonstrate that need and bear the associated costs rather than relying on preferential financial arrangements.

Third, I have serious concerns about civic responsibility and assimilation. As a United States citizen who was born and raised here, I have personally observed behavior among many recent Indian immigrants who arrived in the United States over approximately the last seven to ten years that I consider inconsistent with basic expectations of civic responsibility, respect for shared public spaces, and assimilation into American society. Examples include leaving trash in shopping carts and failing to clean up after themselves in public areas.

These observations have shaped my views. I do not believe that individuals should be exempt from criticism because of their nationality, ethnicity, or immigration status. My intention is not to single out or generalize about any particular group, but rather to speak candidly about behaviors I have personally witnessed and the concerns those experiences have raised.

Immigration should involve more than access to economic opportunities. It should also involve respect for the country receiving immigrants, its laws, its communities, and its civic culture. I believe newcomers have a responsibility to make a genuine effort to integrate into American society rather than treating the United States solely as a place to advance their economic interests while disregarding American laws, civic responsibilities, community standards, and basic expectations of public conduct. Living and working in this country should come with an expectation of respect for the society, institutions, and communities that make those opportunities possible.

While OPT is an employment authorization program, its consequences extend beyond the labor market to broader questions of immigration policy, civic responsibility, community integration, and the long-term interests of American society. I believe these broader considerations deserve significant attention when evaluating whether the program continues to serve the public interest.

My position is not that immigrants should be judged solely by their country of origin. My position is that immigration policies should prioritize the interests of American citizens and workers, impose stricter financial requirements on employers and participants in employment-based immigration programs, and reinforce the principle that living and working in the United States carries responsibilities as well as opportunities.

For these reasons, I support the proposed $70,000 F-1 OPT fee as a potential restriction on the program, while emphasizing that my preferred long-term policy would be to severely limit OPT eligibility or discontinue the program altogether.

My concerns are not limited to the OPT program. They extend to the H-1B visa program and the H-4 dependent visa category as well. I am deeply concerned about reports of visa fraud, misuse of employment authorization, and exploitation of loopholes within these programs.

American workers and American citizens should come first. Access to American employment opportunities should not be treated as an entitlement.

So, DHS and ICE, I urge you to take immediate action to severely restrict or eliminate OPT, impose significant restrictions on the H-1B and H-4 visa programs, investigate credible allegations of fraud and abuse, hold violators accountable, and strictly enforce immigration laws without further delay.

comments.commentText:
The proposed rule presents serious questions concerning the scope of DHS's delegated authority and the reasonableness of the agency's decision-making.

The issue is not whether DHS has authority to administer the F-1 nonimmigrant classification, oversee SEVP-certified institutions, investigate fraud, or regulate practical training. It plainly possesses substantial authority in those areas.

The issue is whether those general authorities permit DHS to impose an extraordinary financial obligation on educational institutions as a prerequisite to recommending otherwise eligible F-1 students for OPT, when the amount is not tied to the costs of administering the program or to an identified compliance violation, and when DHS expressly intends to use the financial obligation to discourage participation in OPT and alter the economic relationship between OPT and the H-1B program.

The Department's own explanation establishes that the proposed charges are intended to operate as a substantial deterrent.

DHS acknowledges that the fees may be passed on to individual students, other students, or employers. It also acknowledges that the proposed structure will materially affect participation, but that the extent of the resulting reduction cannot be confidently predicted.

The Department has not adequately demonstrated that the particular amounts and payment triggers are authorized by Congress, reasonably connected to the statutory purpose of F-1 admission, or supported by a sufficiently reasoned explanation of their consequences.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee increases. These fees are excessive, unreasonable, and fundamentally unfair to international students who are already paying enormous amounts of money to pursue their education in the United States.

International students often pay significantly higher tuition rates, receive limited access to financial assistance, and contribute substantial amounts to American universities, local businesses, and the broader economy. Many have invested years of their lives and significant financial resources into obtaining an American education, following immigration regulations, and preparing to contribute their knowledge and skills to the U.S. workforce.

It is a long-established opportunity for eligible international students to gain practical experience directly related to the education they have already paid for. It is especially unjust to change the financial expectations surrounding practical training after students have already committed years of study and substantial tuition payments based on an established educational framework. Students who have followed the rules, maintained lawful immigration status, and invested in their futures should not suddenly face extraordinary financial barriers to obtaining legitimate professional experience.

These proposed fees appear grossly disproportionate to the administrative process involved in recommending practical training. Their magnitude raises serious concerns that they would discourage participation rather than simply recover legitimate administrative costs. Such an approach undermines fairness, educational opportunity, and the United States' ability to attract and retain talented, hardworking individuals.

International students should not be treated merely as sources of tuition revenue while being denied realistic opportunities to apply the education they have purchased. A system that welcomes their financial contributions but places unreasonable barriers in front of their professional development is neither fair nor sustainable.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw these proposed fees and preserve an accessible, reasonable, and transparent OPT process. Students who respect the law, invest in American education, and seek to contribute productively to American society deserve fair treatment, not punitive financial obstacles.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As an SVA community member, I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. I recognize DHS's responsibility to prevent fraud, protect U.S. workers, and maintain the integrity of the immigration system. However, fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for any subsequent recommendation are disproportionate to the misconduct they seek to prevent. They risk restricting legitimate educational and professional opportunities without proven effectiveness.

1. The fees are not a targeted response to fraud

The proposal aims to encourage schools to be more selective when recommending students for OPT (91 FR 64582). Yet the fee applies regardless of a school's compliance history, the employer, the position, or any evidence of misconduct. The initial payment is required before a school makes its first OPT recommendation, rather than being tied to a specific employer or job offer (91 FR 64577).

DHS cites cases involving shell companies, false employment records, and nonexistent worksites, including an investigation involving over 10,000 students employed by highly suspect employers (91 FR 64570-64571). These cases warrant enforcement, but do not establish that all OPT students and institutions pose comparable risks. A uniform fee penalizes legitimate participants alongside those involved in misconduct.

A more proportionate approach would address these vulnerabilities through employer verification, site visits, risk-based audits, improved data-sharing, and accountability for employers and institutions implicated in violations.

2. Existing oversight gaps call for targeted reforms

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) identified OPT oversight gaps. In 2014, it found that 38 percent of examined OPT records lacked an employer name, while ICE lacked sufficient information to assess consistently whether employment related to students' fields of study or complied with unemployment limits (GAO-14-356). In 2019, GAO recommended stronger fraud-risk controls and fraud-specific training for designated school officials (GAO-19-297).

These findings support complete employment records, employer and worksite verification, risk-based monitoring, and better training. A fee cannot establish whether a student is employed, whether a position relates to their studies, or whether an employer is legitimate. DHS should explain why these direct oversight measures are insufficient before imposing a blanket financial barrier.

3. The economic and educational consequences are substantial

DHS acknowledges that it cannot confidently predict how much the fees would reduce OPT participation (91 FR 64582-64583). Its analysis estimates annualized costs of $32 million to $8.2 billion, with a primary estimate of $4.1 billion and a ten-year estimate of $35.1 billion (91 FR 64579). It also recognizes potential losses in student earnings and work experience, employer productivity, and institutional enrollment (91 FR 64588-64589).

The proposal particularly disadvantages non-STEM students. DHS's low-participation scenario anticipates that institutions may be less willing to pay $70,000 for students eligible for only one year of OPT than for students who may qualify for a STEM extension (91 FR 64582-64583). This disadvantages legitimate fields without that extension. The arts and cultural sector contributed $1.17 trillion, or 4.2 percent of U.S. GDP, in 2023. NAFSA estimated that international students generated $42.9 billion in economic activity and supported over 355,000 jobs in 2024-2025.

As an SVA community member, I have seen international students enrich educational environments through the exchange of ideas and practices. Post-graduation professional experience is an important part of studying in the United States. Making OPT financially inaccessible risks weakening the link between education and professional development and discouraging emerging international talent from choosing the United States.

Conclusion

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue targeted, evidence-based oversight. Reforms should distinguish legitimate participation from documented misconduct, strengthen employer verification and institutional accountability, and assess effects on students, schools, and U.S. employers. Protecting OPT's integrity should not require a prohibitive financial barrier for those participating lawfully.

References
DHS, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (2026).
GAO, GAO-14-356 (2014).
GAO, GAO-19-297 (2019).
BEA, Arts and Cultural Production Satellite Account, 2023 (2025).
NAFSA, International Students Contributed $43 Billion to the U.S. Economy in 2024-2025 (2025).
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are disproportionate and penalize legitimate participants.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a US citizen and student in year 6 of a 6-year PhD program at Yale University. I respectfully oppose the proposed fee and ask DHS to withdraw it, for the reasons below.

1. The rule says OPT has become "a channel ... to circumvent employment visa caps" (64573). Universities, nonprofit research institutes and government research labs are H-1B cap-exempt (8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)); they can file at any time of year, so there is no cap to circumvent and no
lottery to avoid. A university paying $70,000 so its own graduate can take a postdoctoral position in its own laboratory is a transfer from research funds to the Treasury with no integrity effect. DHS should exempt employment with H-1B cap-exempt institutions, along with pre-completion OPT and doctoral graduates, from any measure it adopts, and should explain in the final rule how the circumvention theory applies to employers who face no cap.

2. The transition rule protects only students who already hold a DSO recommendation on the effective date (64577-64578). A student in the first year of a multi-year program has years of reliance and none of it is protected; footnote 124 concedes current students "are in a different position" and then offers them nothing. The alternative DHS "especially encourages" comment on, charging $70,000 again at each degree level (64577), would charge a student who completed a bachelor's, a master's and a PhD in the United States three times, with no connection to any fraud theory in the rule. DHS should reject the degree-level alternative and grandfather every student enrolled in a U.S. program on the effective date.

3. Every example in Section IV.A is an IT consulting or staffing worksite. DHS offers no instance of a PhD graduate, a postdoctoral researcher or a research university involved in OPT fraud. A fee that does not distinguish a national-laboratory postdoc from a "phantom employee" at a residential address (64571) is not "targeted" (64576). At minimum, DHS should exempt doctoral graduates, pre-completion OPT and employment with H-1B cap-exempt institutions, and grandfather every student enrolled on the effective date.

I ask DHS to respond on the record to each alternative proposed by commenters, as the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 603(c)) and Executive Order 12866 section 1(b)(8) require.

As an alternative, I suggest: Match SEVIS employer names and EINs against IRS and state business registrations and hold any
employer with no filings. Shell companies with "no employees present" and "missing employment records" (64571) fail this check at no cost to students or schools. Or: Replace the fee with a wage rule: require every OPT employer to attest to paying the actual or prevailing wage for similarly situated U.S. workers, as STEM OPT employers already must on Form I-983 (64570), with referral to the Department of Labor for violations. This addresses
"depressed wages" (64574) directly; a fee passed to the student lowers the student's pay and makes the problem worse.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee. Any integrity measure that follows should act on employers, where the evidence of abuse lies; should rest on a cost basis if it takes the form of a fee; should exempt pre-completion OPT, doctoral graduates and employment with H-1B cap-exempt institutions; and should protect every student enrolled on the effective date. Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed fee and asks DHS to withdraw it, citing negative impacts on research.
