comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100: Comment in Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

Hello, I am an American citizen and student at a prestigious American university. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS not to finalize this rule for the following reasons:

1.DHS claims that the OPT fees will combat fraud but fails to explain how a universally applied $70,000 fee discriminates against bad actors from qualified students. DHS describes fraud associated with shell employers, fake worksites, and OPT used as an "informal and unlimited employment benefit" (Section IV.A). However, the fee applies identically to all F-1 students recommended for OPT, including those seeking legitimate jobs related to their field of study. The fee does not identify or penalize bad actors. DHS argues that a financial commitment makes abuse "less attractive to bad actors" (Section IV.C), but the rule also makes OPT significantly less attractive for highly qualified and bright international students. Instead, the fee is likely to deter far more legitimate candidates from applying for OPT, rather than preventing fraud operations from bad actors who can afford it.

2.The rule does not factor in costs to students, employers, and universities. DHS estimates fee payments of $8.41 billion to $16.48 billion per year after the transition period (Section VII.A.5.c). The rule also states that they "cannot precisely quantify opportunity costs" due to "limited data on the value placed on OPT," (Section VII.A.5.b). DHS should not impose unreasonably high costs on a program without any comprehensive data or cost-benefit analysis of the program’s economic benefit. There is no question that international students have contributed a great deal to the American economy through employment and innovation over the past several decades. DHS lacks a comprehensive analysis on how the benefits of potential fraud reduction offset the economic losses caused by deterring talented international students from studying and working in the US. Further, American universities will lose revenue and competitiveness from talented international students who choose to study and work in other countries. DHS must measure the negative impacts on U.S. businesses, on university enrollment, and on research and innovation.

3.DHS dismisses fraud enforcement alternatives without showing how a one-time fee supposedly accomplishes more. DHS considered site visits and increased reporting requirements and rejected them for being too complex and costly. They concluded that "Solutions requiring self-attestations, reporting, or reliance on an honor system, without more, are insufficient" (Section IV.C). The rule does not explain how a one-time fee verifies the legitimacy of employment with a legitimate employer. DHS also states that without the fees DHS "cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud" (Section IV.A). However, a thorough analysis of the practical costs of fraud enforcement is missing.

4.DHS cannot use revenue from the proposed fees to combat fraud. The rule explicitly states that fees "would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt", and that the funds are "not specifically earmarked for ICE SEVP or immigration enforcement activities" (Section IV.C). Therefore, DHS cannot rely on this revenue to pay for investigations and additional reporting requirements that could be used to identify fraud. If DHS's goal is to prevent fraud, they must explain how a fraud prevention program would be funded without revenues from the proposed fees.

Considering the above points, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rules under Docket ICEB-2026-0100. Instead, DHS should conduct a thorough analysis on how fraud associated with the OPT program can be prevented without causing economic losses and negatively impacting honest students seeking legitimate employment through OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they deter legitimate students and fail to combat fraud effectively.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student who recently completed a PhD in computer science in the United States after seven years of study. My Optional Practical Training application is currently pending with USCIS, and I have accepted a software engineering position. My wife is also an F-1 PhD student who will need OPT. I write to oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT.

A fee of this size is not an administrative charge; it is a ban by another name. No university can pay $70,000 for every international student it recommends for OPT. Schools will stop recommending OPT, or will recommend it only for a small number of students. The students hurt most will be those at smaller schools and those from less wealthy backgrounds — exactly the people OPT was meant to give a fair chance.

The United States trained me. My research, my degree, and my job all exist because American universities admitted me and American employers want to hire me. OPT is the bridge between that education and that work. If this fee takes effect, graduates like me will take our training to Canada, Europe, or back home instead. That does not protect American workers; it hands American-trained talent to America's competitors.

The rule says the fee is paid by schools, not students, but that distinction will not survive contact with reality. Schools will pass the cost to students, raise tuition, or stop offering OPT recommendations. Either way, the student pays — with money or with the loss of the opportunity itself.

DHS states the fee will combat fraud and protect U.S. workers, but the proposal does not show that a $70,000 fee is calibrated to the actual cost of administering OPT, nor that it targets actual fraud. The agency estimates $8.7 to $16.9 billion in annual transfers under this rule — an extraordinary burden to place on universities and students without evidence that it addresses a real problem at anywhere near that scale.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. If a fee is needed, it should reflect the actual administrative cost of processing an OPT recommendation, not a sum designed to end the program.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessively high, function as a ban, and harm students and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Washington State University
comments.commentText:
See attached letter.
On behalf of Washington State University (WSU). I write to express our strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed $70,000 Optional Practical Training (OPT) application fee and $30,000 renewal fee. These unprecedented costs would create significant barriers for international students and damage America's higher education, research, and workforce development systems.
OPT is a longstanding component of the F-1 student program that allows international graduates to apply their academic training in professional settings while contributing to the U.S. economy. The proposed fee structure transforms this opportunity into an unattainable burden for most students and would significantly diminish the attractiveness of the United States as a destination for global talent.
For public land-grant universities such as WSU, the impact would be particularly severe. International student enrollment is already challenged by visa denials, SEVIS terminations, and global instability. The opportunity to gain professional experience through OPT remains one of the strongest incentives for international students to study in the United States. Eliminating practical access to OPT would further hinder recruitment and enrollment efforts at institutions across the country.
The consequences would extend far beyond campus boundaries. According to NAFSA data, international students at WSU contributed approximately $47.2 million to Washington's economy and supported more than 400 jobs during the 2024-25 academic year. Reductions in international enrollment would negatively affect local communities, employers, and state economies while diminishing America's ability to attract and retain highly skilled talent.
International students also play a critical role in graduate education and federally funded research. At WSU, they serve as teaching assistants, researchers, and innovators who support instruction and advance scientific discovery in fields including agriculture, engineering, health sciences, veterinary medicine, and emerging technologies. Policies that discourage talented students from studying and working in the United States will weaken research capacity, reduce innovation, and undermine U.S. competitiveness.
For these reasons, WSU strongly urges the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the accessibility and effectiveness of the OPT program.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create barriers and damage education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 additional OPT fee. I think this proposal is not only unreasonable for students, but also very harmful to small businesses and startups in the United States.

Many people think about large technology companies when discussing international graduates, but there are also many small companies, research labs, and startups that need young talented workers. These organizations usually have limited budget and cannot afford to pay such expensive fees. If this proposal becomes a rule, many small businesses may simply stop considering international graduates, even when they are the best candidates for the job.

This will create an unfair situation in the American job market. Large companies may have more financial resources to deal with these costs, while smaller companies will lose access to talented graduates. I don't think a government policy should make it even harder for small businesses to compete with large corporations.

Also, many startups are created by university graduates who have new ideas and want to build something useful. Practical work experience is an important part of learning how to turn these ideas into real products. If students cannot afford OPT, some of these ideas may never become businesses in the US. This means less innovation, less opportunities for new companies, and potentially fewer jobs created in the future.

What concerns me most is that these fees do not seem connected to the actual cost of providing OPT. Charging $70,000 for an educational training recommendation is extremely excessive. It does not make sense to place such a huge financial barrier on people who already completed their education in American universities.

I believe the US should encourage innovation and fair competition, instead of creating policies that only wealthy individuals and large companies can afford. This proposal may end up hurting the same American businesses and economic growth that the government should be protecting.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule entirely. These fees should not be implemented because the long-term damage to American small businesses, innovation, and job creation could be much greater than any expected benefit.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are unreasonable and will harm small businesses, startups, and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Hispanic Neuropsychological Society
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

The Hispanic Neuropsychological Society Executive Committee respectfully opposes the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation.

We believe that the proposed fees will have a negative impact on our field. Clinical neuropsychology requires extensive specialized training, including two-year postdoctoral fellowships after doctoral education, to prepare highly skilled neuropsychologists for the workforce. OPT is a key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships. The proposed fees would place substantial financial burdens on institutions that could employ international trainees, severely restricting access to this training. Programs could respond by eliminating fellowship positions or excluding otherwise qualified candidates.

The consequences would extend beyond individual trainees. Collaborations with international professionals contribute to U.S. clinical care and research, bringing expertise in brain–behavior relationships and linguistic and cultural considerations that strengthens neuropsychological assessment, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training could undermine workforce development and reduce the availability of clinicians and researchers equipped to advance the field and meet the needs of the U.S. population.

The Executive Board of the Hispanic Neuropsychological Society urges DHS to 1. reconsider the proposed fee structure; 2. Provide a transparent justification for the proposed amounts; and explore less burdensome alternatives that maintain appropriate oversight without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.

Thank you for considering our comments.

Executive Board
Hispanic Neuropsychological Society
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees place a heavy financial burden and harm workforce development.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 | Optional Practical Training Fees

To the Department of Homeland Security,

I am a domestic PhD student at Yale University, where I work on political economy. I am writing in my personal capacity to oppose the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

Under section V.A, a school would have to pay $70,000 before it could recommend an F-1 student for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation after the initial fee has been paid. A university making 100 initial recommendations would face $7 million in new charges. DHS acknowledges in section IV.C that schools could pass those costs on to students or employers. Schools with limited budgets could also decline to recommend otherwise eligible students. In practice, access to training would depend heavily on who can come up with the money and who cannot. This produces structural unfairness.

That would affect my education at Yale. My research examines how economic interests shape public policy and whose interests governments represent. An explanation for why some groups have more influence than others might make sense in the United States. In seminars, international colleagues bring knowledge of political institutions and histories that helps bolster the accuracy of the work I am to produce. If uncertainty about access to practical training leads some prospective students to pursue their degrees elsewhere, domestic students like me will lose opportunities to learn from and collaborate with them.

DHS argues in section IV.C that the fees would make schools scrutinize OPT recommendations more closely. The ability to raise $70,000 is a poor test of whether a placement offers legitimate training. For example, consider a graduate offered a position at a small nonprofit research center evaluating how changes in labor policy affect workers. The placement would give the graduate a chance to apply their research skills to an important public policy question, yet it could break down simply because the school and the center cannot cover the fee. DHS should address fraud and protect workers through targeted audits of schools and employers, checks that students’ work relates to their degrees, and enforcement of applicable wage and training requirements.

The proposed 60-day transition in sections V.C and VI also gives little to no weight to students who chose their programs years ago with OPT available and are now approaching graduation. If DHS proceeds with either fee, it needs to exempt students who are already enrolled or participating in OPT when the final rule takes effect.

I urge DHS to withdraw both proposed fees. Students who qualify for practical training should have a meaningful chance to pursue it, including at universities and employers with limited resources. Lacking financial support should not be a barrier for students.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I submit this comment as someone who has worked in international education. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. A $70,000 charge on a student's first OPT recommendation, followed by $30,000 for each later recommendation, including the STEM extension, would end OPT for nearly every student while leaving the program on the books.

The rule places the fee on the school and lets the school pass it to the student or an employer. No school can absorb it across the roughly 194,000 F-1 students who reported OPT employment in 2024, and few students can pay it themselves. Employers are the party most often assumed to bear the cost, but the timing of the rule works against that assumption: the DSO recommendation comes before the student files Form I-765, and a student does not need a job offer to apply for post-completion OPT, so at the moment the fee is due there is often no employer to pay it. Where an employer does exist, a firm hiring a recent graduate at an entry-level salary has no reason to add $70,000, or $100,000 with a STEM extension, to the cost of that hire. It will hire someone else, or hire the same graduate later in Toronto or London.

DHS justifies the fees as a means to combat fraud and protect U.S. workers. Fraud in OPT reporting is a real problem, and DHS is right to pursue it. A flat charge, however, cannot tell a sham employer from a legitimate one; it falls equally on the engineering graduate hired by a manufacturer and on the student reporting work for a shell company. DHS already holds targeted tools in SEVIS employer reporting and in the STEM OPT training plan and its site visit authority. NAFSA's November 3 comment letter makes this point: DHS should use SEVIS data more effectively and pursue enforcement aimed at demonstrated noncompliance. The fees would not even fund that enforcement, since the receipts would go to the Treasury rather than to SEVP. On worker protection, research by Madeline Zavodny and by the Niskanen Center has not found that international STEM graduates reduce employment for U.S. workers. As NAFSA's chief executive, Fanta Aw, stated on October 7, international students "don't take opportunities from Americans, they create them."

Post-study work authorization is part of what a prospective student weighs when choosing where to study, and competing destinations, including Canada and the United Kingdom, offer it. The students this rule would turn away are the ones the United States has the strongest interest in keeping: graduate students in STEM fields who move from OPT into American research labs and companies. Graduate engineering and computer science programs depend on international enrollment to fill research assistantships and to sustain course sections that domestic students also take. A rule that closes the main route from a U.S. degree to U.S. work experience will reduce applications, and the cost will fall on universities and on the domestic students they serve.

The NPRM states that DHS may end OPT absent the fees. A fee set at this level reaches that same result without the reasoned analysis that an outright termination would require. NAFSA also questions whether DHS has statutory authority to impose charges that bear no demonstrated relationship to the cost of administering or enforcing the program. I share that concern. A charge designed to suppress lawful activity functions as a tax, and Congress has not authorized DHS to tax OPT.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If the agency has evidence of specific fraud patterns, it should publish that evidence and propose measures aimed at those patterns.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule due to the excessive fee amounts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

The existing grace period provides an essential safeguard for skilled professionals who lose their jobs due to layoffs, corporate restructuring, or other circumstances beyond their control. Eliminating this protection would create unnecessary hardship and uncertainty for workers who have complied with U.S. immigration laws.

Finding new employment and completing the immigration transfer process requires time. Even when an employer is ready to hire, immigration filings involve legal preparation, administrative procedures, and coordination among multiple parties. Removing the grace period would make it significantly harder for qualified workers to transition between employers through no fault of their own.

This proposal would also negatively affect U.S. businesses by reducing their ability to recruit experienced international talent already residing in the country. It could discourage skilled professionals from pursuing long-term careers in the United States, weakening the nation’s global competitiveness.

The current 60-day grace period is a reasonable and limited protection, not an indefinite extension of immigration status. It recognizes the practical realities of employment transitions while maintaining immigration compliance.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period. Immigration policy should promote fairness, economic stability, and the retention of skilled talent rather than impose disproportionate consequences on workers facing unexpected job loss.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes eliminating the grace period and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule establishing $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees for each F-1 nonimmigrant student recommended for OPT through a Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP)-certified educational institution.

The proposed rule should be withdrawn. Alternatively, DHS should substantially revise the proposal, publish a supplemental regulatory and economic analysis addressing the material deficiencies identified below, and provide a meaningful opportunity for public comment before taking final action.

The concerns are not limited to the dollar amount. The proposed rule creates a mandatory financial condition on an educational institution, makes payment a prerequisite to entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS, and prohibits USCIS from granting employment authorization when the required payment has not been made.

The proposed financial obligations are not calculated by reference to the actual cost of processing an OPT recommendation, a demonstrated compliance violation, or an identified risk associated with a particular employer or institution.

Instead, DHS expressly states that it selected the initial fee to align with H-1B program fees, in part to discourage students and employers from using OPT to avoid H-1B program fees.

DHS further acknowledges that the receipts will be deposited into the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, that ICE cannot retain or use the funds for OPT administration under the authority it invokes, and that the deterrent effect is intended to operate regardless of whether Congress subsequently appropriates the money for immigration enforcement.

The agency's stated objectives include fraud prevention, program integrity, and protection of U.S. workers. Those are legitimate regulatory objectives. However, the existence of a legitimate objective does not establish that the particular financial condition proposed is authorized by Congress, reasonably related to the statutory purpose of F-1 admission, or supported by a sufficiently reasoned administrative record.

The proposed rule raises substantial issues under the Immigration and Nationality Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, the Regulatory Flexibility Act, and the requirements governing federal information systems.

Full Comment attached.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessively high and urges withdrawal of the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sakthivel Rajaram
comments.commentText:
As a parent of a student pursuing higher education in the United States, I strongly oppose the proposed excessive fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT\.

My child came to the United States as an H\-4 dependent and has since transitioned to F\-1 student status to pursue higher education\. Our family has invested significant time, effort, and financial resources in supporting his educational journey\. His long\-term goal is to pursue a career in medicine and contribute to the healthcare profession in the United States\.

Like many other families, we believe in the opportunities provided by American education\. We have made considerable sacrifices to help our child build a future through education, hard work, and professional development\.

OPT and STEM OPT are important pathways that allow international graduates to gain practical experience in their respective fields\. These opportunities are particularly valuable for students pursuing science, technology, healthcare\-related research, and other specialized professions\.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee would create an unreasonable financial burden on educational institutions, employers, and ultimately international students and their families\.

I am particularly concerned about the following impacts:

1. **Financial burden on families:** Families already pay substantial tuition and living expenses\. Excessive OPT fees could make it financially impossible for deserving students to continue their professional journeys\.
2. **Impact on future healthcare professionals:** Students pursuing medicine and healthcare\-related careers require opportunities to gain practical experience, participate in research, and develop their professional skills\.
3. **Uncertainty for international students:** Students and families make long\-term educational and career plans based on existing immigration pathways\. Significant financial barriers could disrupt these plans\.
4. **Loss of global talent:** The United States benefits from attracting talented students who can contribute to healthcare, scientific research, technology, and innovation\.
5. **Impact on American competitiveness:** Unreasonable restrictions could encourage talented international students to pursue their education and careers in other countries\.

I fully support the government’s responsibility to maintain the integrity of immigration programs and prevent fraud\. However, these objectives should be achieved through reasonable compliance measures rather than excessive financial barriers that disproportionately affect legitimate students and their families\.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider and withdraw the proposed OPT and STEM OPT fees and preserve reasonable access to practical training opportunities for eligible international graduates\.

As a parent, I want my child and other international students to have a fair opportunity to complete their education, pursue their professional ambitions, and contribute positively to American society\.

**Please ensure that the United States remains a country where education, dedication, talent, and hard work are rewarded rather than limited by excessive financial barriers\.**

Thank you for considering my comments\.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing in my personal capacity to express my strong concerns about the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations.

For the past two years, I have served as a Designated School Official (DSO), working directly with international students as they navigate their education and the responsibilities of maintaining F-1 status. I take seriously my responsibility to protect the integrity of the F-1 program, support institutional compliance, and help students understand their obligations. I also see firsthand the knowledge, experiences, and perspectives international students contribute to our campuses and communities.

I firmly believe that regulatory integrity and educational opportunity should reinforce one another, not be treated as opposing goals.

What concerns me most is the proposal's approach to addressing fraud and institutional oversight. If DHS has identified SEVP-certified institutions that have failed to meet their responsibilities, those institutions should be held accountable through targeted monitoring and enforcement. Why should institutions fulfilling their regulatory obligations face extraordinary financial burdens because oversight may have been inadequate elsewhere? Broad financial deterrents should not replace evidence-based accountability.

As a DSO, I know that compliance requires ongoing education, professional judgment, and careful advising. Requiring DSOs to verify payment before entering OPT recommendations in SEVIS adds another administrative responsibility without clearly demonstrating how it will improve oversight. I also question how these substantial fees were determined, where the revenue will go, and what evidence supports their effectiveness in reducing fraud.

Beyond these regulatory concerns, I believe deeply in the importance of connecting theory with practice. Education should not end at the classroom door. Practical training allows students to apply their knowledge, develop professional competencies, and contribute meaningfully to their fields. The National Association of Colleges and Employers (NACE) identifies communication, critical thinking, teamwork, and professionalism as essential career-readiness competencies. These opportunities should be accessible to all eligible students, including those studying on F-1 visas.

I also believe the benefits are reciprocal. International students bring cultural perspectives, experiences, and approaches to problem-solving into American workplaces while learning from their colleagues and professional environments. Everyone has something to contribute, and everyone has something to learn. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2015) recognizes integration as a reciprocal process, while the Institute of International Education's Open Doors research documents international students' substantial contributions to American higher education.

At a time when we emphasize preparing students for a globally connected workforce, I find it counterproductive to create barriers that could restrict these valuable experiences. American students, colleagues, employers, and communities also benefit from intercultural collaboration. These competencies are increasingly imperative, not optional.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fees and prioritize transparent, proportionate, and evidence-based oversight that holds noncompliant institutions accountable without penalizing those meeting their responsibilities. We can protect the integrity of the F-1 program while preserving meaningful educational opportunities. Doing so strengthens our students, institutions, workforce, and communities.

References: NACE, Career Readiness Competencies (naceweb.org); National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2015), The Integration of Immigrants into American Society (doi.org/10.17226/21746); Institute of International Education, Open Doors (opendoorsdata.org).

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 / RIN 1653-AB01

I am writing on behalf of an international legal professional and prospective judicial clerk to a United States District Judge impacted by the proposed rule. I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees NPRM in its entirety.

First, the proposed $70,000 initial charge and $30,000 subsequent fee function as an unauthorized tax rather than a permissible user fee or regulatory charge. The exaction is not tied to agency adjudication costs, provides no service to universities, and routes unearmarked proceeds directly into the general U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. § 3302—violating the separation of powers and exceeding ICE's statutory authority under INA § 214(a), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a). This structure replicates the exact legal flaws identified in recent federal court vacaturs of similar executive exactions (California v. Mullin).

Second, the rule is arbitrary and capricious under the APA (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)). DHS fails to quantify purported benefits, relies on inflated and methodologically flawed fraud figures, targets universities rather than the bad-actor employers committing alleged fraud, and ignores overwhelming empirical economic evidence (such as research by Dr. Madeline Zavodny and Dr. Michael Clemens) establishing that OPT strengthens the U.S. labor market and economy without displacing native workers. Furthermore, the rule inflicts catastrophic net-margin losses on higher education and destroys master's and professional degree pathways—including international J.D. graduates seeking to complete federal judicial clerkships—without statutory authorization or reasoned consideration of reliance interests.

At a minimum, DHS must extend the truncated 30-day comment period, exempt U.S. government and judicial employment, grandfather students enrolled prior to the rule's effective date, and establish objective, appealable refund standards.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sam F
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. While protecting American workers and preventing fraud are legitimate objectives, these extraordinary fees would impose substantial economic burdens without sufficient evidence that they are necessary, proportionate, or effective.

1. Economic costs outweigh unproven benefits

DHS’s regulatory impact analysis estimates approximately $12.8 billion in annualized transfers and $4.1 billion in annualized economic costs under its primary scenario. Transferring billions of dollars from educational institutions to the federal government does not create equivalent economic growth or productivity.

DHS has not adequately demonstrated that the proposed fees would generate benefits sufficient to justify these costs. Such a consequential policy requires stronger empirical evidence and a transparent cost-benefit analysis.

2. Fees disconnected from administrative costs

A $70,000 fee is 140 times a $500 application fee. The proposed payments would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than directly funding OPT processing or fraud investigations.

If stronger oversight is the objective, DHS should identify actual enforcement costs and establish proportionate fees. Without a demonstrated relationship between the amounts charged and the intended benefits, these fees function primarily as financial barriers.

3. Harm to American jobs and local economies

According to NAFSA, international students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 American jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year.

NAFSA also reported a 17% decline in new international student enrollment in fall 2025, associated with an estimated $1.1 billion reduction in economic contributions and nearly 23,000 jobs lost or not supported.

These figures do not prove that OPT fees would cause equivalent losses. However, they demonstrate the economic importance of international education. DHS should assess whether additional financial barriers would discourage enrollment, reduce university revenue, and harm American businesses.

4. Disproportionate burden on small businesses

Small American businesses and startups often cannot absorb expenses that large corporations can.

Consider a small employer hiring a STEM graduate at a $60,000 annual salary. A $70,000 OPT fee would exceed that employee’s annual salary. Combined with a subsequent $30,000 fee, the total would equal approximately 167% of annual salary.

This hypothetical example illustrates how the proposal could make hiring international graduates financially impractical for smaller employers, concentrating access to talent among large corporations and weakening competition.

5. Damage to American technological competitiveness

According to data summarized by The Conference Board, temporary visa holders earned approximately 61% of U.S. research doctorates in computer and information sciences, 54% in engineering, and 51% in mathematics and statistics in 2024.

Imposing extraordinary costs on practical training could push talented graduates toward competing countries. America risks educating highly skilled individuals while losing their future contributions to innovation and economic growth.

6. Insufficient evidence of fraud prevention

The proposal does not adequately explain why these fee amounts would prevent fraud or protect American workers. Compliant students with legitimate employment would face substantial burdens regardless of their individual risk.

Targeted employer audits, improved SEVIS reporting, risk-based compliance reviews, and stronger enforcement against fraudulent arrangements would address misconduct more directly.

DHS should explain why these less burdensome alternatives would be insufficient.

7. Unfair treatment of existing OPT participants

Students already participating in post-completion OPT made educational, financial, and employment decisions under the existing regulatory framework.

Imposing a $70,000 fee on an existing OPT participant seeking a STEM OPT extension would create an extraordinary and unforeseeable burden.

DHS should explicitly grandfather existing OPT participants, allowing them to pursue otherwise eligible STEM OPT extensions under the fee framework in effect when their initial OPT authorization was granted.

At minimum, DHS must establish clear transition provisions and protect individuals whose eligibility dates depend on previously issued employment authorization.

The proposed fees threaten American competitiveness, impose disproportionate costs on universities and small businesses, and create serious fairness concerns without adequately demonstrated benefits.

Fraud prevention and worker protection should rely on targeted, evidence-based enforcement rather than extraordinary financial barriers.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and develop a more proportionate, economically justified approach.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees are excessively burdensome, disproportionate, and economically harmful.

Back in July, the report on the White House’s proposed 2027 DHS budget began by stating that “[the] DHS is the third largest agency in the federal government in terms of civilian personnel”. It seems hard to imagine that, if the threat of widespread fraud in the OPT program is really serious enough, additional money could not be diverted from the department’s other activities to help with the increasing need.
The Department of Homeland Security has done a good job of defining the legal parameters of the program, meaning that it will not be difficult to detect violations of the rules after due investigation. Simply imposing steep fees on any applicants, however, is a blunt instrument at best. All students, whether or not they have any intention of breaking the law, will be penalized in exactly the same way. There is no way to make distinctions between those who have, or have not, displayed their willingness to obey our nation’s laws. Rather, our immigration system should reward such loyalty. Many of my age-peers seem not to care or even know, and if they don’t meet someone like my friend it’s harder to wake them up to the scary reality.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student in the third year of my PhD.

I oppose the proposed fee and ask DHS to withdraw it, for the reasons stated here:

According to DHS, the rule “does not need to define which OPT experiences provide genuine educational value,” and schools are expected to recommend only “the most promising students” (64574-64575). Existing regulations give a DSO no authority to rank students by promise; the DSO’s role is to confirm eligibility. The rule thus invents a merit gate, entrusts it to more than 2,000 institutions, and provides no standard for applying it. Money will become the standard by default. A school choosing whom to fund will prefer students who can repay the fee, or whose employers will, and those are the students with the highest-paid industry placements. The first to lose out will be students bound for research, nonprofits, public agencies, clinics or startups. Selection of that kind tracks wealth and field, not fraud risk. And since every student the rule covers is a foreign national, its burden falls wholly along national-origin lines, an effect the proposal never analyzes. Any measure administered by schools needs published eligibility standards, a written decision and an administrative appeal. A fee lacking all three is arbitrary and should be withdrawn.

DHS asserts that the comment period and delayed effective date allow students “ample time ... to apply for a change of status, depart the United States, or make any other necessary arrangements” (64578). This concedes that the rule is expected to drive out students who have violated no rule, and it cannot be squared with the claim that the fee ensures “legitimate participants continue to benefit from its opportunities” (64576). DHS should say how many lawful students it expects to leave and include that loss in its analysis. A rule whose expected effect is the departure of compliant participants should be withdrawn.

The amount has no cost basis. DHS says only that the figure was chosen to be “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” and to deter use (64575). Under the general fee statute, 31 U.S.C. 9701, agency charges must be based on the cost to the government and the value of the service to the recipient. The Supreme Court has held that this statute authorizes a fee, not a tax, because taxation is a legislative function (National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). The only fee Congress has authorized for F-1 students, the SEVIS fee, must be “based on” the cost per alien (8 U.S.C. 1372(e)). The H-1B payment that DHS treats as its benchmark was vacated as a tax by a federal court in June 2026, a ruling the rule does not mention. DHS should address that decision and explain how a general-fund receipt backed by no service satisfies 31 U.S.C. 9701. Any fee that survives should be cost-based, set by a published cost study of SEVP’s OPT oversight, collected with Form I-765, and retained for enforcement, as the SEVIS fee is.

DHS explains that the fee operates by making participation “less attractive to bad actors” and by establishing “a tangible stake” that distinguishes lawful participants from those “who may seek to exploit the program” (64576). A charge meant to punish or deter conduct is a sanction. Agencies may impose civil penalties only where a statute provides for them, and only through the process that statute specifies. The rule cites no penalty provision. DHS should identify one or withdraw the fee.

So that the public can verify the figures, I ask DHS to release the data underlying Tables 2-17, which appear only as images, along with the per-institution fee analysis the rule says it ran in Python (64593-64594).

I also ask DHS to respond on the record to each alternative that commenters propose, as required by the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 603(c)) and Executive Order 12866 section 1(b)(8).

As an alternative to the proposed fee, DHS could compare SEVIS employer names and EINs against IRS and state business registrations and place a hold on any employer with no filings. Shell companies with “no employees present” and “missing employment records” (64571) would fail that check, and neither students nor schools would bear any cost.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee. Any integrity measure that follows should:

1) target employers, where the evidence of abuse lies;
2) rest on a cost basis if it takes the form of a fee;
3) exempt pre-completion OPT, doctoral graduates and employment with H-1B cap-exempt institutions; and
4) protect every student enrolled on the effective date.

Thank you.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Congress authorized DHS to administer the F-1 nonimmigrant program, regulate practical training, and administer immigration-related fees within statutory limits. Congress did not clearly authorize ICE to impose a $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent financial exaction on educational institutions as a mechanism to discourage participation in OPT, effectively determining access to employment authorization through an unprecedented economic barrier.

The NPRM identifies three principal sources of authority:
6 U.S.C. § 112 — general DHS authority.
8 U.S.C. § 1103(a)(1), (3) — administration and enforcement of immigration laws.
8 U.S.C. § 1184(a) — authority to prescribe conditions governing nonimmigrant admission.

The problem is that these provisions do not expressly establish an OPT fee, authorize ICE to impose a $70,000 institutional payment obligation, or authorize the agency to use a financial deterrent to restructure the economics of the F-1 employment system. DHS does not merely claim that the fees reimburse administrative expenses. Its own explanation states that the fees are intended to discourage students and employers from using OPT to avoid H-1B program fees, caps, and prevailing-wage requirements. The agency also states that the proposed fee would reduce the OPT applicant pool and effectively eliminate certain categories of OPT participation.

A. Section 1184(a) does not automatically authorize unlimited financial conditions.
DHS relies on its authority to prescribe the conditions of nonimmigrant admission. But regulating the conditions of admission and creating an enormous financial exaction are different exercises of governmental power.

The agency needs to explain why authority to regulate the duration and conditions of nonimmigrant status necessarily includes authority to impose a six-figure cumulative financial obligation on educational institutions for exercising their role in the OPT process.

The distinction becomes particularly important because the proposed fee is not connected to a particular employer, a particular job, a particular compliance violation, or an individualized fraud determination.

B. Sections 1103 and 112 are not blank checks.
General authority to administer and enforce immigration legislation cannot independently establish every substantive power DHS might consider useful.

Otherwise, the agency could use general administrative language to create virtually any financial condition it considers beneficial to immigration enforcement.

That interpretation would eliminate the distinction between administering a statutory program and creating a new regulatory scheme with major economic consequences.

C. The Major Questions Doctrine Requires Clear Congressional Authorization
The proposed rule independently presents a major question under the Supreme Court's decisions in West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022), and Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023). Under the Major Questions Doctrine, an agency asserting extraordinary power over matters of vast economic and political significance must identify clear congressional authorization for the power it claims. DHS estimates that the proposed fees could generate approximately $12.4 billion in annual transfers under its primary economic scenario and approximately $109.4 bil. These are not ordinary administrative processing charges.

Most importantly, DHS is not merely exercising authority to administer an existing statutory program. It is claiming the power to fundamentally alter the economic accessibility and practical operation of that program through an unprecedented financial mechanism.

Nothing in the general administrative provisions cited by DHS clearly authorizes this extraordinary exercise of power.

Under West Virginia, a merely plausible textual basis is insufficient when an agency asserts consequential authority of this magnitude. DHS must identify clear congressional authorization.

The proposed rule does not satisfy that requirement.

DHS must identify the statutory authority permitting it to collect these payments, determine their legal classification, and explain why the applicable federal fiscal statutes permit the proposed collection and disposition.
Technical Clarification:
1. What is the specific statutory provision authorizing the Secretary to establish this particular OPT financial exaction?
2. What is the specific delegation authorizing ICE to exercise that authority?
3. What is the specific statutory provision permitting ICE to condition SEVIS recommendations on payment?
4. What is the specific statutory provision permitting DHS to make payment a prerequisite to USCIS employment authorization?
5. What is the statutory basis for the amount selected and the disposition of the collected funds?
comments.reason: Argues DHS lacks statutory authority to impose excessive OPT fees designed as an economic barrier.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal while preserving access to legitimate OPT and STEM OPT.

Regarding sections IV.A–C and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are important goals, but ability to pay such a large fee is not a reliable measure of educational merit, compliance, or the legitimacy of a training opportunity. A blanket financial barrier would burden compliant schools and students as well as bad actors. DHS should explain why these particular amounts are necessary and proportionate, and compare their expected effectiveness with targeted enforcement alternatives.

Section IV.C expressly acknowledges that schools may pass these costs to students, employers, or other students. Making schools the formal payer therefore does not resolve the affordability problem. The proposal could make practical training inaccessible to qualified students with limited resources and could discourage smaller employers, universities, and nonprofit research organizations from offering legitimate training opportunities. DHS should evaluate these effects, including consequences for research, institutional budgets, international enrollment, and U.S. competitiveness, rather than treating reduced participation itself as evidence of improved integrity.

Regarding section IV.B, DHS should distinguish between documented misconduct and lawful participation in practical training. Protecting workers would be better served by enforcing applicable compensation and non-displacement requirements, verifying genuine employers and training arrangements, investigating suspicious worksites, and penalizing proven violations. DHS should evaluate these measures as alternatives to fees that exclude participants regardless of their compliance.

Regarding section V.C and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), a 60-day transition would give already-enrolled students and institutions little opportunity to adjust educational and financial plans. DHS should meaningfully address reliance interests and protect currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants from newly imposed fees if it proceeds with any fee change.

Please withdraw the proposed fees, retain OPT and STEM OPT, and pursue evidence-based, proportionate oversight focused on actual fraud and worker protection. Any future fee proposal should provide a transparent justification for its amounts and a thorough assessment of less burdensome alternatives and distributional effects.

I am an international graduate student, and I'm writing to respectfully oppose the proposed OPT fee rule. I ask DHS to withdraw the $70,000 initial fee and the $30,000 subsequent fee and to address fraud through targeted enforcement instead.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee regulation. While protecting the integrity of the immigration system and preventing employment fraud are legitimate policy objectives, imposing fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorization is neither a proportionate nor a rational solution.

A few important considerations deserve serious attention:

Economic consequences: International students contribute substantially to the U.S. economy through tuition, housing, consumption, research, and other economic activities. Creating an extraordinarily expensive barrier to post-graduation employment risks discouraging talented students from pursuing American higher education in the first place.
Research and innovation: International graduates contribute to STEM research, healthcare, engineering, biotechnology, computer science, and university research laboratories. Restricting access to practical training risks weakening the very research ecosystem that has helped maintain American scientific competitiveness.
Disproportionate financial burden: A $70,000 initial institutional fee, followed by another $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation, is an extraordinary financial barrier. Universities, particularly public universities and smaller research institutions, cannot reasonably be expected to absorb these costs for every eligible graduate.
Policy should be evidence-based: If fraud, noncompliance, or exploitation exists within OPT, the appropriate response is targeted auditing, stronger employer verification, transparent reporting requirements, and enforcement against documented violations. A blanket financial barrier does not distinguish legitimate participants from fraudulent actors.
Legal and regulatory concerns: OPT has a longstanding regulatory framework. In Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (2022), the D.C. Circuit upheld DHS's authority to establish the OPT framework. Any major regulatory change should therefore be supported by a clear legal rationale and a defensible assessment of its consequences.
International competitiveness: The United States invests in attracting some of the world's brightest students through its universities. It is counterproductive to recruit international talent, collect substantial tuition and education-related revenue, and then create prohibitive barriers to obtaining relevant professional experience after graduation. Other countries will benefit from this talent if the United States makes remaining professionally competitive here unnecessarily difficult.

The central issue is not whether OPT should be regulated. It should. The question is whether regulation should be proportionate, evidence-based, and consistent with America's long-term economic and scientific interests.

My position is straightforward: prevent fraud, enforce existing requirements, and protect American workers through legitimate oversight, but do not effectively eliminate a lawful professional training pathway through financially prohibitive institutional fees.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue targeted, transparent, and economically responsible alternatives.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, citing severe economic and innovation consequences.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Briana Stone
comments.commentText:
My name is Briana Stone, and I am a research assistant in the Department of Health Policy and Management at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. I am a U.S. citizen, and I write to urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees.

Although I am not an international student, these fees would directly affect me, my colleagues, and my field. I work closely with international doctoral students, postdoctoral fellows, and staff; we co-author analyses, share code and data, and train one another. OPT is often how a new graduate stays to finish a project or starts a postdoctoral position. A $70,000 fee would close that path. It exceeds the full first-year postdoctoral stipend on NIH training awards ($63,480 in FY2026) and is more than double the predoctoral stipend ($29,364). Grant-funded research groups cannot absorb that cost for each trainee, and few early-career researchers could pay it themselves. Graduates trained here would take their skills elsewhere, and many future scientists would never come: 92% of institutions surveyed by the Institute of International Education said that without OPT, international students would likely choose other countries, and new international enrollment had already fallen 17% in fall 2025.

DHS says this rule will protect U.S. workers. As an American early-career researcher, I am one of those workers, and my opportunities depend on the projects, grants, and collaborations that international colleagues help build. Our department studies how Americans get and pay for health care, from insurance coverage and Medicare and Medicaid to the cost and quality of care. That work relies on advanced training in statistics, economics, and data science, fields where international students earn a large share of U.S. degrees: temporary visa holders earned 38% of U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2024, including a majority in mathematics and statistics. Losing them would slow research that affects every American patient and taxpayer.

I support efforts to prevent fraud, but a flat fee cannot distinguish a sham employer from a university research lab; it screens students by wealth rather than merit. A study of 2,300 U.S. science and engineering departments found that foreign doctoral students raise U.S. research output, and that visa policies favoring applicants with more money over those with the strongest qualifications harm it. Targeted tools already exist. STEM OPT requires E-Verify, a formal training plan, and employer attestations that the student will not replace a U.S. worker and will be paid comparably to similar U.S. workers, and it permits DHS site visits.

International students and graduates are vital to American science because:
-They broaden our research environments. Colleagues trained abroad bring new methods, questions, and firsthand knowledge of other health systems. The same study found that departments with doctoral students from more diverse origins produce more publications and citations.
-They drive innovation and U.S. scientific leadership. Immigrants have won 40% of the Nobel Prizes awarded to Americans in chemistry, medicine, and physics since 2000, and 31% in economics. International students also contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024-25.
-Global cooperation strengthens America’s standing. Graduates who return home become partners and leaders who know and trust U.S. institutions. In public health, these ties become the networks through which outbreaks are detected early and data are shared, protecting Americans at home.
-They make American researchers better. Working with international colleagues has broadened my own training, and international students often serve as teaching and research assistants who train the next generation of American scientists.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. At a minimum, DHS should exempt OPT employment at universities and nonprofit and government research organizations, which Congress already exempts from the H-1B cap and training fee. It should also address fraud through targeted enforcement rather than a fee on every student.

Sincerely,
Briana Stone, MSPH
Research Assistant, Department of Health Policy and Management, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
Submitted in my personal capacity; my views do not represent Harvard University.

Sources: NIH NOT-OD-26-044; .Baer J, Ekin S. Fall 2025 Snapshot on International Student Enrollment. 2025. Accessed November 8, 2026. https://www.iie.org/publications/fall-2025-snapshot-on-international-student-enrollment/; NSF NCSES, Doctorate Recipients from U.S. Universities: 2024; Stuen, Mobarak & Maskus, Economic Journal (2012); NFAP, Immigrants and Nobel Prizes: 1901-2025; NAFSA International Student Economic Value Tool.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yash Lala
comments.commentText:
My name is Yash Lala.
I am a citizen, and am currently a 4th year PhD student at Yale's Computer Science department.
My research focuses on improving the power efficiency of our computing devices, in turn facilitating the competitiveness of the US's AI, mobile computing, and large-scale-computing capabilities.

I'm writing in response to Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 (aka: the proposed optional practical training fees).
I request the DHS consider withdrawing this proposed fee.

This proposal would drastically reduce my lab's ability to remain competitive with foreign researchers and maintain American technological dominance.
I graduated from UCLA in 2022. Out of the ~9300 students in my graduating class, I know of only one other student that went on to a PhD in core systems research.
This is to say that very few Americans are interested in pursuing the specialized training required to work on the kinds of problems blocking our industry today.
The majority of my colleagues are international students; they are the one in ~10k, siphoned off from other countries.
With few exceptions, I see these colleagues enter American industry directly after graduating.
This siphoning is a boon to our computing sector, and has thus far allowed US systems research to remain competitive w/ countries with much larger population sizes.
(The most prestigious systems journals, for example, are almost exclusively American or in English; eg. ASPLOS, SOSP, OSDI, NSDI, etc!).

This proposal will cut off this brain drain, as a side effect of its implementation mechanisms.
Specifically:

- In 64576, the DHS states the proposed fees make participations "less attractive to bad actors", by establishing a "tangible stake" against potential immigrants trying to exploit the system.
But these fees are not applied in a targeted manner!
The DHS draws no distinction between a post-doctoral scholar at a national laboratory and a fraudulent "phantom employees" at residential addresses (as described in 64576).
In order to avoid throwing the former out with the latter, the DHS should consider excepting doctoral graduates, pre-completion OPTs and employers w/ H1B cap-excempt institutions.

- The utility of drawing this distinction is borne out by the DHS's provided examples of fraud, in Section IV.A. Every example of fraud is restricted to either (a) staffing
worksites or (b) IT consulting; the DHS has provided no instances of PhD
graduates, postdoctoral researchers, or research universities involved
in OPT fraud.

- Fees that are imposed to deter conduct are, definitionally, sanctions.
Agencies are permitted to impose these sanctions in the form of civil
penalties only where permitted by existing statutes (and following the
process defined by these statutes).
The DHS must either withdraw the fee, _or_ cite an explicit penalty provision (which is not included in the current rule).

I implore the DHS to consider the following requests:

- I ask the DHS to quantify the benefits of the proposed rules, specifically the expected effects on US workers and the expected numbers of fraudulent authorizations the DHS expects to prevent.
These two points are required in Executive Order 13563 and 12866, but are absent from this proposal.

- I ask the DHS to enact any new measures incrementally, going sector by sector in the order that DHS identifies fraud (namely the IT consulting and staffing worksites fields, as the DHS notes in Section IV.A).
After a year, the DHS should publish results on the efficacy of this program, and expand the program from this initial pilot only w/ data demonstrating its success.

- I ask DHS to respond on the record to each alternative proposed by commenters, as the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 603(c)) and Executive Order 12866 section 1(b)(8) require.

Thank you for considering this comment.

-- Yash

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal entirely.

International students are an integral part of America's educational and economic landscape. They bring diverse perspectives, specialized knowledge, and professional skills that strengthen American universities, businesses, research institutions, and local communities. They contribute to innovation, economic growth, and America's global competitiveness.

International students make substantial financial investments in the United States through tuition, housing, transportation, and everyday expenses. Target fraud, not legitimate international students.

However, imposing extraordinary fees on every university recommending legitimate graduates for OPT is an unfair and disproportionate response. It penalizes compliant students and institutions for misconduct committed by others.

If fraud is the concern, DHS should investigate the actual perpetrators, including unscrupulous staffing companies and employment consultancies operating in India and elsewhere that facilitate fabricated employment, fraudulent documentation, and other immigration violations. These organizations should face serious investigations, financial penalties, and disqualification from employment programs.

To the Department of Homeland Security,

As a United States citizen and a formulation scientist manager working in research and development, I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. My concerns extend beyond the impact on international students to the broader consequences for American businesses, scientific innovation, and economic competitiveness.

I have personally witnessed how immigration challenges can disrupt American research and development teams. One of the scientists who reports directly to me is not a U.S. citizen and has faced significant visa-related challenges, including uncertainty about her ability to remain in the country and fears of deportation. She possesses specialized technical expertise that is extremely valuable to our research team, and the uncertainty surrounding her immigration status has forced us to consider difficult alternatives.

One possibility is transferring her to one of our company's international sites in a country with more accommodating visa requirements. While this might allow her to continue her career, it would represent a significant loss for our U.S.-based team. We would lose not only her technical expertise but also the institutional knowledge, ongoing research contributions, and collaborative relationships she has developed. Replacing this expertise would require considerable time and resources, potentially delaying research projects and reducing our team's productivity.

Although her circumstances are separate from this specific OPT proposal, they illustrate a broader concern: restrictive immigration policies can push highly skilled professionals, and potentially the work they support, outside the United States.

The proposed fees risk making these challenges even worse. American companies, particularly those engaged in scientific research, technology, and advanced manufacturing, depend on access to specialized talent. A $70,000 fee could make hiring international graduates financially impractical for many employers, particularly smaller companies and startups. Restricting access to this talent does not automatically create equivalent opportunities for American workers, especially in highly specialized fields where expertise can take years to develop.

The proposal could also undermine the competitiveness of American universities. International students contribute to academic research, university finances, and local economies. If the opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation becomes prohibitively expensive, talented students may increasingly choose to pursue their education and careers in other countries. The United States risks losing not just individual graduates but also the innovations, businesses, and economic activity they might otherwise contribute.

I recognize the importance of protecting American workers and preventing immigration fraud. However, imposing substantial fees across the board does not directly address fraudulent activity. More targeted measures, including stronger employer verification, compliance monitoring, and enforcement against documented abuses, would address these concerns without creating unnecessary barriers for legitimate employers and graduates.

Furthermore, DHS acknowledges in its economic analysis that it cannot confidently predict how significantly OPT participation would decline under the proposed fees. Given the potential consequences for American businesses, universities, and research institutions, these uncertainties deserve more thorough consideration before implementing such a consequential policy.

As an American citizen and a manager responsible for building and retaining a highly skilled scientific team, I believe protecting American workers and attracting global talent are not mutually exclusive goals. My firsthand experience has shown me that losing skilled professionals to immigration barriers can directly harm American teams and the work they perform.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue more targeted, evidence-based approaches that protect program integrity while preserving America's ability to attract and retain highly skilled talent.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Professor G
comments.commentText: Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566) I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees as currently structured. The fees address a symptom rather than the underlying design that has produced large volumes of OPT recommendations from certain programs. Since the 2016 STEM OPT expansion, which lengthened the extension and highlighted CIP codes such as 52.1301 (Management Science), 52.1302 (Business Statistics), 52.1399, and later analytics codes such as 30.7102, many business schools have scaled one-year specialized master’s programs (management studies, quantitative management, business analytics, and similar). These programs are frequently classified under the qualifying CIP codes, marketed for the resulting 36-month work-authorization window, and filled with high shares of full-pay international students. The combination of STEM eligibility and full-tuition revenue has made these programs substantial budget contributors at numerous institutions. A standard business administration code (52.0201) does not confer STEM eligibility; schools obtain it by reclassification under the codes listed above. The proposed fees would raise the cost of each OPT recommendation. Schools could absorb the cost, pass it through, or reduce the number of recommendations. That may shrink volume, but it leaves the eligibility rules unchanged. Students in these programs would still qualify for the STEM extension, and the economic incentive to maintain large international cohorts around the work-authorization feature would remain. A more direct approach is to remove the business-related CIP codes that currently qualify (including 52.1301, 52.1302, 52.1399, and 30.7102) from the DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List. Graduates would retain standard 12-month OPT but lose the 24-month STEM extension. This would eliminate the primary product feature that drove the scale of these specialized master’s programs after 2016, without imposing a new fee structure on every SEVP-certified school. Core STEM fields (engineering, mathematics, biological and physical sciences) would be unaffected. The fees as proposed do not redirect revenue to fraud detection or enforcement; they are deposited in the Treasury. If the objective is to reduce the use of specialized business master’s as high-volume OPT pathways, revising the STEM list targets the rule that created the volume. I urge the Department to withdraw or substantially revise the fee proposal and instead address STEM eligibility for the business CIP codes identified above.
