comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject:Comment on Proposed OPT Fees, DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01

Dear Department of Homeland Security, I respectfully urge you to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and keep Optional Practical Training accessible to international students who follow the rules. Thank you for considering this comment.

Introduction: I'm an F-1 graduate with a U.S. Master's Degree working in AI Infrastructure and Software Engineering. This rule directly affects students like me.

Background: I'm commenting on the proposed changes to 8 CFR Part 214 that would charge $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT.

Analysis: Few students can pay fees this large, so in practice the rule would end OPT. Employers, especially startups, would stop hiring F-1 graduates. Students who paid full U.S. tuition relying on OPT would be penalized after the fact. Trained talent would go to Canada, the UK, Australia, and Germany instead. A flat fee on every student also doesn't separate fraud from honest graduates.

Recommendations: Withdraw the fees. If new funding is needed, set any small amount of fee at the documented processing cost. Fight fraud with targeted tools like employer verification and E-Verify.

Conclusion: These fees would end OPT for most students and hurt U.S. employers without targeting fraud. It will also hurt the economy. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, arguing they would end the program and harm students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule for two main reasons.

First, a higher fee does not necessarily improve fraud detection. Universities may reduce the number of students recommended for OPT because of the financial burden, but that does not mean they will become better at detecting fraud. Students attempting fraud who have sufficient financial resources may still be able to pay the fee, while universities may remain unable to identify the fraud. A higher fee does not automatically mean greater responsibility or competence in fraud detection. USCIS already reviews OPT applications through Form I-765, and existing monitoring procedures continue throughout the OPT period. DHS should strengthen these existing processes rather than impose an enormous financial burden on universities.

Second, reducing OPT participation does not necessarily protect American workers. I work at a US university and understand how important international student tuition is to university funding. Such a high fee could discourage international students from studying in the U.S., reducing university revenue and potentially leading to layoffs of American employees. Universities also support local businesses and communities, so these financial consequences could extend well beyond campus.

A policy intended to protect American jobs could ultimately eliminate them. I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the high fee harms universities and workers without improving fraud detection.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed rule establishing $70,000 and $30,000 fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). I believe the proposal lacks sufficient evidence to justify fees of this magnitude and fails to adequately account for the consequences for American universities, students, employers, and local economies. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I am an international Ph.D. student at a U.S. research university, with an academic background in construction engineering, computer science, and artificial intelligence. Throughout my doctoral studies, the majority of my fellow doctoral students have been international. I have witnessed firsthand the sacrifices these students make to pursue advanced education and contribute to research and teaching in the United States. Many doctoral students live on modest stipends, work long hours, and have little opportunity to accumulate substantial savings. They dedicate years of their lives to research, often contributing to federally funded projects, university instruction, and technological innovation. For many, OPT provides an important opportunity to gain professional experience after graduation and apply their education before determining the next steps in their careers.
The proposed fees appear disconnected from these economic realities. Although DHS discusses the amounts in relation to H-1B fees, the proposal does not convincingly establish why $70,000 or $30,000 is proportionate to the risks associated with OPT or demonstrate that these amounts would effectively prevent fraud. The ability to pay an exceptionally high fee is not a reliable measure of whether a student or employer is complying with immigration regulations. A financial barrier this large risks excluding legitimate participants without directly addressing the misconduct DHS seeks to prevent.

On a personal note, I never imagined that I would come to regret my decision to pursue my Ph.D. in the United States. I came here with genuine admiration for this country, its universities, and the opportunities it offered to people willing to work hard and contribute. I invested years of my life in that belief. I could not have anticipated the amount of uncertainty, anxiety, and emotional distress that repeated changes in immigration policies and expectations would bring. It is deeply painful to feel that the future you worked so hard toward can become increasingly uncertain through decisions entirely beyond your control.
I cannot change the years I have already invested or the difficulties I have experienced. But I sincerely hope that future generations of international students will not have to look back on their decision to study in the United States with the same regret. I hope they can preserve the admiration, trust, and excitement that once led so many of us to choose this country. I respectfully ask DHS not to proceed with this proposal and not to make that hope even harder for the next generation to sustain.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Augusto Reis
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an MBA student in the United States, and I oppose this proposed rule. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

First, the fee has no relationship to the problem it claims to solve. DHS says the $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee are meant to combat fraud. But the revenue goes to the U.S. Treasury, not to fraud detection, SEVP oversight, or faster processing. A fee that funds nothing related to fraud cannot be justified as a fraud-fighting tool. Ability to pay is not evidence of compliance. A student at a well-funded school, or whose employer can absorb the cost, passes through the gate, while a legitimate student at a smaller school is locked out. That does not screen for fraud; it screens for money.

Second, the amounts are disconnected from any real cost. No one believes processing an OPT recommendation costs $70,000. For most students this exceeds a full year of tuition, and for many schools it exceeds what they could ever pay per student. DHS acknowledges schools may pass the cost to students or employers, which in practice means OPT simply becomes unavailable for the large majority of F-1 students who cannot produce $70,000. A rule designed so that almost no one can use the program is a repeal of OPT by another name, and repealing a program of this scale deserves a full economic analysis, not a fee rule with a 30-day comment period.

Third, the proposal is unworkable as written. The rule is ambiguous about how many times the $30,000 subsequent fee applies, whether a student who transfers schools or moves to a higher degree level triggers a second $70,000 "initial" fee, and how refunds would work in practice. If the agency itself cannot describe how the fee operates, schools and students cannot comply with it.

Finally, this hurts the United States, not just international students. I came here because the U.S. offers the best graduate education in the world and a real path to apply it afterward. My classmates and I pay full tuition, spend in our local economies, and fill roles American employers struggle to staff, especially in quantitative and technical fields. OPT is what makes the investment of a U.S. degree make sense. Remove it, and the next class of students will take their tuition, their spending, and their talent to Canada, the UK, or Australia instead. That is a loss for U.S. universities, U.S. employers, and U.S. workers, not a protection for them.

If DHS has evidence of specific fraud in OPT, it should target that fraud directly: audit the specific employers and schools involved, enforce the reporting rules that already exist, and use the SEVIS fees it already collects for that purpose. A blanket fee that punishes every legitimate student and school for the conduct of a few bad actors is neither fair nor effective.

For these reasons, I ask DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees are disconnected from costs and urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

International students come to the United States legally, follow immigration regulations, invest thousands of dollars in their education, and contribute to the American economy. We pay tuition, support local businesses, and bring knowledge, creativity, and different perspectives to this country.

The United States has become a global leader in innovation, technology, business, and education partly because it has welcomed talent from around the world.

We should not forget that influential figures such as Elon Musk, who studied at the University of Pennsylvania, Sundar Pichai, who studied at Stanford University and later became CEO of Google, and Satya Nadella, who earned advanced degrees in the United States and became CEO of Microsoft, all came from other countries.

Thousands of international students may never become famous entrepreneurs or CEOs, but they still contribute to American communities, businesses, research, and economic growth.

As an international student, I believe that education should open doors to opportunities, not create financial barriers.

Optional Practical Training gives students a chance to apply what they have learned, gain professional experience, and contribute their skills to the American workforce. Imposing fees of this magnitude could make participation unaffordable for many educational institutions and students.

America's strength has never come from talent born within its borders alone. It has also come from the ideas, determination, and contributions of people who arrived from around the world with dreams of building something meaningful.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider this proposal. The United States should continue to be a country where talent, hard work, and opportunity matter.

comments.commentText: I am an F1 student undertaking a PhD who works on campus as part of their degree. I am submitting this comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. The OPT program is one of the few ways for students such as myself to contribute our new skills to the workforce before applying for a more durable (and expensive) work status such as the 0 visa or green card. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This proposed rule by the DHS (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100) would undoubtedly negatively affect the United States of America in a multitude of ways. It is completely short-sighted. From what I understand, the logic is that limiting international students ability to pursue a career here in the United States would provide more opportunity to American citizens. This logic is flawed and narrow-minded. I urge DHS to immediately withdraw this proposed rule.

One of the greatest assets this country has is its vast, highly regarded University System. The smartest, most capable, highest achieving people come from all around the world, students and professors alike, come to teach and learn in this country.

So let me get this straight... we have a group of wildly successful, high achieving, innovative, boundary-pushing, and hard-working young people who are ready and willing to contribute to our society and economy, and we want them to leave??

It's clear foreign graduates do quality work, create jobs, boost the economy, and rise the tides for everyone around them. Wouldn't we rather them stay here and do this in our country rather than immediately returning home with all this newfound knowledge and ability? Thinking of jobs as spots on the high school football team that can be taken from you is naive, to say the least.

These are the exact types of immigrants I've always been told we wanted in this country. It's really hard for me, then, not to believe this proposal is founded in ideals of nationalism and racism and packaged as care for the average American.

The other thing that bugs me is the pay-to-win aspect of it all. We're America... I thought we loved an underdog? I thought we love a rags-to-riches success story? My heart breaks a little bit every time I'm reminded the American Dream is less accessible than ever. Apparently wealthy foreigners are welcome to stay, but the individuals who earned it, the ones who worked their ass off to get here, the ones that defied all odds, the ones that inspire me - they need to leave the second they graduate. I don't know... seems pretty un-American to me. Or maybe it's the most American thing of all time :(

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Beth Vargas
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule of the US Department of Homeland Security that would impose an undue burden of a tax upon international students. (Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100) This impacts students and universities across the United States who want to enhance classroom learning with experiential learning through internships and entry level positions. International students maintaining legal F-1 status benefit from these opportunities through Optional Practical Training (OPT). Students already pay high fees to cover the cost of processing applications for OPT. This new fee will discourage them from coming to the United States at all and they will no longer have the opportunity to learn and to contribute to our country.

I have worked in higher education for the past 39 years, specifically in the area of international education. I consider this work a vocation because I know how my life was changed by the opportunity to study abroad as a young adult and I have seen literally thousands of students grow, mature, and become world citizens because of global learning. I also know that these opportunities are often limited to wealthy students who have been educated in elite schools from pre-school up through college. I attended a well-funded private college and have worked at a large Ivy League University, but I am proud that for the past 27 years I have worked in the largest system of public higher education in the world. Our mission is Global Learning for All: Educating for a Sustainable Future. Global learning cultivates individuals and societies helping students comprehend the world beyond their borders and a giving them a sense of responsibility for the challenges humanity faces. Global learning imparts skills needed to work across differences to forge mutual understanding and devise solutions to those challenges. The State University of New York has made a commitment to equity that has led to the recognition that universal global learning is integral to a high-quality public education.

I am writing this in the last hours before the comment period closed. With only 30 days to provide a comment and with the proposed rule published in October, the timing of its publication seems designed to limit the number of responses. University faculty and administrators are in the busiest part of the academic year, doing the meaningful work of supporting and educating students. We are grading mid-term exams and advising students, guiding them through research and creative activity, preparing them for graduation and careers beyond that milestone, which seems much more important than taking time to comment on a cumbersome, expensive and unnecessary rule that is opposed to the value of global learning.

Chancellor John King set out a goal for every SUNY undergraduate student to complete a paid internship or research opportunity before graduation, highlighting the importance of experiential learning.

The burden of paying a new DHS fee will take away critical internship opportunities from international students. It will send these students to other, more welcoming countries, harm the dynamic cultural environment of our campus, and have a negative economic impact on our university, the state of New York, and our nation.

At SUNY New Paltz, where I work, the financial impact will be significant. We calculated the cost if New Paltz had to make these OPT fee payments over the 2025 calendar year when we saw 63 Optional Practical Training applications processed at an initial cost of $70,000, so the total cost would be $4,410,000. With 42 OPT STEM applications processed the same year at a cost of $30,000 each, the total would be $1,260,000. That means that for a small liberal arts college the one-year fee for Optional Practical Training comes to $5,670,000.

As a Designated School Official since 1987, I have worked to protect the integrity of the immigration system and combat fraud. I have supported the policies of the Immigration and Naturalization System since before it became part of DHS. I entered student data into the SEVIS system when it was first created and I have complied with ever-changing regulations. I am committed to continuing to assure that students and scholars understand and follow the law of this country. Recent DHS proposals do not protect American workers, they do not combat fraud, and they do not benefit our country. There is more information about international students available to DHS than any other group of immigrants or non-immigrants in the United States. When a student moves across the hall in her dormitory, we notify DHS. When she changes her major, we update her record in SEVIS. The US government has every detail about her post completion work authorization. This expensive and overly cumbersome regulation will do nothing but restrict the contributions of international students to this country. I urge you to revoke this proposal. Thank you.

comments.commentText:
I am a faculty member at a large research university, and over my career I have worked extensively with international students and postdocs. I have come to understand the irreplaceable value these people have in our scientific research system here in the United States --- without them, we would have many unfilled research positions and we would fall catastrophically behind other nations in scientific innovation. The ability for graduate students to work immediately after their degrees through OPT is an essential component of that research system --- without it, students we have just invested years and hundreds of thousands of dollars in training will have to immediately leave the country and contribute the skills they gained here in the United States to the economies of other countries. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed OPT fee structure. Preventing fraud, maintaining immigration system integrity, and protecting American workers are important objectives. However, fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT would impose substantial barriers to legitimate educational training. DHS should consider whether more targeted measures could achieve its objectives with fewer adverse consequences.

1. Financial capacity is not a reliable measure of program integrity.

The proposal would condition access to OPT on substantial payments by educational institutions, with costs potentially passed to students or employers. Ability to pay does not establish whether a student is qualified, an employer is legitimate, or training has educational value. Conversely, inability to pay does not indicate fraud or misuse.

This approach risks excluding qualified, compliant participants based on financial resources rather than eligibility. Institutions with limited resources may restrict OPT recommendations because of budget constraints. DHS should demonstrate how the proposed amounts would distinguish legitimate participation from abuse and explain why less burdensome safeguards would be insufficient.

2. Benefits to American workers require a fuller assessment.

Reducing OPT participation does not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in opportunities for American workers. Employers may hire domestic workers, but they may also leave positions unfilled, scale back projects, or move work abroad. The economic consequences depend on which responses occur.

DHS should examine these possibilities across occupations, regions, and employer sizes. It should also consider how international graduates may complement American colleagues through research, specialized expertise, and business growth. Protecting workers requires attention to actual employment outcomes, rather than treating reduced participation as sufficient evidence of success.

3. The potential costs extend to American institutions and communities.

Practical training connects academic education with degree-related experience. Making that opportunity financially inaccessible could reduce the attractiveness of U.S. education and encourage graduates to apply their skills elsewhere.

Potential consequences include lower international enrollment, reduced university revenue, disruption to research, and decreased spending in surrounding communities. Institutions could redirect resources from teaching, student services, or research to cover the fees. Smaller employers and nonprofit organizations may face particular difficulties if asked to fund participation.

These are material risks that warrant analysis before adoption. DHS should assess them alongside anticipated benefits and explain why the proposed amounts represent an appropriate balance.

4. Protect students who have already made educational commitments.

The proposed 60-day transition does not adequately account for educational decisions made over several years, including tuition payments, degree planning, and research arrangements. Those commitments cannot readily be reversed within two months.

If DHS proceeds, it should exempt currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants from the new fees for their remaining otherwise-eligible OPT, including STEM extensions. This would preserve eligibility requirements while avoiding substantial, unexpected costs after students have committed to an American education. Such protection would mitigate disruption but would not resolve the broader concerns with the proposal.

5. Targeted safeguards offer a more direct response.

DHS should evaluate stronger employer verification, risk-based audits, verification of training relevance, and enforcement against fraudulent institutions and employers. Enforcing applicable wage and working-condition protections would address exploitation more directly than a financial barrier imposed across compliant and noncompliant participants alike.

Any fee should have a transparent justification, including its relationship to necessary program costs, expected effectiveness, and consequences for access. DHS should compare reasonable alternatives and explain why a less burdensome approach would not meet its objectives.

For these reasons, I recommend that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure and develop a targeted, proportionate approach. Effective oversight should preserve legitimate practical training while addressing demonstrated misconduct and protecting the interests of American workers, educational institutions, and the economy.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee structure, arguing it creates substantial barriers and risks excluding students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)) and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

The fee funds no enforcement. Section IV.C states the money goes to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt, and ICE cannot keep it. It adds no investigators, site visits, or employer checks. DHS named the tools that work (training plans, site visits, more reporting) and set them aside because they take resources. Verifying employers before OPT begins would target the fraud directly.
The fee punishes the many to reach the few. DHS cites about 10,000 students at highly suspect employers (Section IV.A). About 360,000 students used OPT and STEM OPT in 2024. Even if every case is fraud, that is under 3 percent.
Schools cannot screen out fake employers. Students need no job offer for initial OPT, so the school pays before any employer exists. The fraud DHS describes is employer fraud, and the fee makes schools screen by who can pay.
The rule shows no link between OPT and American unemployment. The 6.1 percent figure for computer science graduates comes from a presidential proclamation, with no study tying it to OPT. The 2017 wage study DHS cites measures 2001, seven years before STEM OPT existed. The foreign-share figures cover all foreign-born workers. DHS admitted in 2016 it had no quantified estimate of OPT’s effect on U.S. workers, and this rule provides none.
OPT does not bypass the H-1B cap. DHS compares all 165,524 STEM OPT participants in a year to the 85,000 new H-1B visas allowed each year, which measure different things. OPT is temporary, and STEM OPT employers already attest they will not replace U.S. workers and will pay the same as similar U.S. workers (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)).
Payroll tax savings do not justify the fee. Congress created the FICA exemption (26 U.S.C. 3121(b)(19)), and it lasts only five calendar years. On an $80,000 salary, the employer saves about $6,120 a year. The fee is over ten times that.
The fee does not match the H-1B. An H-1B is a multi-year work visa. OPT is temporary training that can be as short as a summer internship.
Practical training has been part of student status since 1947, as the rule notes, and the D.C. Circuit upheld OPT in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (2022). Current students chose and paid for U.S. programs under these rules.
The fee would weaken U.S. education and innovation. Canada, the UK, and Australia let graduates work after study, and top students would go there. International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported over 355,000 U.S. jobs in 2024-2025 (NAFSA). Almost one in four U.S. billion-dollar companies has a founder who came as an international student (NFAP, 2026). DHS based the 2016 STEM OPT rule on the view that educational exchange and STEM innovation strengthen the U.S. economy and U.S. workers. This fee would send talented graduates, and the companies they would build, to other countries.
The fee selects by wealth and stacks quickly. A well-funded fraud scheme can pay $70,000. Most students and entry-level employers cannot. Pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT together cost $130,000, with no refund once the work permit is issued, even if the job offer is withdrawn.
Small and public schools are hit hardest. DHS estimates 56 percent of SEVP-certified schools are small entities and offers them no exemption.

I also oppose the Section V.A alternative of charging $70,000 again at each new degree level.

DHS can address fraud and protect U.S. workers without any fee. Instead, DHS should:

Check all OPT employers with the STEM OPT training plans and worksite visits that already exist.
Require all OPT employers to pay the same as similar U.S. workers, as STEM OPT employers already must.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and protect the education and innovation that OPT supports.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

Imposing additional fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) would harm U.S. interests. First, some international students rely on OPT to complete practical training needed for professional qualifications or licensure. Additional fees could discourage prospective students from choosing U.S. institutions in the first place, reducing the substantial economic benefits that international students bring to American universities and local communities.

Second, OPT provides time-limited work authorization for practical training directly related to a student’s field of study. Although OPT participants may compete with U.S. workers for some positions, it would be misleading to assume that every OPT placement displaces an American worker. Any additional fee should therefore be justified by evidence of a specific problem and a clear explanation of how the fee would address it.

Additional fees could also place a disproportionate burden on graduates with limited financial resources, making access to practical training depend more heavily on the ability to pay. They could make lower-paid but educationally valuable training opportunities less accessible and weaken the appeal of a U.S. education.

Before imposing new charges, the government should weigh the expected fee revenue against potential losses in international enrollment, tuition revenue, and local spending. If the objective is to protect U.S. workers, policymakers should explain how the proposed fees would advance that goal and consider more targeted measures. Any policy change should also account for students who have already committed substantial resources to a U.S. education under the existing framework.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000/$30,000 OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the rule. My points cite the NPRM's own text.

1. Revenue measure without a cost basis or identified authority (Sec. IV.C, pp. 64575-76). DHS says proceeds go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, ICE will not retain or use them, and the fee works as a "deterrent." It chose the amount to "closely align with the H-1B fees," the $100,000 charge a federal court vacated as an unauthorized tax (State of California v. Mullin, D. Mass. June 2026; stay denied by the First Circuit, July 2026). INA 214(a) concerns the "time and conditions" of a student's admission. DHS should identify the statute authorizing a per-student charge on schools unrelated to any cost of administering OPT.

2. The mechanism does not match the problem (Secs. IV.A, V.A). The fraud described is employer-side: shared addresses, homes listed as worksites, "phantom employees" (p. 64571). But initial OPT requires no employer (p. 64569), so a school paying $70,000 cannot tell whether an employer is legitimate. The headline figure is also inconsistent: the text says 10,000+ students (p. 64571); footnote 56 says 10,000 "highly suspected employers," citing a video. "Suspected" is not fraud. Even read as students, that is roughly 3% of the ~360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants DHS counts (p. 64573), yet the fee reaches every school and student.

3. The analysis cannot support a rule DHS says will transfer ~$12 billion a year (Sec. VII.A). DHS "cannot confidently predict" the participation response (p. 64582); its annualized cost range runs from $32 million to $8.2 billion, and the "primary" figure is the average of two scenarios (pp. 64579, 64583). It dismisses reliance because "only about 20 percent" of F-1 students use OPT (p. 64578), dividing by all 1.4 million students, including those not yet eligible; the relevant share is among graduates. It cites the FICA exemption as a hiring incentive (pp. 64573-74), yet footnote 108 concedes it ends after five calendar years in F-1 status, as is common for PhD graduates.

4. Reliance interests are dismissed (Sec. VI). Students chose multi-year programs, including 5+ year doctorates, knowing OPT existed. Only those already recommended are protected (pp. 64578-79); DHS concedes current students are "in a different position" than prospective ones (fn 124). I ask DHS to (a) exempt everyone enrolled as of October 8, 2026; (b) reject charging $70,000 again at each degree level (p. 64577); and (c) clarify what a student whose first OPT predates the effective date owes for later OPT, since the text conditions the $30,000 on having "paid the initial" fee.

5. Less burdensome alternatives were not seriously considered (p. 64576). DHS weighed one alternative. Options matching its own findings: E-Verify and basic business verification for all OPT employers (already required for STEM OPT, fn 52); data matching on shared addresses and residential worksites; enforcement against shell employers and visa mills; risk-based treatment of schools; or a cost-based fee dedicated to SEVP oversight. I offer these without conceding the fee is lawful or necessary.

6. Procedure. A 30-day comment period for an "economically significant" rule (p. 64579) is too short, particularly with information-collection comments due December 7. I request an extension of at least 30 days.

7. Impact. As a PhD student in a STEM field at a U.S. university, I see OPT as the main route by which U.S.-trained researchers keep working here. A flat fee with no distinction for doctoral researchers or high-wage research roles contradicts DHS's stated aim of keeping "highly qualified" participants (p. 64572) and would likely push this talent abroad. DHS itself said in 2008 that STEM OPT addressed a competitive disadvantage for U.S. high-tech industries (fn 102).

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and asks DHS to withdraw or revise the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Optional Practical Training Fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2))

I am an F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT, interning at a tech company as an AI/ML engineer, doing work directly related to my degree. I write to agree with the Department's goals — and to oppose this fee, because the fee does the opposite of what the Department says it will do. I ask the Department to withdraw this proposal.

I agree that fraud in OPT should be stopped. DHS cites fraud found in site visits to STEM OPT employers, and no honest student defends fake employers, fake job offers, or fake training plans. I agree that the immigration system should have integrity, and I agree that American workers should be protected. Those are goals worth pursuing.

But I deny that a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT achieves any of them. A flat fee does not punish fraud. It punishes everyone. Fraud is committed by a small number of bad actors — employers who invent jobs and schools that look the other way. The proposed fee charges the same $70,000 to every student at every school, including the 294,253 students on OPT in 2024-25 who are doing real work for real employers. A fraudster who already fakes employment will not be stopped by a fee. The student who followed every rule will be. The Department already has the tools that actually target fraud: site visits, employer verification, SEVIS reporting, and the E-Verify and training-plan requirements for STEM OPT. Those tools go after the people breaking the rules. A universal fee goes after everyone except them — and the Department's own numbers show it: this rule would move $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion a year from schools to the federal government, a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. That is not the cost of processing a recommendation. DHS says it chose $70,000 because it is 'comparable to the H-1B fee' — not because it measured what a recommendation costs. That is a price on being an international student.

This fee will not protect American workers. It will hurt them, because it does not fall on international students alone. The Department itself says schools may pass the cost on to F-1 students, all students, or employers. That means American students can pay higher tuition and fees because of a rule that has nothing to do with them. The Department counted 2,478 schools with students on OPT. A large university might spread the cost around. A small college cannot pay $70,000 per student, and it cannot ask its students to. It will simply stop recommending OPT. Its international students will lose the program entirely, and its American students will lose classmates, lab partners, and the employers who came to that campus to hire.

Employers will feel it too. The engineers, researchers, and analysts they hire out of OPT will not be there to hire. And the jobs international students support are real and counted: in the 2024-25 academic year, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs, according to NAFSA. For every three international students, one American job is created or supported. Most of us pay full tuition, pay rent, and spend in the communities where we study. When a $70,000 fee drives students to Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia — and a 2025 survey of 8,000 international students found that a majority say post-study work opportunities strongly influence where they choose to study — the United States does not only lose tuition. It loses the people it spent years educating, and hands them to its competitors, along with the jobs and spending they bring.

So I agree with the Department's goals and I deny its method. If the Department wants to stop fraud, it should use the enforcement tools it already has, publish what its site visits found, and go after the employers and schools that break the rules. If it wants to protect American workers, it should protect the 355,736 jobs that international students support, not put a $70,000 price on the students who sustain them. And if any fee is charged at all, it should reflect the actual cost of processing a recommendation, not $70,000.

This rule affects everyone — international students, American students, small colleges, employers, and the communities that host us. Please withdraw it.

Respectfully submitted,
An F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT

I am a Machine Learning Engineer currently working in the U.S. on STEM OPT. Under the NPRM's grandfathering I may be unaffected, so I write on behalf of the graduates and employers who will follow. I oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the rule.

1. The fee targets the part of OPT that already has safeguards. The fraud the NPRM describes involves shell employers and unverified worksites. STEM OPT already requires an E-Verify employer, a Form I-983 training plan, and employer attestations (fn 52); initial OPT does not. A $30,000 charge on STEM extensions penalizes the most closely supervised stage of OPT. The one alternative DHS considered was extending STEM-style safeguards (p. 64576). DHS should explain why a fee is better than the oversight it already applies, and why it was not applied to initial OPT instead.

2. The cost lands on workers and small employers. DHS says schools may pass the fee to F-1 students, all students, or employers. Because no DSO recommendation or EAD can issue until it is paid, the fee works as a barrier to work authorization. For a new graduate, $30,000 is a large share of a first-year salary. For a small company or research lab, it is a hiring cost that can decide whether it takes on a trainee at all. STEM OPT lets employers train U.S.-educated graduates for up to 24 months; a fee at this level will push employers toward hiring elsewhere.

They bring knowledge, experiences, and perspectives shaped by different educational and cultural backgrounds, enriching campus life, fostering intellectual exchange, and strengthening academic communities. In architecture education specifically, international students contribute valuable knowledge of different construction methods, building traditions, material practices, and architectural precedents from around the world. These perspectives are essential to an academic discipline that is inherently global and benefits from cross-cultural exchange.

Furthermore, international students' tuition payments provide meaningful financial support for university operations, faculty, academic programs, and research. Reducing international enrollment would therefore affect not only prospective international students but also the broader university community, including currently enrolled domestic and international students, who may face fewer academic resources, reduced program offerings, and diminished institutional capacity. The proposed fee risks weakening the very universities that have made American higher education globally competitive.

2. The proposed fee does not appear to be appropriately aligned with its stated purpose of preventing employment fraud.

If the stated objective of the proposed rule is to combat employment fraud, the collection and use of the proposed fees should be directly connected to that objective. However, the proposed fee places the financial burden on universities and students without establishing a clear and proportional relationship between the fees collected and the prevention or investigation of employment fraud. A fee should not be imposed on institutions and students under the justification of addressing fraud unless its purpose, allocation, and actual use are demonstrably aligned with that goal.

3. The proposed rule places financial responsibility on universities and students for potential misconduct occurring at the employer level.

If employment fraud occurs, the relevant misconduct is generally associated with the employer's actions and the actual employment arrangement. Universities and students should not be made financially responsible for misconduct over which they have limited control. Placing the burden of additional fees on universities and students, rather than addressing potential violations at the employer level, is an inequitable allocation of responsibility. Any policy intended to prevent employment fraud should hold the responsible parties accountable and direct enforcement efforts toward the actual sources of misconduct, rather than imposing broad financial penalties on educational institutions and international students.

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. International students are an integral part of American universities, contributing to academic excellence, research, international exchange, and institutional sustainability. A policy that places additional financial burdens on universities and students risks discouraging international enrollment and undermining the academic breadth, educational quality, and global standing that distinguish American higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Optional Practical Training Fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2))

I am an F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT. I write about the students this proposal would catch in the middle — the ones who already made their choices under the rules that exist today. I ask the Department to withdraw this proposal, and at a minimum to protect students who are already enrolled and already on OPT.

The Department says this rule is prospective: the fees would apply only to recommendations dated on or after the effective date, 60 days after a final rule is published. Calling it prospective does not make it fair. I decided to come to the United States, enrolled in a master's program, and took on years of tuition debt under the framework that existed when I made those decisions. My family borrowed heavily to pay for my education. My father has worked as a laborer in a different country for more than 10 years, away from our family, so that I could study. I am already on post-completion OPT. If a final rule takes effect 60 days after publication, that is not enough time for anyone to change a decision made years ago. A student cannot undo a degree, a loan, or a move across the world in 60 days. The Department should explicitly protect currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants, including anyone who will need a later recommendation or extension, instead of changing the price of the program after the money is already spent.

The fee would also make students more dependent, not more protected. The Department says schools may pass the cost to students or employers. A student who cannot pay $70,000 will have to find an employer willing to pay it for her — and an employer who pays that much for a worker has power over that worker. A policy that is supposed to protect American workers should not create a system where a foreign student's right to work depends on a single employer who bought it. That is the opposite of protection. The ability to pay a fee is not evidence of compliance, and the inability to pay is not evidence of misconduct.

And the fee does not even fund the oversight it is supposed to support. The proposal states that the fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury and would not be retained by ICE or specifically earmarked for immigration enforcement. So the money does not pay for site visits, employer verification, or fraud investigations. It is only a financial deterrent — a price that keeps people out. If the Department wants better oversight, it should fund oversight. A fee that goes to the general Treasury while doing nothing for enforcement is not an integrity measure. It is a barrier.

Finally, this fee will reach far beyond students. Universities, teaching hospitals, research laboratories, and small employers rely on OPT graduates. A teaching hospital that cannot afford $70,000 per resident loses a doctor it trained. A research lab loses the researcher it spent years educating. A small employer in an underserved community loses the only applicant with the skills it needs. These are not the fraudsters the Department describes. They are the institutions and communities the fee would quietly break.

I support protecting American workers and stopping fraud. But a rule that changes the terms after students have already committed, that makes students dependent on whoever can pay, and that does not fund the enforcement it claims to serve, does none of those things. Please withdraw this proposal. At the very least, protect the students who are already here, already studying, and already working under the rules they were promised.

Respectfully submitted,
An F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT
comments.reason: The commenter asks the Department to withdraw the proposal and protect existing students from the fees.

comments.commentText:
**Re: Public Comment on Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)**

Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am an international graduate of a U.S. university, and I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees under 8 CFR 214.13(i).

I invested virtually all my savings in obtaining an American education, believing that I would have a fair opportunity to gain professional experience in the United States after graduation. I followed the immigration rules, paid substantial educational and living expenses, and hoped to contribute my skills and future earnings to the American economy. The proposed fees threaten to make that opportunity financially unattainable.

Requiring institutions to pay $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations creates an extraordinary financial barrier. Even if schools are formally responsible for payment, they may pass these costs to students or simply stop recommending them. Either outcome would make access to practical training depend more on financial resources than qualifications, merit, or compliance with immigration law.

I recognize DHS's stated objectives of preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, imposing such substantial fees on students who have complied with existing requirements does not, by itself, distinguish fraudulent activity from legitimate employment. DHS should explain why less burdensome, targeted enforcement measures would be insufficient.

The proposal also raises serious reliance concerns. Students like me made life-changing financial decisions based on the existing educational and OPT framework. Introducing these fees after students have already committed their savings risks undermining reasonable expectations and causing severe financial hardship.

Beyond individual consequences, the policy could discourage future international enrollment, reduce educational spending, and deprive American employers of skilled graduates willing to work, pay taxes, and contribute to their communities.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, pursue evidence-based fraud prevention measures, and meaningfully assess the economic and educational consequences. At minimum, DHS should protect currently enrolled students and recent graduates through appropriate transitional exemptions.

International graduates who have invested in American education and followed the rules deserve a fair opportunity to contribute—not an additional financial barrier that makes their investment impossible to realize.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my serious concerns regarding the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT authorizations and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT extensions.

$70,000 is an extremely high and arbitrary hurdle for international students (or institutions, which are meant to be responsible for ensuring this fee is paid per OPT student applicant). I work with the international students who would be directly impacted by this rule, and I personally understand how detrimental this rule would be on our F-1 students and their positive contributions to the United States.

First and foremost, the economic, educational, and cultural benefits of international students studying in the United States has been well documented.
For example, prior to recent international student enrollment shifts at U.S. institutions, the Institute of International Education, Inc published this statement about the benefits of international students in higher education: https://www.iie.org/research-initiatives/open-doors/economic-impact-of-international-students/
“The continued growth in international students coming to the U.S. for higher education had a significant positive economic impact on the United States. International students contributed $45 billion to the U.S. economy in 2018, according to the U.S. Department of Commerce. Open Doors 2019 reports that about 62 percent of all international students receive the majority of their funds from sources outside of the United States, including personal and family sources as well as assistance from their home country governments or universities. Students from around the world who study in the United States also contribute to America’s scientific and technical research and bring international perspectives into U.S. classrooms, helping prepare American undergraduates for global careers, and often lead to longer-term business relationships and economic benefits.”

The majority of international students enter the U.S. on an F-1 student visa. OPT providing work authorization for employment in the student’s degree field is one of the reasons why so many international students choose to make the U.S. their destination for their college education. With all the time, effort, and money that goes into completing a degree program here in the U.S., students naturally look for an extension of their studies to get practical training in their field, which is the core purpose of this authorization.

Upon graduation from their program, students will have limited funds and are eager to find employment to gain this additional experience. How will they clear the financial hurdle of $70,000 before even finding employment? How can any university have the means to cover the $70,000 fee for each international student applicant interested in applying for OPT, especially when many universities are already struggling financially? What student fresh out of college would be able to find an employer willing to pay such a fee?

The only outcome of this proposed OPT fee will be a further decline in international student interest in U.S. institutions (already sharply decreasing in the post-pandemic years), which will handicap the U.S. on the competitive global stage as students choose to take their talents and skills elsewhere. The U.S. economy will suffer with the loss of the economic benefit these students contribute during their studies and post-graduation in jobs that are crucial for maintaining the United States’ competitive edge, especially since many of these students study in crucial STEM fields that are highly valued in today’s race for AI and tech dominance.

It is my understanding that this proposed fee was conceived in part to address concerns of fraud. What is not clear is how a $70,000 fee for initial OPT would resolve these concerns. It would not target only those very few who might take duplicitous advantage of OPT work authorization; instead, it would have the effect of simply deterring almost every student from applying for OPT while allowing a few wealthy or fortunate applicants to proceed with the authorization.
Instead of implementing a hefty fee to discourage all OPT applicants, perhaps DHS could develop a more targeted approach to screening applicants and enhanced vetting using the tools already at their disposal, such as the SEVIS system, which already closely monitors and records F-1 student activity.
In the end, it is difficult to discern any positive benefit of such a capricious and incredibly high fee. OPT is a valuable authorization that many F-1 students use to further their education and develop crucial skills, much to the advantage of the U.S. economy, prosperity, and cutting-edge innovation.

I request that DHS consider less burdensome alternatives to this approach; one that won’t have such a wholesale detrimental effect on our students, our institutions, and our country.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Optional Practical Training Fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2))

I am an F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT, interning at a tech company as an AI/ML engineer, doing work directly related to my degree. I write about a part of this proposal that has received little attention: the fee is non-refundable, and the school must pay it before the recommendation is even made. I ask the Department to withdraw this proposal. At a minimum, a fee of this size must be refundable when the training it pays for does not happen, and refund decisions must be appealable.

Under the proposal, the school pays $70,000 before the designated school official recommends the student for OPT. The payment comes first; the recommendation, the adjudication, and the employment authorization document all come after. Under the proposal's refund rules, a refund is available only if the student never received the employment authorization document and the school removes the recommendation. Once the document is issued, the fee is non-refundable under any circumstances, and refund decisions cannot be appealed.

That means the school — and, if the cost is passed on, the student — pays $70,000 for an outcome that is not guaranteed, and bears all of the risk if it does not happen. If the employment authorization is denied, the money is gone. If the student cannot find qualifying work in time — and on post-completion OPT, a student has only 90 days of unemployment — the money is gone, and the student loses the OPT as well. If the employer withdraws the offer, the money is gone. In every one of these cases, the government keeps $70,000 for a training period that never took place, and no one can appeal.

That is not how a fee for a government service should work. A fee should pay for a service that is provided. Here the government takes the money first, controls every step that follows, and keeps the money even when the service is not delivered. For a fee of a few hundred dollars, that might be a nuisance. For $70,000 — more than many families earn in a year — it is a serious financial risk that no school or student can plan around. A small college that pays $70,000 for a student whose authorization is then denied has lost money it cannot recover, for nothing.

The Department should explain why a fee of this size is non-refundable and why refund decisions are unappealable. If the Department proceeds, the fee should be refunded whenever the OPT does not happen — when the employment authorization is denied, when the recommendation is withdrawn, or when the student is unable to use it. Refund decisions should be appealable like any other decision involving this much money. Better still, the fee should be charged only after the employment authorization is issued, so that no one pays for a training period that never begins.

A rule that asks schools and students to pay $70,000 in advance, keeps the money when the training never happens, and offers no appeal, is not a fee. It is a gamble that only the government can win. Please withdraw it.

Respectfully submitted,
An F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT
comments.reason: The commenter asks the Department to withdraw the proposal due to excessive and non-refundable fees.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 – Request for Grandfathering Protections for Existing OPT Participants

I respectfully urge DHS to establish clear grandfathering protections for international students who enrolled in U.S. universities or received their initial OPT Employment Authorization Document (EAD) before the final rule's effective date.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Benjamin Krebsbach

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to Optional Practical Training for international students. These changes would impose unjustified financial and administrative burdens on students, universities, and employers while undermining the United States' ability to attract and retain talented graduates.

The proposed increase in application fees, from the current $470 to $69,530, is completely unreasonable. Such a dramatic increase is massively disproportionate to the administrative costs of processing applications and would effectively make OPT inaccessible. The proposed fee is so exorbitant that it is difficult to imagine any university or institution being able to absorb the cost on behalf of its students, particularly small liberal arts institutions like Carleton College where I attend. More than simply discouraging OPT participation, this policy would more broadly discourage international students from pursuing higher education in the United States in the first place. Countries such as China, Australia, and the United Kingdom are actively competing to attract international students. Making the United States a less affordable and welcoming destination risks driving talented students toward these alternatives, along with the economic, intellectual, and cultural contributions they would otherwise bring here.

The proposed changes would also create significant uncertainty for American employers. Faced with the possibility of exorbitant fees, shifting regulatory requirements, and potential penalties or prosecution for noncompliance, employers may become increasingly reluctant to hire international graduates, even when those graduates are qualified for the positions. This would effectively undermine the purpose of OPT by making employment opportunities less accessible and placing international students at a disadvantage in the job market. It would also discourage employers from investing in international talent, ultimately making American businesses and institutions less competitive.

These consequences extend well beyond international students themselves. At Carleton, international students make invaluable contributions to our campus and surrounding communities. In 2024, international students contributed $518 million to Minnesota's economy and supported approximately 3,530 jobs. At Carleton alone, international students contribute an estimated $12 million to Minnesota's economy and help support 50 jobs on our small campus. Their contributions are not merely financial, with international students enriching classroom discussions, participating in faculty-led research, and providing domestic students with valuable cross-cultural experiences and perspectives with massive educational value in an increasingly interconnected world. Restricting OPT would therefore harm not only international graduates but also American employers, universities, domestic students, and the communities that benefit greatly from them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule. Beyond its extraordinary price, the NPRM contains four analytical and design flaws requiring a specific response. These comments address Sections V, VI, and VII (91 FR 64566).

1. Financial deterrence is not evidence of fraud detection.

In Section VII.A.5.b(2), DHS estimates an additional 0.5 hours of DSO review per OPT application, including SEVIS fee updates, and 0.5 hours of administrator time to process payment. These are incremental workload estimates, not evidence of more effective fraud investigations. Yet DHS predicts that the fees will improve scrutiny and deter abuse.

What evidence links a $70,000 payment by a school to better detection of fraudulent employment? How would DHS distinguish improved compliance from schools simply refusing to recommend eligible students? DHS should compare the fee approach against targeted audits, employer verification, and risk-based reviews using measurable enforcement outcomes. A financial barrier is not a substitute for evidence of effectiveness.

2. The opportunity-cost model confuses social value with ability to pay.

In Section VII.A.5.c, DHS uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the opportunity cost of lost participation. DHS acknowledges that true costs could be higher or lower, but assumes stakeholders can share costs whenever OPT's benefits exceed the fee.

This assumption ignores liquidity constraints and coordination failures. OPT can generate value for a student, employer, university, and the broader economy without any single party having the cash, budget authority, or mechanism to fund $70,000 up front. Benefits may accrue over years, while payment precedes the DSO recommendation. Inability to pay does not establish that an OPT opportunity is worth less than the fee.

DHS should test alternative estimates using wages, enrollment sensitivity, institutional financing constraints, and uncertainty ranges rather than treating its proposed charge as a proxy for lost social value.

3. The structure discourages the training it claims to safeguard.

Section VII.A.5.d(3) acknowledges that dividing the same maximum 12-month ordinary OPT allowance between pre-completion and post-completion training can cost $100,000, versus $70,000 if used only after graduation. DHS even anticipates that schools will discourage pre-completion OPT due to this fee differential.

This is a perverse incentive. Two students may use the same total authorized training time, yet the one gaining earlier degree-related experience creates an extra $30,000 obligation. DHS should explain how discouraging legitimate practical training during enrollment advances program integrity. The same aggregate OPT entitlement should not be penalized merely for being used in two stages.

4. The transition rules penalize lawful prior participation.

Sections V.C and VI describe prospective application, yet the transition analysis in Section VII.B assumes a $70,000 initial fee for a STEM OPT recommendation when no initial fee was paid previously. Someone already lawfully authorized for post-completion OPT could thus face the initial fee when seeking an extension, solely because the fee did not exist at the time of their first authorization.

This is not equivalent to a first-time OPT applicant. Existing students, schools, and employers have made commitments under prior rules. A 60-day delay after publication may not allow a school to budget $70,000 per affected student; STEM extension applicants cannot simply choose an earlier eligibility date. Nor should access to the $30,000 subsequent fee depend on payment of a fee that could not previously have been paid.

DHS should grandfather students who received initial OPT authorization or a DSO recommendation before the effective date. Otherwise, it should explain why previously authorized students are treated as first-time fee payers and quantify the impact on existing cohorts.

Based on the above reasoning, I urge DHS to withdraw this rule. At minimum, it should substantiate the anti-fraud mechanism, replace the unsupported opportunity-cost proxy, eliminate the pre-/post-completion penalty, and establish explicit grandfathering. Regulation should distinguish actual compliance from financial exclusion and economic value from ability to pay.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule, citing financial deterrence and analytical flaws.

comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, “Optional Practical Training Fees” (RIN 1653-AB01)

I am a second-year Ph.D. biochemistry student studying mammalian chemoreceptors. I am writing to oppose the proposed fees in 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), which would require schools to pay $70,000 before an initial OPT recommendation for an F-1 student and $30,000 before each subsequent recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension.

Throughout my training, I have met many incredibly smart and skilled international researchers. My very first mentor in research was an international scientist who taught me every skill and technique I needed to get started, and many of my colleagues are international students I learn from every day. Without them, my scientific journey would not have been the same. This rule would make it extremely difficult for people like them to continue their education and careers in the United States.

Although the fee is assessed on schools, the proposal contemplates that schools may recover it from students or employers. In biomedical research, those employers are often universities themselves, which cannot pay up to $100,000 per international hire. The practical result is that OPT would survive only for a select few, likely those with the most financial resources.

International researchers bring specialized skills and expertise that are hard to replace in their fields, and OPT is how many of them continue contributing to U.S. research after graduating. Pricing them out of OPT will discourage talented students from applying to U.S. programs at all, significantly reducing our biomedical research productivity.

DHS says the rule is meant to combat fraud, strengthen integrity, and protect U.S. workers, but I fail to see how it accomplishes these goals. Removing people from roles that require specialized skills does not create openings for Americans. It leaves the work undone. If the goal is a stronger domestic research workforce, the answer is greater investment in the NSF and NIH.

I'd also like to ask DHS to explain how the $70,000 figure was determined. Students already pay the Form I-765 filing fee, and I have not seen a justification tying this amount to the actual cost of processing an OPT recommendation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This proposed rule would be harmful for America and higher education in this country. The following three points illustrate the most likely result had such a rule become effective.

1. College education and other types of higher education are effective and helpful when students get to practice and apply what they learned in the classroom to the workplace. Being able to work for a year to enable that application through OPT is a significant part of the education America has been offering to international students.
2. Raising the fees to apply for OPT to $70k would place the financial pressure on those international students. Although the rule proposes that the fees could be paid by the university, the employer, or the student. It is likely that the pressure would fall on the student. $70k is a significant amount of money that many international student cannot afford, or even when it’s affordable for some, they might refuse to do that simply because it’s not cost-effective and to pay would be a bad financial investment/decision.
3. Therefore, raising OPT fees to $70k and then $30k for the two years of STEM OPT would discourage international students from investing in higher education in America. Even international students with greater financial resources will think through their options and likely make the investment in other countries or areas, such as England, Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Japan.

The consequences mentioned above would be harmful for America for the following reasons.
1. America used to attract one of the brightest minds and brains from all over the country to receive one of the best education opportunities in this country. As a result, they have been contributing to the academic and professional development in this country. Such development includes academic breakthroughs, technological innovations, professional contributions, and so on. Those accomplishments help American universities and society and the status of the country in academia as well as the professional world. When policies discourage those students and push them to other countries, the result is harmful to American universities and society.
2. Tuition from International students has been contributing to the establishment and development of U.S. universities. Generally, and on average, an international student pays more tuition to contribute to the universities financially compared to an American student. Tuition from international students also takes up a significant portion of all the income going in. Not receiving tuition from international students will hurt universities financially, thereby hurting the quality of education Americans receive. Moreover, when universities cannot get enough money from international students, they might need to raise tuition fees for American students, making higher education even less affordable for local students.
3. Losing international students in American campuses will disable an educational environment filled with diversity and different perspectives from around the world.

In addition, the rationale for the proposed rule is insufficiently justified. One of the stated purposes of the proposed rule is to protect American workers and their employment opportunities. While restricting international students’ access to employment may create opportunities for American workers in certain circumstances, preventing international students from applying their classroom education in the workplace does not necessarily increase overall employment opportunities for Americans. International graduates also contribute their knowledge and skills to American businesses, potentially supporting innovation, economic growth, and job creation. Therefore, the potential benefits to American workers should be weighed against the broader economic and educational consequences of restricting OPT participation.

Simply substituting American workers for international graduates is not a sustainable solution to the challenges facing the American labor market. Rather than merely redistributing existing employment opportunities, policies should address the underlying causes of limited job availability and promote economic growth and job creation. Restricting international graduates’ access to employment does not address these structural challenges.

Policymakers have limited time, energy, and intellectual resources. They should devote those those limited resources to developing policies that address the underlying structural causes of the challenging American job market, rather than focusing on superficial measures that fail to address the root causes of the problem and can create additional problems.

For all the reasons mentioned above, I urge the Immigration and Customs Enforcement Bureau to reconsider the proposed rule and withdraw it.

I am an F-1 doctoral student in computer science, writing in my personal capacity to comment on the proposed rule that would require a fee of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation, payable by the school before issuing the recommendation.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this fee schedule or reduce it substantially for the following reasons.

First, although the fee would formally be charged to schools, DHS itself acknowledges that these costs may be passed on to students or employers. Alternatively, universities would have to absorb substantial expenses that many institutions cannot reasonably afford. At this level, the fee would create a financial barrier that could prevent otherwise fully qualified students from accessing practical training, regardless of their academic merit or compliance with immigration regulations.

Second, the proposed amounts appear disproportionate to the stated objectives. DHS describes the fees as a deterrent to fraud and compares them with other employment-based immigration fees. However, the proposal does not adequately demonstrate why charges of $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary to achieve these objectives, or why less burdensome compliance and enforcement measures would be insufficient. Students already pay separate USCIS filing fees for employment authorization. Legitimate students should not face prohibitive financial barriers as a substitute for targeted fraud prevention.

Third, OPT provides an important opportunity for STEM doctoral graduates to apply their research training in U.S. universities, laboratories, and industry. Under the proposed schedule, an initial OPT period followed by a STEM OPT extension could require a total of $100,000 in fees. Such costs could discourage universities from supporting qualified graduates and reduce opportunities for international researchers to contribute to the U.S. research workforce. The potential effects on graduate enrollment, scientific research, and the retention of highly trained researchers deserve serious consideration.
