comments.title: Comment Submitted by Edward Cunningham
comments.commentText:
I am writing as a Canadian student who genuinely loves the United States and wants nothing more than to build my future here. I grew up in Canada, went to university in Scotland for two years, and eventually transferred to the University of Oklahoma. I am now pursuing graduate studies in accounting in Texas. Having lived and studied in three different countries, I can confidently say there is nowhere else I would rather be than America. One of the primary reasons I left Canada was because I felt it had lost some of the things America still celebrates, like the ability to work hard, take risks, make something of yourself, and actually celebrate success. I genuinely believe America is the greatest country on Earth, and a big part of that is because it rewards ambition and gives people the opportunity to succeed.
Don't get me wrong, as someone who is not American, I absolutely believe there should be stricter immigration requirements and that American citizens should come first when it comes to employment opportunities. I have no issue with greater oversight, stricter requirements, or having to work harder to earn the opportunity to stay here. In fact, I think it should be harder than it currently is. However, I think the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training fee is too far. I understand the fee would fall on universities rather than directly on students, but the consequences for students like me would effectively be the same. This is especially frustrating in accounting, where firms need qualified professionals and graduates need practical experience to begin their careers. I am not asking for preferential treatment or for an American to lose an opportunity because of me. I am simply asking for a reasonable chance to compete, prove myself, and contribute.
For me specifically, my ambitions go well beyond just getting a job. I want to eventually build a business in America, create jobs in America, and contribute to the economy. I would also love to serve my community as a parttime law enforcement officer someday, if I get the honor of becoming a citizen. I genuinely love this country and want to give back to it. I fully support protecting American workers and preventing abuse of the immigration system, but I think there are much more reasonable ways to accomplish that through stricter eligibility requirements, better enforcement, and affordable fees rather than effectively pricing qualified students out of the opportunity altogether.
I say all the time that America is the greatest country on Earth, and I mean it. If America wants to continue attracting ambitious, hardworking people who genuinely want to contribute, I think it needs to give them a realistic opportunity to do so. Make us earn it, hold us to high standards, and put Americans first. I have absolutely no issue with any of that. But please don't make the financial hurdle so high that people who genuinely love this country and want to help make it even better never get the chance. I want to work harder than anyone else, succeed here, and give back to the country that has made so much possible. America is the greatest country on Earth, and I want to do my part to keep it that way.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states that the proposed $70,000 OPT fee is too far and harms students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by April Valentine
comments.commentText:
Concerning ICEB-2026-0100-0001

For more than 15 years, I have served as a Designated School Official at various higher education institutions, classified as private liberal arts, a Predominately Black Institution, and an R1 ranked university. Regardless of the college or university at which I have served, the F-1 students who chose, applied, and were admitted to study there pursued their degrees with the expectation of having the eligibility to apply for real-world training experience through OPT.

Per SEVIS By The Numbers, “...[there were]194,554 pre- and post-completion optional practical training (OPT) students with both an employment authorization document (EAD) and who reported working for an employer in 2024." There were also "165,524 foreign students participating in STEM OPT in 2024." More than 2 million students earned undergraduate degrees in 2024-2025 according to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center while another 1.4 million earned an associate’s degree.

Time does not allow me to research the number of master’s and doctoral degrees awarded in the same year. However, I will state that from an equity and fairness lens, imposing a “fee” on institutions to pay for students, or having those students pay a “fee” to the university to subsequently send the funds to the US Treasury, not the USCIS, would be neither fair nor equitable to the international students who will have fulfilled the same degree requirements as their American citizen peers.

It is also important to note that this tax imposition will place an undue burden on several units within colleges and universities. Staff in the International Student Services, Business Office, Accounts Payable, and potentially other units would have to coordinate to create entirely new systems to ensure the tax is paid. In addition, what institution has a minimum of $70,000 to pay for one student to pursue an initial period of OPT? Who can determine which student is worthy of the opportunity should the student be able to pay the tax? Can USCIS guarantee an approved petition? For so many reasons, I write in opposition to the imposition of this tax.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that imposing a high fee on F-1 students for OPT is unfair and inequitable.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international graduate student, and I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees. I understand that DHS wants to reduce fraud, improve the OPT program, and protect American workers. However, charging schools $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for later OPT will not solve these problems.

Most international students spend years studying and paying tuition in the United States. OPT gives us a limited period to use what we learned in a job related to our degree. It is an important part of our education, not a guarantee of permanent employment.

The proposed fees are far too high. Many public universities and smaller colleges will not be able to pay them. These schools may stop recommending students for OPT or pass some of the cost to students. As a result, students could lose access to OPT because of money, even when they followed every rule.

If fraud is the concern, DHS should investigate suspicious employers and applications. It could require better employer records, conduct more audits, and punish people who break the rules. Charging every school a large fee treats honest students and schools as if they have done something wrong.

The fee also does not directly protect American workers. It does not address wages, working conditions, or dishonest employers. Instead, it could push educated graduates out of the country after American universities spent years training them.

Please withdraw this proposal and consider more focused ways to prevent fraud. Any fee should be reasonable and based on the real cost of managing the program. Students who follow the law should still have a fair chance to gain practical experience related to their education.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are too high and asks DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment as a concerned citizen with extensive professional experience interpreting and applying F-1 student regulations and advising international students regarding immigration compliance, employment authorization, and practical training benefits.
I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. While DHS states that the proposal is intended to strengthen program integrity, deter fraud, and protect U.S. workers, the proposed rule does not adequately demonstrate how fees of this magnitude are reasonably connected to those objectives.
The proposed fees would function not as administrative charges, but as substantial barriers to participation.
Of particular concern is the rule's limited discussion of the extensive compliance infrastructure already embedded within the F-1 program. In my experience, OPT and STEM OPT are not programs lacking oversight. Rather, they are benefits subject to multiple layers of monitoring, reporting, review, and enforcement involving students, employers, educational institutions, SEVP, USCIS, and DHS.
Throughout the post-completion OPT period, including the 24-month STEM extension period, universities already perform significant compliance functions that support the integrity of the OPT and STEM OPT programs at no cost to DHS. DSOs review training plans, evaluate regulatory eligibility, maintain records, monitor reporting obligations, counsel students regarding compliance requirements, and update SEVIS records accordingly. The proposed rule does not account for these substantial institutional investments, which effectively supplement federal oversight efforts and contribute to program integrity on a daily basis.
In this regard, universities effectively serve as partners in the administration of this benefit. The work performed by Designated School Officials provides an important layer of review that supports program integrity. Yet the proposed rule does not meaningfully address this or explain why such measures are insufficient to address the concerns identified by DHS.
The likely effect of this proposal is not merely increased program integrity. Rather, it appears to discourage participation by otherwise eligible students, reduce the attractiveness of U.S. higher education, and diminish the ability of U.S. employers to recruit graduates who have been educated U.S. institutions. Students weighing educational opportunities increasingly compare options across multiple countries. Policies that significantly restrict access to practical training opportunities may influence enrollment decisions and redirect talented students elsewhere.
Access to practical training should be based on eligibility, compliance with regulatory requirements, and educational objectives. In my experience, compliance challenges are best addressed through education, advising, monitoring, targeted enforcement, and data-driven oversight. Broad financial barriers imposed on all participants are a blunt policy instrument that risks substantial unintended consequences while offering limited evidence that they will achieve the agency's stated goals.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule or substantially revise it. At a minimum, DHS should provide additional evidence supporting the proposed fee levels, conduct a more robust analysis of the consequences for students, educational institutions, and employers, and evaluate less restrictive alternatives capable of advancing program integrity without effectively eliminating access to practical training opportunities.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed exorbitant OPT fees, arguing they create major barriers and lack justification.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees in DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100. In Section VII.A, DHS says the fees would help reduce fraud. I’d like to know what DHS would count as evidence that the policy worked.

Say the number of OPT placements drops by half, and the number of fraud cases DHS finds also drops by half. That would be fewer cases, but DHS would still be finding fraud just as often relative to the size of the program. And if DHS changes how many placements it checks, the number of cases it finds could change for that reason too. A lower case count by itself would tell us very little about whether the fee is making the program more reliable.

Before requiring schools to pay $70,000 for an initial recommendation, DHS should estimate how many legitimate training placements the fee would eliminate for every fraudulent placement it prevents. I’d also like to see DHS compare that estimate with what it could achieve by checking employers with suspicious records and auditing a sample of other placements. That would give DHS a better way to tell whether fraud is actually becoming less common. I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue enforcement that targets the conduct it wants to stop.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and asks DHS to withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly believe that imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 subsequent OPT fee is a disproportionate and counterproductive response that would harm legitimate students, American educational institutions, and the broader U.S. economy.

1. The proposed fees create an unreasonable financial barrier
Optional Practical Training is an educational opportunity designed to allow international students to apply their academic knowledge in a professional environment. It is not a guarantee of employment, permanent residency, or an exemption from existing immigration requirements. Requiring an educational institution to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation, followed by another $30,000 for subsequent training, would make this opportunity financially inaccessible for many qualified students. Although the proposed rule formally places the payment obligation on universities, institutions may be unable or unwilling to absorb these costs. Consequently, students could lose opportunities because of financial considerations rather than their qualifications, academic achievements, or compliance with immigration laws.

2. The proposal risks undermining American higher education and economic competitiveness
International students make significant financial investments in American universities through tuition, housing, transportation, and other living expenses. They also contribute to university research, academic collaboration, and local economic activity. Many students choose American institutions because of their educational excellence and opportunities to gain practical experience in their fields.
A financial barrier of this magnitude could discourage talented students from choosing the United States, reducing international enrollment and weakening the competitiveness of American universities.

3. Financial barriers should not substitute for effective fraud prevention
I fully support stronger oversight, verification of legitimate employment, and appropriate enforcement against individuals or institutions engaging in immigration fraud. However, the ability to pay an extraordinary fee is not evidence of legal compliance, and the inability to pay is not evidence of fraudulent intent.
The proposed fees risk penalizing legitimate students and responsible universities without necessarily addressing the individuals or organizations responsible for actual violations. DHS should instead prioritize targeted employer verification, improved reporting mechanisms, risk-based compliance audits, investigations of suspicious employment arrangements, and meaningful penalties for proven misconduct.
These approaches would more directly address the underlying problems while preserving opportunities for students who follow the law.

4. The proposed rule could disproportionately harm smaller educational institutions
DHS's own regulatory analysis estimates that 841 of 1,389 affected small institutions could experience financial impacts exceeding 1 percent of their estimated annual revenue. These institutions may lack the financial resources to pay substantial OPT fees or obtain external funding. As a result, access to practical training could become dependent on the financial capacity of a student's university rather than the student's academic preparation or eligibility. Such an outcome would create an uneven system that disadvantages students attending smaller institutions, including those serving communities outside major metropolitan areas.

5. DHS should reconsider the proportionality and economic justification of these fees
The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees are extraordinarily high relative to the administrative purpose of recommending a student for practical training.
Furthermore, the proposed rule states that the collected fees would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts rather than retained by ICE to directly fund OPT oversight. This raises an important policy question: How would imposing these extraordinary financial obligations more effectively prevent fraud than targeted enforcement measures? I respectfully request that DHS provide a clearer evidence-based justification demonstrating that these specific fee amounts are necessary, proportionate, and more effective than less burdensome alternatives.

6. The United States should protect both American workers and legitimate educational opportunities
Protecting American workers and supporting international education should not be treated as mutually exclusive objectives. America's strength has long depended on its ability to educate talented individuals, encourage innovation, and create opportunities through institutions that uphold high academic and professional standards. International students who comply with immigration requirements should be evaluated based on their qualifications, conduct, and eligibility, not on whether their university can afford an extraordinary government fee.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees create unreasonable financial barriers and harm students and the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dahlia Halabi
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,I’m writing this comment to express my opposition to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published October 8, 2026. I am a graduate student studying Bioengineering at Harvard University. While I am a US-born citizen, I benefit greatly from the Optional Practical Training (OPT). The OPT makes way for talented, motivated individuals to bring innovative ideas to our country’s research institutions, and over the course of my undergraduate studies and now my PhD in engineering, I have worked with and learned from non-citizen students and trainees who entered the US motivated by the OPT. These international students and trainees make the US research environment competitive; they bring unique skills and perspectives to our laboratories and classrooms and contribute extensively to the research scene and to pedagogy while they study. Importantly, the OPT program allows STEM PhD students on F-1 visas to remain in their labs after completing their degrees to train other scientists, many of them domestic students. The OPT has attracted many of my international student colleagues to the US universities I have studied at, allowing for there to be sufficient demand for challenging, specialized STEM courses and research training programs that I and other domestic students benefit greatly from. The proposed rule is designed to encourage universities to “exercise greater oversight and selectivity” recommending students for OPT, but in practice, it will only make financial capacity the most important factor in determining if a student receives OPT. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ted Cruz
comments.commentText:
Formal Opposition to the Proposed $70,000 Initial OPT Fee and $30,000 Subsequent OPT Fee

Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. While I recognize the importance of protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system, these extraordinarily high fees are disproportionate and could create serious unintended consequences for the U.S. economy.

International students come to the United States, pay substantial tuition, contribute to universities, support local businesses, and invest years of their lives preparing to contribute professionally. OPT provides a pathway for graduates to apply their education, develop practical skills, and contribute to American innovation and economic growth.

Implementing fees of this magnitude would create significant financial barriers for employers and graduates. In particular:

Harm to American businesses and employment: Small businesses, startups, and even established employers may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial fees. This could discourage legitimate hiring, limit business growth, and reduce opportunities for American workers who benefit from productive businesses and expanding industries.
Loss of skilled talent and global competitiveness: International graduates contribute to critical fields, including technology, engineering, healthcare, research, and entrepreneurship. If the United States makes it financially impractical to hire qualified graduates, competing countries will become more attractive destinations for skilled talent, research, and investment.
Unfair financial burden on students and families: International students already pay significant tuition and living expenses, often without access to the same financial assistance available to domestic students. Such excessive fees could undermine years of educational investment and place additional financial pressure on families who have sacrificed considerably to support their children's education.
Disproportionate impact on innovation and economic growth: International graduates do not simply compete for jobs; they also create businesses, contribute to research, pay taxes, purchase goods and services, and support American communities. Restricting their employment opportunities could have broader economic consequences beyond the individual student.
I support strong immigration enforcement and efforts to prevent fraud. However, enforcement should be targeted toward fraudulent employers, unauthorized practices, and violations of immigration regulations—not achieved through excessive fees that penalize legitimate students and employers.

I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to:

Withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees.
Establish reasonable and proportionate fees based on actual administrative and enforcement costs.
Conduct a transparent economic impact assessment, including the effects on small businesses, American employment, universities, and local communities.
Prioritize targeted fraud prevention and employer compliance rather than imposing excessive financial barriers.
Conclusion

The United States has built its position as a global leader through education, innovation, entrepreneurship, and the ability to attract talented individuals from around the world. International graduates who study here and contribute their skills are part of that strength.

Protecting American workers and maintaining immigration integrity are important goals, but policies should strengthen the American economy rather than unintentionally discourage investment, innovation, and legitimate employment.

A fee structure of $70,000 and $30,000 risks turning an opportunity for economic contribution into an unreasonable financial barrier. I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to reconsider and withdraw this proposal and pursue a fair, practical, and economically responsible alternative.

Please protect American competitiveness, support legitimate employers, and preserve opportunities for talented graduates who want to contribute to the United States.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they harm businesses, students, and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an international graduate student at a U.S. university, and I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee [proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2)], along with the requirement that schools pay these fees before a DSO may recommend a student for OPT [proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)]. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

I am qualified to comment because I have lived every stage of the pathway this rule would put out of reach. Over the past eight years in the United States, I studied as an F-1 undergraduate; worked full time at a U.S. firm on OPT, then the STEM OPT extension, and then an H-1B; and have now returned on an F-1 visa for a graduate degree as I prepare to re-enter the U.S. job market.

My U.S. education opened the door to a career I loved, and OPT is what allowed me to walk through it. My employer selected me through the same competitive process as my American peers and invested in my development. Over four years, I grew from a new graduate into a trusted contributor, co-authoring more than five research abstracts and three manuscripts with my colleagues in health economics and outcome research. Those collaborations also gave me lasting friendships and mentors who shaped who I am, at work and in my community. None of this would have been possible without the work authorization that F-1 status provides.

Under the proposed rule, that same path would have required my school to pay $100,000 ($70,000 for my initial OPT and $30,000 for my STEM OPT extension) before I could work a single day. Today, the only OPT-related cost is a filing fee of roughly $500; the proposal would raise it more than a hundredfold. Because students typically request post-completion OPT before graduation, often before receiving a job offer, the $70,000 would be owed before a student knows whether, or where, they will work. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass this cost on to “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers.” For most international students, a charge of this size would put OPT out of reach. For employers, it would make an international graduate far more expensive to hire than an equally qualified domestic candidate, regardless of merit.

This is not abstract for me. I am recruiting for internships and full-time roles right now. From my first job search in college, I know how long and uncertain the process already is for international students, and today’s job market is tighter than the one I entered four years ago. Employers who would gladly hire me on the strength of my experience may simply stop considering candidates who need OPT. A fee of this size would turn a difficult search into a nearly impossible one, for me and for many classmates who are equally ready to contribute here.

DHS states that the fee would ensure “only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate” in OPT and would reduce fraud. I respectfully argue that a flat fee can do neither. It does not measure qualification or detect fraud; it measures only who can pay. I was hired on my qualifications, yet under this rule I would have faced the same $100,000 barrier as anyone else. Meaningful safeguards already exist: during my STEM OPT extension, my employer and I completed a formal training plan, submitted periodic evaluations, and were subject to reporting requirements and possible site visits.

The rule would also weaken U.S. universities’ ability to recruit the most talented students in the world. For prospective international students, the chance to gain practical experience after graduation is a core part of the value of a U.S. degree. A fee of this magnitude sends an unmistakable signal that they are not welcome to stay, and many will choose countries that offer post-study work pathways instead. Fewer international students means less tuition revenue to sustain programs, faculty, and financial aid. And because DHS acknowledges the cost could be passed on to “all students,” American students could end up paying for this rule as well.

The consequences extend to the broader economy and to fields that serve the public. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-2025 academic year. In my own field, healthcare, international graduates contribute to research and innovation that improve patient care and public health. Pricing them out would cost U.S. employers talent they have helped train, and cost the United States its standing as the first choice for the world’s most ambitious students.

I chose the United States eight years ago because it offered a world-class education and a real chance to put it to work. That choice paid off in both directions: I built a career, and my employer, my colleagues, and my community gained someone committed to contributing. This rule would close that door to the

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Charlie Abbott
comments.commentText:
Subject: Strong Opposition to the Proposed $70,000 Initial OPT Fee and $30,000 Subsequent OPT Fee

Docket Number: ICEB-2026-0100

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. Although I understand the government's responsibility to protect American workers and prevent immigration fraud, imposing fees of this magnitude would create an unreasonable financial barrier for legitimate international graduates and the employers seeking to hire them.

International students make substantial investments in the United States by paying tuition, living expenses, and other educational costs. They contribute to universities, local businesses, research institutions, and the broader economy. OPT allows these graduates to apply the knowledge and skills they have developed through their education while contributing to American businesses and industries.

The proposed fees could have several serious consequences:

Negative impact on American employers: Many startups, small businesses, and research organizations cannot afford an additional $70,000 or $30,000 expense to hire a qualified graduate. Employers may choose not to hire international candidates, even when they are highly qualified. This could limit business growth, reduce innovation, and indirectly affect employment opportunities for American workers.
Loss of skilled talent and economic competitiveness: International graduates contribute to important sectors such as technology, engineering, healthcare, finance, and scientific research. Excessively high fees could encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities in countries with more reasonable employment policies. The United States risks losing skilled individuals, future entrepreneurs, researchers, and potential job creators to global competitors.
Unfair burden on students and families: International students already face significantly higher educational expenses and often have limited access to financial assistance. Many families make substantial financial sacrifices to support their children's education in the United States. These additional fees could make it extremely difficult for graduates to secure employment and benefit from the education they have worked so hard to obtain.
Broader consequences for American communities: International graduates contribute through taxes, consumer spending, entrepreneurship, and professional services. Their participation supports local economies and creates opportunities for businesses and communities. Restricting legitimate employment through excessive fees could negatively affect more people than just the international students themselves.
I strongly support protecting American workers, preventing fraudulent employment practices, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, these objectives can be achieved through stronger employer verification, targeted investigations, compliance monitoring, and reasonable administrative fees. Excessive financial penalties should not become a barrier to legitimate employment.

I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to:

Withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees.
Establish reasonable fees that reflect actual administrative and enforcement costs.
Conduct a comprehensive economic impact assessment before implementing such a significant policy.
Consider the effects on American employers, domestic workers, universities, international graduates, and local communities.
Focus enforcement efforts on fraudulent employers and violations rather than placing disproportionate financial burdens on legitimate participants.
Final Statement

The United States has become a global leader because it attracts talent, encourages innovation, supports entrepreneurship, and provides opportunities for people to contribute through education and hard work.

International graduates who study in the United States are not simply seeking employment; they are also potential innovators, researchers, entrepreneurs, taxpayers, and future job creators. Policies that make it financially impractical for American employers to hire them could weaken the very economic competitiveness the country seeks to protect.

I urge DHS and ICE to reconsider and withdraw this proposal. Immigration integrity and the protection of American workers should remain priorities, but they must be balanced with economic growth, fairness, and America's long-term global competitiveness.

Please do not turn legitimate educational and professional opportunities into financial barriers that ultimately hurt American businesses, workers, families, and communities.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed high fees create an unreasonable financial barrier and harm employers and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Zachary Spritzer
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It relies on selective examples, unsupported assumptions, conflicting data, and a flawed cost-benefit analysis. As a current PhD student at a research university, I see firsthand how critical OPT is to advancing research and bringing incredible minds to work in this country.

**1. Selective evidence (Sec. IV.A)**
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests that year, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video. The text says the video identified 10,000 students working for suspicious employers, while footnote 56 says 10,000 suspicious employers. Either way, suspicion is not proof, and 10,000 is only about 3% of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. Most cited cases involve employer fraud uncovered through existing site visits and prosecutions, yet DHS says the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." There is no evidence this fee would have prevented the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

**2. Conflicting data**
DHS claims STEM OPT has "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of roughly 92,000 participants by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, citing 165,524 participants. But its own analysis reports 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, consistent with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study using 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not an analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires comparable wages (Form I-983).

**3. High fees do not prevent fraud (Sec. IV.C)**
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students," but a high fee measures ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Employers already selling job letters can build the fee into their prices, while honest students who cannot afford $70,000 are excluded. DHS provides no evidence that any fee level would reduce fraud.

**4. This is a tax, not a fee**
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, generating an estimated $8.7–16.9 billion annually. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must cover program costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no costs; it is modeled on an H-1B fee to discourage participation. That makes it an unauthorized tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). INA 214(a)'s authority over "time and conditions" cannot justify a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources failing to keep pace with the program, yet none of this money would fund compliance. DHS also suggests it may end OPT without the fees, while admitting it cannot keep the revenue.

**5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)**
DHS leaves benefits unquantified while estimating costs of up to $8.2 billion annually. It caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee, arguing parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. This is circular: much of OPT's value, including innovation, taxes, and local spending, benefits the public, not just whoever pays. DHS also fails to model enrollment losses, an omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

**6. Alternatives dismissed**
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as too slow or costly, despite relying on those tools to uncover the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, also cited by DHS, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative convenience is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

**7. Reliance and unintended consequences**
DHS calls reliance speculative because only about 20% of F-1 students use OPT. That still represents roughly 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt based on the program. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000, versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, penalizing students who combine work and study. Refund denials also cannot be appealed.

**8. Small institutions and states**
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue, and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS offers no relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then says it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, despite requiring 1,044 state institutions to pay.

**9. Process and baseline**
DHS allows 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days for a paperwork change estimated to take five minutes. It also relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) as its baseline and vetting rationale without noting that the rule has been postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nora Lucas
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. These amounts are unrealistic for international graduates, particularly postdoctoral researchers whose annual salaries may be lower than the proposed fees.

Although DHS places payment responsibility on educational institutions, it is unrealistic to expect universities to absorb such enormous costs. Many schools would likely pass these fees on to students or limit the number of OPT recommendations they issue. This would create de facto barriers to OPT, with institutions potentially selecting applicants based on financial considerations or additional criteria not clearly defined in federal regulations. Students who otherwise meet all legal eligibility requirements could effectively lose access to OPT.

Furthermore, it is unclear how imposing $70,000 could reduce the fraud incidents that DHS is claiming to prevent, such as false employment documents, establishment of shell companies, missing employment records, and offshore operation. For instance, per 2024 SEVIS by the Numbers Report, from 200,000 to 300,000 F-1 international students are authorized for OPT every year. However, the proposed rule indicates that around 5% of those F-1 nonimmigrant students were identified to have been engaged with “highly suspect employers.” This suggests the Immigration and Customs Enforcement Bureau is attempting to preemptively criminalize and impose financial penalties to 95% of law-abiding students based on the statistics of a small sample. Therefore, the claim that imposing $70,000 to all OPT applicants will reduce the overall OPT fraud rate is unsubstantiated.

I am deeply concerned by DHS's indication that it may discontinue OPT without these fees. Given the significant contributions this program has made to U.S. research and innovation, it is unreasonable to shut down OPT contingent on approving a nonsensical fee just to prevent a potentially minor fraud rate. International students have invested years of effort and resources in American education and have often contributed to federally funded research. Such a drastic change in policy would be unfair to international students and detrimental to the domestic economy and development.

In sum, although fraud prevention is important, excessive fees are not a substitute for effective oversight. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees are unrealistic and will create financial barriers for international graduates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Comments in Response to Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed rule and urge that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety, and that the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program remains intact.

In Section VII(A)(5)(D)(3) of this proposed rule, DHS specifically requests information on pre-completion OPT applications: "While DHS expects future participation in pre-completion OPT to decline, DHS cannot reasonably predict the extent of this decrease. DHS requests comments and any available data regarding this discussion which could further improve these estimates." (p.64591)

Due to the enormous backlog of USCIS cases, processing times for pre-completion OPT cases appear to have absorbed the brunt of delays in OPT-related I-765 applications. As a DSO at a private institution, I have observed multiple cases where pre-completion OPT cases have remained in pending status over a year after the initial request was submitted. Premium processing cases in this category also experience delays despite the 30-business-days guarantee. With Curricular Practical Training made off-limits to large masses of students and pre-completion OPT being the only viable pathway to hands-on training, students are either opting for premium processing or forgoing opportunities all together, which in turn affects their ability to make the most of their program of study. I fully anticipate that this rule will cause steeper declines in pre-completion OPT applications.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges that it be withdrawn in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Zongdi Xu
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. Requiring $70,000 initially and $30,000 per subsequent recommendation, i.e. potentially $100,000 for post-completion OPT plus STEM extension, would create a financial barrier favoring wealthy students and employers, excluding startups and small firms. With 447,000 information-sector layoffs in 2025 (BLS), placements may end after authorization; the rule bars refunds once documents are issued. Employer-paid fees could also coerce trainees into unsuitable roles.
Regulatory analysis must consider where next-generation deep tech is built: in 2024, temporary visa holders earned 61% of U.S. computer and information science doctorates and 54% in engineering (NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates, fig. 9). These graduates transfer specialized knowledge in chip design, AI infrastructure, and biotechnology into prototype validation, process development, and deployment. Reduced retention could shift study or work abroad, limiting U.S. commercialization, company formation, and training. DHS should estimate impacts by field, school type, employer size, and region, including effects of eliminating the employment-based grace period. To deter fraud while protecting current students, DHS should compare fees with risk-based site visits, employer and duty verification, and enforcement against sham placements. Since fee revenue would go to Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, DHS must justify how fees deter fraud versus legitimate cases and publish supporting evidence. If adopted, the fee should protect enrolled students and current STEM OPT participants, remain affordable, include hardship relief, and be evidence-based.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create financial barriers and harm students and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Opposition to the Proposed Rule Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 on Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an international Graduate Student, in my fourth year of Computer Science PhD, at an Ivy League university.
I have been staying in the USA and contributing to its economy (rent, taxes, commute, etc) for 3 years.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule concerning Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees.
Specifically, the Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 , Section V. A: Establishing a Fee for Initial and Any Subsequent OPT

I am deeply concerned about the financial burden this proposal could impose on international students and its broader implications for American higher education, economic competitiveness, and fairness.
International students like myself, already make substantial financial contributions to the United States through tuition, housing, healthcare, and everyday expenses. Many invest significant resources in obtaining an American education with the hope of applying their knowledge and skills through practical training after graduation.

Imposing excessive additional fees on OPT applicants would create unnecessary financial barriers, particularly for students from middle- and lower-income backgrounds. Access to professional opportunities should not depend primarily on a student’s financial circumstances.

Furthermore, international graduates contribute valuable skills to the American workforce, particularly in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. OPT helps American employers access globally trained talent while allowing graduates to gain practical experience in their fields of study.
Making OPT substantially more expensive risks discouraging talented students from choosing American universities and may ultimately weaken the United States’ competitiveness in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and quantum computing.

Additionally, OPT is intended to provide practical training directly related to a student’s academic studies. Excessive fees would undermine this educational purpose by transforming access to practical training into a privilege determined by university or personal financial resources rather than academic achievement or professional qualifications.

Any proposed fee increases should be supported by transparent, detailed evidence demonstrating their necessity and proportionality to actual administrative costs. The government should also carefully evaluate the potential economic consequences, including reduced international student enrollment, diminished talent retention, and negative impacts on American universities and employers.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider this proposal, conduct a comprehensive assessment of its financial and economic consequences, and avoid imposing disproportionate burdens on international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Officers and Regulatory Specialists,

I am writing to respectfully offer my public comment in opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. As an international student pursuing higher education in the United States under an F-1 visa, I deeply respect the Department’s ongoing commitment to safeguarding national security, maintaining the integrity of our immigration framework, and protecting the American workforce. However, I am compelled to voice my profound concern regarding the proposed assessment of a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee. While I appreciate the intent to deter bad actors and fraudulent entities, imposing such an unprecedented financial burden creates immense personal hardship for law-abiding students while inadvertently harming American higher education and the broader domestic economy.

From a personal perspective, the opportunity to participate in practical training is a vital extension of the academic journey rather than a financial privilege or an employment loophole. International students and their families make extraordinary sacrifices, often liquidating life savings or securing substantial loans, to afford full tuition and living expenses at American universities. Entering an academic program with the understanding that post-graduation training would allow us to apply our classroom knowledge in real-world settings forms a core part of the decision to study in the United States. Assessing a $70,000 fee places an insurmountable barrier before students who have meticulously followed every immigration rule. For the vast majority of scholars, a fee of this magnitude far exceeds an entry-level annual salary, effectively pricing dedicated graduates out of the very training opportunities their education prepared them to fulfill.

Beyond individual hardship, this policy threatens the vitality and global competitiveness of American higher education institutions. U.S. colleges and universities rely heavily on international scholars to foster vibrant, diverse academic communities and to drive cutting-edge research. Because smaller non-profit institutions and public universities cannot absorb these multi-thousand-dollar transfers on behalf of their students, the proposed fees will inevitably lead to a sharp decline in international enrollment. Prospective scholars will increasingly redirect their talents to nations with more welcoming post-study work frameworks, such as Canada, Australia, or members of the European Union. Over time, the loss of international student tuition and intellectual contributions will undermine campus operations, force reductions in academic programming, and diminish the collaborative research environment that benefits domestic students.

Furthermore, dismantling the practical training ecosystem runs counter to the long-term economic interests of the United States. International graduates, particularly those in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, serve as crucial catalysts for technological innovation and economic growth. Restricting their access to temporary practical experience deprives American industries of specialized talent and diminishes the nationwide potential for research and development. While curbing fraudulent shell companies and bad actors is a necessary objective, achieving it through financial exclusion risks penalizing legitimate scholars and eroding the aggregate productivity of the national economy. Fraud is best combated through heightened administrative verification, focused employer site visits, and targeted enforcement against bad actors, rather than an extraordinary fee structure that renders the entire program inaccessible.

In conclusion, I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider and withdraw the proposed OPT fee schedule. Upholding the integrity of the immigration system does not require closing the door on legitimate international talent. By pursuing balanced, targeted oversight measures rather than prohibitive financial demands, the Department can maintain robust security standards while preserving the immense mutual benefits that international scholars bring to American campuses and communities. Thank you for your time, consideration, and dedication to serving the public interest through open dialogue.

Respectfully submitted,
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create severe financial hardship and harm international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
ubject: Strong Support for Proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees Rule
I am writing to express my strongest support for the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to introduce a fee structure for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. As a parent, I have witnessed firsthand how the current, un-tariffed OPT program actively harms the career prospects of recent American graduates.
My daughter is currently on the verge of completing her hard-earned higher education. Despite her qualifications, dedication, and readiness to enter the workforce, her prospects of securing a job have been severely diminished. She is entering a entry-level labor market that has been heavily distorted by the OPT program.
Under the current system, foreign graduates under OPT function as a massive pool of subsidized, cheap labor for corporations. Because employers are exempt from paying FICA (Social Security and Medicare) taxes for OPT workers, hiring a foreign graduate provides an automatic, unfair financial discount to companies over hiring qualified American citizens and permanent residents. This financial loophole incentivizes corporations to bypass local talent in favor of lower-cost foreign labor, driving down entry-level wages and locking American graduates out of the very economy they just trained to enter.
My daughter, like thousands of other young Americans, is facing an uphill battle because she cannot "compete" with corporate tax avoidance and artificially suppressed wages. The current system creates an uneven playing field where American students pay exorbitant tuition, only to find themselves structurally disadvantaged upon graduation.
By implementing the proposed $70,000 employer fee for initial OPT participation and the $30,000 fee for STEM extensions, DHS will finally neutralize this artificial economic distortion. These fees will compel corporations to prioritize domestic talent, ensuring they only utilize the OPT program for its original, intended purpose: filling genuine, specialized talent shortages, rather than sourcing cheap, tax-exempt entry-level labor.
This rule is a necessary step toward restoring fairness, protecting young American workers, and ensuring that our higher education system actually leads to viable career paths for domestic graduates. I urge DHS to finalize and implement this proposed rule without delay.

Respectfully submitted,
Sanjay Sharma
(California)
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong support for the proposed OPT fees rule to protect American graduates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Medha Kler
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student. I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it or substantially revise it.

1. The remedy does not match the problem (Sec. IV.A, IV.C). DHS’s fraud evidence centers on shell employers, nonexistent worksites, and visa mills. It cites an investigation identifying more than 10,000 students at “highly suspect” employers, roughly 5% of the 194,554 students with OPT in 2024. A flat $70,000 fee applies to every school and every student, including the large majority with legitimate employers, and does nothing to stop a fraudulent employer. DHS should target abusers through employer verification, E-Verify participation, site visits, and decertification of schools that operate as visa mills.

2. DHS dismissed targeted alternatives without evidence (Sec. IV.C). DHS rejected expanded site visits, reporting, and training plans because a fee is faster and cheaper for the government. DHS provides no data that a fee reduces fraud rather than just participation.

3. The fee does not fund enforcement (Sec. IV.C). DHS states the fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and ICE will not retain them. The rule adds no oversight capacity.

4. The regulatory analysis does not quantify benefits and understates harms (Sec. VII.A, Tables 1 and 10). DHS lists monetized benefits as “Not Estimated,” yet projects annualized costs of about $4.1 billion (up to $8.2 billion). It concedes it “cannot precisely quantify” opportunity costs. A rule designed to shrink participation needs a quantified justification.

5. Small institutions bear a severe burden (Tables 15 and 17). DHS estimates that 841 of 1,389 small affected institutions (60.5%) would see impacts above 1% of revenue in the transition year, and 98 would exceed 20% post-transition. Many of these schools will simply stop recommending OPT, and their students will lose access.

6. The fee structure creates perverse incentives (Sec. VII.A.5.d(3)). DHS acknowledges that a student using both pre- and post-completion OPT triggers $100,000 in fees versus $70,000 for post-completion only, and it expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT. That reduces work-based learning during the degree, contrary to the program’s purpose.

7. I oppose the alternative on which DHS requested comment (Sec. V.A). Charging the $70,000 fee again each time a student moves to a higher degree level would deter students from pursuing advanced study.

8. Students who relied on current rules should be exempt (Sec. VI). DHS dismisses reliance interests as “speculative,” but students like me chose programs and financed multi-year, six-figure tuition based on the existing OPT framework. At minimum, the rule should not apply to anyone enrolled before the final rule is published. [Add 2–3 sentences on how this affects your own decisions or plans.]

9. The comment period is too short. DHS itself designates this an economically significant rule, yet allowed only 30 days. I request that DHS extend or reopen the period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and urges DHS to withdraw or revise it.

comments.title: MM37 Comment Submitted by Sara Es
comments.commentText:
I am a current F-1 graduate student. I recognize that Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a temporary, discretionary benefit—not an entitlement to employment or a guarantee of authorization. I am not asking DHS to preserve OPT unchanged or arguing that the agency cannot regulate the program. I ask DHS to distinguish future students, who can make informed decisions under new rules, from current students, who have already made substantial commitments in reliance on the framework in place when they began their studies.

For many years, eligible F-1 students have been able to seek up to 12 months of post-completion OPT, with an additional 24-month extension for graduates of qualifying STEM programs. This was not a promise of a job, but a known part of the academic-to-professional pathway that students could reasonably consider when deciding to study in the United States and planning their careers. Students already here have committed years of their lives and substantial resources to tuition, housing, relocation, and living expenses. Many have left jobs, paused careers, and moved away from their families. These commitments cannot be undone by giving students 60 days' notice after a new rule is finalized.

The proposed rule would impose a $70,000 fee for an institution's initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for a subsequent recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. Although the institution would formally pay the fee, the proposal allows schools to pass the cost to students, the student body generally, or employers. It also allows a school or DSO to decline to recommend a student for OPT rather than pay the fee. In practice, OPT could become inaccessible to students who planned their education around the existing framework, even if the fee is not billed directly to them.

This is especially important for STEM students. Practical training is not simply an opportunity to remain in the United States or obtain a job after graduation; it bridges academic learning and professional practice. It allows graduates to learn how scientific and technical knowledge is applied in workplaces, how projects and teams operate, and how research and technical skills become practical solutions. For students who intend to return home, this experience can be essential to applying their education in local industries, developing new ventures, or becoming entrepreneurs. University coursework alone cannot always provide the same exposure to professional methods and practical constraints.

I am particularly concerned that the proposed transition rule uses the date of the DSO recommendation—not the date a student began the degree—as the trigger for the new fees. A student who began a multi-year degree before the rule was proposed could therefore face this new financial condition simply because they will not be eligible to request OPT until after it takes effect. This is prospective only in a formal sense: it imposes a new condition on students whose educational decisions and substantial investments were made under the prior framework.

DHS acknowledges in Section VI and footnote 124 that current F-1 students who have already moved to the United States are in a different position from prospective students. That difference should have practical consequences. OPT need not have been the sole reason a student chose to study in the United States for its established availability to have been an important part of their academic and professional planning. The fact that not every F-1 student ultimately uses OPT does not diminish the reliance of those already enrolled who planned their path around it.

I respectfully ask DHS to revise Sections V.C and VI so the proposed fees apply only to students who begin a new degree program after the final rule's effective date. F-1 students enrolled in their current degree programs before publication of this proposal on October 8, 2026, should remain under the existing OPT framework for that program, including initial post-completion OPT and any eligible 24-month STEM OPT extension—even if their DSO recommendation is issued after the new rule takes effect. They would remain subject to existing OPT eligibility, training, and oversight requirements; this request is only for protection from the newly proposed fees.

This approach would allow DHS to implement a new policy for future cohorts while treating current students fairly. Students enrolling after the effective date can assess the changed conditions before committing years of time and substantial resources. Those who have already made these commitments should not have the terms of their educational pathway changed midway through their studies.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against the prohibitive proposed OPT fees that disrupt current students' plans.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule and to urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw it.

The proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one are not tied to the cost of administering the program. They are roughly 140 times the current fee of about $500, and DHS has not shown that they reflect the cost of any service it provides. Because the proceeds would be deposited in the general Treasury, the fees function as a revenue measure rather than a cost-based charge, which goes beyond DHS’s authority under INA 214(a) and invites legal challenge.

DHS also failed to adequately analyze the rule’s impacts. It estimates that 2,478 schools would pay between $8.4 and $16.5 billion in annual fees, yet it dismisses the effects on universities, employers, and U.S. competitiveness as too speculative to consider. Failing to weigh important aspects of the problem is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The remedy does not match the stated problem. DHS cites fraud and abuse, but the fee applies equally to every OPT student, nearly all of whom follow the rules, and DHS has not explained how the fees would be used to detect or prevent fraud. Targeted enforcement against bad actors would address the concern without penalizing compliant students and schools.

The proposal is also ambiguous. It does not clearly state whether a STEM extension would cost $30,000 or $70,000 for a student whose first OPT began before the rule takes effect. DHS also floats re-charging the $70,000 fee when a student begins OPT at a higher degree level, an alternative I urge it to reject. These points should be clarified before any rule is finalized.

Finally, the rule will discourage participation in practical training. DHS itself anticipates that charging separately for pre-completion and post-completion recommendations could discourage pre-completion OPT. Combined with fees of this size, the rule will push schools to limit OPT access and weaken the pipeline of international talent that U.S. employers and universities depend on.

For these reasons, I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should substantially reduce the fees, tie them to documented costs, and publish a full analysis of the impacts on students, schools, and employers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees are excessive, unauthorized, inadequately analyzed, and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to Bureau’s proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees," published on October 8, 2026.

I submit these comments from a critical and deeply personal perspective: I am on an H4 visa. I have paid taxes, and raised my family here. Currently, I have one child attending an American university and another who has recently "aged out" of dependent status. While this rule is framed as a regulatory adjustment for educational institutions, its real-world impact is a devastating financial and humanitarian blow to lawful, high-skilled immigrant families who have followed every rule to contribute to this country.
I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal based on the following severe consequences:

1. Critical Threat to "Aged-Out" Children and Family Unity
Children of long-term H-1B visa holders who grow up in the United States face a precarious future when they turn 21 and "age out" of their dependent H-4 status. For these young adults, transitioning to an F-1 student visa and subsequently utilizing the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program is the primary legal pathway to maintain status, remain with their families, and enter the workforce in the only country they call home. By levying an astronomical $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for extensions, this rule effectively destroys the only viable survival pipeline for aged-out children. It forces unnecessary separation of legal immigrant families, punishing children who have grown up as part of the American fabric.

2. Extreme Financial Duress on Immigrant Households
Universities will be forced to pass these massive new institutional OPT fees directly down to students, this rule creates an insurmountable financial penalty. For a family already managing the high costs of higher education, an unexpected $70,000 to $100,000 surcharge just for a child to gain post-graduation practical training is a financial impossibility.

3. Destruction of the Career Entry Pipeline for the Next Generation
My child currently in college deserves a predictable, fair, and merit-based landscape upon graduation. If universities are forced to restrict OPT recommendations, or if the financial barriers prevent students from applying, the entry-level career pipeline for foreign-born graduates will effectively die. Legitimate students who have worked hard in American classrooms will be barred from gaining the practical experience required to launch their careers, leaving them stranded despite their family's legal status and immense financial investment in American higher education.

4. Misaligned Enforcement and Economic Harm
While the agency’s stated goal is to enhance oversight and curb fraud, punishing compliant, world-class American universities and lawful student applicants is an arbitrary mechanism. It does nothing to target actual bad actors. Instead, by crippling the STEM OPT pipeline, the rule will starve the very American industries—such as technology, engineering, and healthcare—that rely on high-skilled talent. This harms the long-term economic stability of the companies that sponsor legal workers, ultimately damaging the broader American economy.

This proposed rule introduces unprecedented, disproportionate financial barriers that target the most vulnerable segment of the legal immigration community: the children of high-skilled workers. It forces family separation and imposes impossible financial burdens on families who have acted entirely in good faith. I respectfully urge to withdraw this harmful proposal in its entirety.
Thank you for your time and consideration of these comments.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition and urges the agency to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule.

comments.commentText:
This policy is throwing the baby out with the bathwater. That is probably the aptest description of what it is doing. In our obsession with preventing H1B abuse, we risk destroying higher education and our talent pipeline altogether. There are much better ways to prevent OPT fraud without shooting ourselves in the foot.

First, let’s look at what we are gaining. Yes, we might shut down shell companies and prevent OPT fraud. But how much does that help US workers if the students involved are not actually working—and therefore not taking anyone’s job? Given that students on OPT are allowed only 90 days of unemployment to search for a job, all they are doing is buying more time to search for a legitimate job. That does not excuse fraud, but it should make us question whether this tunnel vision on OPT fraud is proportionate to the problem. (Also, European countries like Denmark allows them to stay for 3 years to find a job! We were being extremely stingy with the amount of time!)

We should also keep the scale in perspective. So far, only 10,000 of OPT fraud cases are found. How large a share of the international student population do they represent?

Now let’s look at how much we stand to lose:
* The large fee could deter companies from hiring OPT students altogether. Students will choose to go to Europe and Canada instead—or, at worst for US competitiveness, China. Schools will admit fewer international students and lose a sizeable source of funding. Financial aid for domestic students could also suffer.
* We lose out on top talent. International students make up a substantial share of PhD students in the US. Would people like Elon Musk or Noubar Afeyan, a co-founder of Moderna, still choose to come here? Why go to a country where you cannot get hired?
* And if, by some miracle, they still choose to come, why train them only to send them away? What is the point?
Just look at where the world’s top AI researchers originally come from and tell me the US is not shooting itself in the foot by making it harder for international students to stay. We should go after fraud. But undermining the entire talent pipeline in the process is naive at best and idiotic at worst.
The cure is worse than the illness itself.

Why not just do a real-time E-verify + Tax Data tax check so that OPT with shell companies cannot clear?

I respectfully submit this comment to express my concern regarding the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

I understand and respect the Department’s responsibility to protect the integrity of the OPT program and address fraud or misuse. However, the proposed fee structure of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT could have an extraordinary impact on international students and their families. These amounts are part of the proposed rule and are not currently effective.

I ask that you also consider the unique circumstances of children who came to the United States with their parents at a young age. Many parents came to this country legally for employment and brought their children with them. These children may have completed their elementary, middle, and high school education in the United States and then continued through an American college or university. For many of them, the United States is the only home they truly know.

Their education, family, community, friendships, professional relationships, and personal lives have been built here. Asking these young adults to pursue education or early-career opportunities in another country is not necessarily a realistic alternative. They may have little educational, professional, or social connection to another country, despite their immigration status.

Families have also made substantial financial and personal investments in their children's education in the United States, including college tuition and living expenses. After years of education, OPT provides these graduates with an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to their field of study. Under existing rules, eligible F-1 students can generally receive up to 12 months of OPT, with eligible STEM graduates potentially qualifying for an additional 24-month extension.

A potential combined fee burden of $100,000 associated with initial and subsequent OPT would be beyond the reach of many ordinary families and could create a system in which practical training opportunities depend heavily on financial resources rather than education, merit, skills, or professional potential.

I respectfully ask DHS to carefully consider the unintended consequences of these proposed fees, particularly for students who have spent most of their formative years in the United States. I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud and misuse of the OPT program, but I believe those goals can be pursued through stronger compliance, oversight, verification, and enforcement without creating an overwhelming financial burden for legitimate students and their families.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fee amounts and explore a more proportionate approach that protects the integrity of the OPT program while recognizing the circumstances of students who have been educated and raised in the United States.

These students are not simply seeking an employment opportunity. For many, they are trying to begin their adult lives in the country where they grew up, studied, built relationships, and became part of their communities.

Thank you for considering the impact this proposed rule may have on these students and their families.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees would have an extraordinary negative impact on students and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michael Walfish
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal entirely.

1. Excessive Financial Burden

International students already make substantial financial investments in American education, including tuition, housing, insurance, and living expenses. Many depend on education loans and family savings. Although institutions may formally bear these proposed fees, the costs could ultimately be passed to students through additional charges or reduced opportunities. A $70,000 fee is an extraordinary financial barrier for graduates who have already invested years in their education.

2. Damage to Quantitative Finance and Wall Street

This proposal could seriously damage the quantitative finance industry, including hedge funds, investment banks, proprietary trading firms, asset management companies, and financial technology startups.

Quantitative finance depends on highly specialized talent in mathematics, statistics, computer science, machine learning, artificial intelligence, financial engineering, and computational modeling. International graduates from American universities contribute valuable expertise as quantitative researchers, quantitative developers, algorithmic traders, financial engineers, and risk analysts.

A $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could make hiring international graduates financially impractical. Smaller hedge funds, proprietary trading firms, and financial startups would be particularly disadvantaged because they cannot absorb such extraordinary costs.

3. Threat to American Financial Competitiveness

The United States is a global leader in financial markets partly because it attracts exceptional international talent. New York and other American financial centers depend on access to highly skilled professionals who contribute to market innovation, financial research, and technological development.

If hiring international graduates becomes prohibitively expensive, financial institutions may increasingly move recruitment, research, and development activities toward competing financial centers such as London, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

At a time when artificial intelligence, algorithmic trading, and advanced computing are transforming financial markets, restricting access to specialized talent could weaken America's competitive advantage and benefit foreign financial markets.

4. Negative Impact on American Employers and Innovation

The proposed fees would not only affect international students. They could also hurt American businesses, universities, research institutions, and employers. Companies may choose not to hire qualified graduates because of the additional financial burden. This could reduce innovation, limit employment opportunities, and weaken the talent pipeline supporting American technology and finance.

5. Disproportionate Approach to Fraud Prevention

I recognize DHS's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect program integrity. However, imposing extraordinary fees on legitimate students and employers is not a proportionate solution. Fraud should be addressed through targeted investigations, institutional oversight, compliance requirements, and appropriate penalties for proven violations rather than excessive financial barriers affecting everyone.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal entirely.
