comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposal. A lawful agency fee must be tied to the cost of a service provided to an identifiable recipient
(Independent Offices Appropriation Act, 31 U.S.C. 9701). The NPRM contains no cost analysis
linking $70,000 or $30,000 to any government cost. The current Form I-765 adjudication fee is
about $500 — the proposal is roughly 140 times that cost.
Worse, the NPRM admits the amounts are punitive and deterrent rather than cost-based: it states
that schools may pass the fee on to students and that doing so "would further discourage misuse
of OPT" (91 FR at 64576). The proceeds would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts; the
NPRM concedes "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected"
(91 FR at 64577) — not one dollar would fund the fraud enforcement the rule claims to serve. A
charge designed to deter behavior and raise general revenue is a tax, and the power to tax
belongs to Congress alone. DHS's own estimates put annual transfers at $8.4–16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4
billion per year , across 2,478 affected institutions (91 FR at 64584). Under the major questions
doctrine, an agency action of this economic and political magnitude requires a clear statement of
congressional authorization (Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023); West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S.
697 (2022)). INA § 214(a)'s general authority to prescribe the "time and conditions" of admission
has never before been read to authorize multi-billion-dollar per-student exactions.
The closest precedent has already been struck down: in June 2026, a federal court vacated the
administration's $100,000 H-1B charge as an unauthorized tax, and courts have since declined to
stay or have separately enjoined it. The OPT fee shares the same defects.No reasoned basis for the amounts. The NPRM offers no explanation of why $70,000 and
$30,000 are the correct figures rather than any others.
Circular cost-benefit analysis. DHS "assumes these opportunity costs are equal to or less
than the proposed fee per OPT instance" (91 FR at 64585) — valuing a lost year of skilled
professional work at exactly the amount of the fee DHS invented.
Gross mismatch of means and ends. DHS's own evidence shows fraud concentrated among
a small minority of bad actors — even its 2026 probe identified roughly 10,000 suspectparticipants out of about 194,554 OPT employment authorizations in 2024 (around 5%). The
fee punishes the other ~95% across every field and treats compliant universities identically to
bad actors. Targeted tools (site visits, training plans, employer verification) were considered
and rejected as too administratively burdensome (91 FR at 64577). Convenience is not a
reasoned basis for a blanket punitive fee.
Irrational compounding. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and then post-completion
OPT triggers $70,000 + $30,000 = $100,000 for one person, although any fraud risk is per
person, not per recommendation.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees are unlawful, punitive, and exceed agency authority without cost justification.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Theresa McCromick
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

To the Department of Homeland Security,

As the Chair of the Department of Chemistry at Portland State University (PSU), I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed fee increases for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and to urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

Our graduate program relies heavily on talented international students, who use OPT to transition from their academic training into the U.S. workforce. However, the current proposal fails to examine how public research universities—and the state governance structures that fund them—will be impacted. In its federalism discussion, DHS lists the effect on state governments as “N/A” and notes that it did not consult state officials. This overlooks the financial reality of public access institutions like PSU, where half of our funding comes from the state and the other half comes from student tuition.

Graduate students earning stipends of less than $30,000 per year cannot reasonably afford a $70,000 fee. Absorbing this cost would fall to the university, ultimately forcing tuition increases for all students. The far more likely outcome is a sharp decline in international enrollment. Furthermore, the international students who do attend will be forced to leave the U.S. after graduation rather than staying to contribute their advanced skills to our local, state, and federal economies. Depleting both our graduate student pool and our domestic scientific workforce will severely harm American competitiveness in scientific research and development.

While this fee increase is framed as a measure to deter fraud, robust anti-fraud protections are already in place. In my role helping process OPT applications for PSU chemistry students—all of whom I know personally—I have never encountered an application that was improper or failed to benefit the U.S. economy. While bad actors may exist elsewhere, existing vetting mechanisms already ensure that the applications reaching my desk are entirely legitimate.

At PSU, the majority of our chemistry graduates go on to support the domestic semiconductor industry. This proposal directly threatens our program and our ability to train the STEM workforce in this critical national sector.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal in its entirety. I also strongly oppose the alternative proposal on which DHS requested comment, which would assess the $70,000 fee repeatedly at each higher degree level. Any fee structure should be calibrated strictly to the actual administrative cost of program oversight, rather than serving as a punitive revenue measure. Neither students nor public universities can absorb these costs, and implementing them will disproportionately disenfranchise state research institutions.

Sincerely,

Theresa McCormick, PhD
Chair, Department of Chemistry
Portland State University

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Patric Gerard
comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

Optional Practical Training Fees (Proposed Rule)Introduction

I am an American citizen submitting this comment in strong support of the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. I am particularly concerned about the long-term effects of large-scale guest-worker programs on employment opportunities for U.S. students and workers, especially in STEM fields. While the proposed fees are a useful interim step, I believe OPT should be terminated altogether.Background

This comment addresses the proposed rule that would require SEVP-certified schools to pay a $70,000 fee for the initial OPT recommendation of an F-1 student and $30,000 for any subsequent recommendation (including STEM OPT extensions). The fees would be paid by the school before a Designated School Official could recommend the student for OPT in SEVIS. I support these fees as proposed and urge the agency to finalize them promptly.Analysis

OPT was never authorized by Congress. It was created by administrative rulemaking and expanded over time into a multi-year work authorization program for foreign students after they complete their studies. The F-1 visa category was intended for temporary study, not as a pathway to U.S. employment. There is no clear statutory basis for granting open-ended work authorization under OPT, no prevailing-wage requirement, and no numerical limit on the number of participants.This structure disadvantages American workers. Employers hiring certain OPT participants can avoid the employer share of Social Security and Medicare (FICA) taxes, creating a direct cost advantage over hiring a U.S. worker for the same role. In practice, this functions as a subsidy for employing foreign graduates rather than Americans. Data consistently show that a large share of U.S. STEM graduates do not end up working in STEM occupations; large-scale OPT and related guest-worker programs contribute to this mismatch by increasing labor supply in precisely those fields without corresponding protections for domestic workers.The program also creates incentives for “pay-to-stay” and other schemes that weaken the integrity of the student visa system. Schools and employers have financial reasons to maximize OPT participation, while American graduates face increased competition for entry-level and early-career positions without the same tax or regulatory advantages. The proposed fees would raise the cost of these recommendations, deter low-value or fraudulent participation, and force schools and employers to internalize more of the external costs currently borne by U.S. workers.I recognize that fees alone do not solve the underlying problem. The better policy outcome is for Congress to end OPT entirely (for example, through legislation such as H.R. 2315, the Fairness for High-Skilled Americans Act). Until that occurs, the fees in this proposed rule are a practical and justified measure that reduces the scale of an unauthorized program and prioritizes American students and workers.Recommendations
Finalize the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees as written, without reducing the amounts or creating broad exemptions.
In the preamble to the final rule, clearly restate that the F-1 category was never intended to serve as a work pathway and that OPT lacks explicit statutory authorization.
Coordinate with the Department of Labor and Congress on permanent reforms that would eliminate OPT work authorization and close related loopholes, rather than treating fees as a permanent substitute for ending the program.
Monitor and publicly report on the effect of the fees on the volume of OPT recommendations, STEM OPT extensions, and any displacement effects on U.S. graduates.
Conclusion

I support the proposed OPT fees because they will raise the cost of an administratively created work program that Congress never authorized, reduce the tax subsidy that favors foreign graduates over Americans, and better protect U.S. students and workers. The fees are a necessary interim step. The preferable long-term solution remains the complete termination of OPT. Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong support for the proposed OPT fees and urges the agency to finalize them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Vicky Boss
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees. I oppose the proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I am a graduate student at Northeastern University, currently interning at TikTok on large-scale advertising systems, and I expect to graduate in Spring 2027. OPT is the practical training my degree is designed to lead into, and the only lawful way for me to continue that field-related work after graduation. If schools cannot pay $70,000 to recommend OPT, I would lose that path entirely, despite having completed my U.S. degree and training in the U.S.

1. The charge is a tax, not a fee. A lawful agency fee must be tied to the cost of a service provided to an identifiable recipient (31 U.S.C. 9701). The proposal contains no cost analysis linking $70,000 or $30,000 to any government cost. The current Form I-765 adjudication fee is about $500, so the proposal is roughly 140 times that cost. Worse, the proposal admits the amounts are punitive and deterrent rather than cost-based: it states that schools may pass the fee on to students and that doing so "would further discourage misuse of OPT" (91 FR at 64576). The proceeds would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts; the proposal concedes "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected" (91 FR at 64577), so not one dollar would fund the fraud enforcement the rule claims to serve. A charge designed to deter behavior and raise general revenue is a tax, and the power to tax belongs to Congress alone.

2. An exaction of this scale requires clear congressional authorization. DHS's own estimates put annual transfers at $8.4-16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion per year, across 2,478 affected institutions (91 FR at 64584). Under the major questions doctrine, an agency action of this economic and political magnitude requires a clear statement of congressional authorization (Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023); West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)). INA section 214(a)'s general authority to prescribe the "time and conditions" of admission has never before been read to authorize multi-billion-dollar per-student exactions. The closest precedent has already been struck down: in June 2026, a federal court vacated the administration's $100,000 H-1B charge as an unauthorized tax. The OPT fee shares the same defects.

3. The rule is arbitrary and capricious. The proposal offers no explanation of why $70,000 and $30,000 are the correct figures rather than any others. Its cost-benefit analysis is circular: DHS "assumes these opportunity costs are equal to or less than the proposed fee per OPT instance" (91 FR at 64585), valuing a lost year of skilled professional work at exactly the amount of the fee DHS invented. The means also mismatch the ends: DHS's own evidence shows fraud concentrated among a small minority of bad actors, roughly 10,000 suspect participants out of about 194,554 OPT employment authorizations in 2024, around 5%. The fee punishes the other roughly 95% across every field and treats compliant universities identically to bad actors. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and then post-completion OPT triggers $70,000 + $30,000 = $100,000 for one person, although any fraud risk is per person, not per recommendation.

4. It punishes the wrong people. The fraud DHS describes concerns fake employers and shell companies falsifying employment, not a university's recommendation. Taxing the school's recommendation does nothing to catch fraudulent employers; it only deters compliant universities from recommending legitimate students.

5. OPT is not "optional" for many graduates. For many F-1 students, OPT is the degree-related practical training that completes their education: the supervised, field-related work experience their degree program is designed to lead into, and in many fields the only lawful way to do it after graduation.

6. A less restrictive alternative already exists. STEM OPT already requires formal training plans, employer reporting, and site visits. Extending verification requirements to post-completion OPT would target fraud directly, at its actual source. DHS rejected such measures as administratively burdensome, but the agency's convenience does not justify shifting $12.4 billion per year onto students and universities. International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 355,736 American jobs in 2024-25 (NAFSA); new international student enrollment had already dropped by 17 percent from fall 2024 to fall 2025. Finalizing this fee would lock in that decline and hand U.S.-trained talent to competitor countries.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and asks DHS to withdraw it due to high fees.

I am writing in opposition to this proposed rule.

Read its design carefully, because the design is the confession. If DHS wanted to recover the cost of OPT, it would charge the student, as it already does with the $410 filing fee for the I-765. Instead, this rule charges the school $70,000, payable before the school official is even permitted to enter the recommendation. That structure has one purpose: to make universities do the excluding. No student will ever receive a denial under this rule. No official will ever have to look at a 23-year-old and say her future is cancelled. Her school will simply stop participating, OPT will die in a budget meeting, and the Department's hands stay clean. That is not fee-setting. It is a ban built with plausible deniability, by people who did not want to defend a ban in the open.

Consider who pays the price. F-1 students are the most documented, most tracked, most compliant people in the immigration system. Their addresses are on file. Their employers are reported. Their status is verified term by term. They broke nothing. They paid full tuition, followed every rule they were handed, and made decisions that cannot be undone — turning down other countries, taking on debt, building years of a life here — in reliance on the terms they were offered. This rule touches no one who broke the law. It lands only on the people who obeyed it, because they are the ones standing in the open, where they are easy to reach. That is not enforcement. It is punishing compliance because compliance is convenient to punish.

The amount itself admits the intent. $70,000 is more than a year of tuition at most universities, more than many graduates will earn in their first year of work. The act being "paid for" — an official entering a recommendation into an existing database — costs almost nothing. Nobody at DHS calculated $70,000. Somebody chose it, the way you choose the height of a fence: high enough that nothing gets over. A price set above what anyone can pay is not a price. It is a wall, described in the language of accounting so its builders can call it bookkeeping.

And the charge returns. $30,000 more for every later recommendation, including the STEM extension. Even in the fantasy where one wealthy school pays once, the toll comes back two years later. The cruelty is not a side effect of this design. It recurs on schedule, because it is the design.

Behind all of this are students who are mid-degree right now, 19 and 20 years old, who chose this country in good faith. They cannot un-borrow the loans. They cannot recover the years. This rule reaches back into decisions already made by people with no power and no vote, and reprices their future at a number chosen to be impossible. There is a word for changing the terms on the powerless after they can no longer walk away, and that word is not "fee."

Withdraw this proposal. If the Department wants to end OPT, let it say so in plain words and take responsibility for saying it. The students this country invited are owed at least that much honesty.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed rule functions as a ban and harms compliant F-1 students and universities.

Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, “Optional Practical Training Fees” (RIN 1653-AB01, 91 FR 64566)

I am an international PhD student (F-1) at Yale University, where I have trained since 2022. My work bears directly on the biology of autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia, conditions that affect millions of Americans. I am also a Teaching Fellow for Yale’s neuroanatomy lab course and coordinate neuroscience workshops for New Haven high school students. I am submitting this comment because the proposed rule would directly determine whether I, and scientists like me, can continue doing this work in the United States after graduation.

1. The fee structure would effectively close OPT to biomedical researchers [8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)]

The proposed rule would require SEVP-certified schools to pay $70,000 before a DSO may recommend a student for initial OPT, and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension. For a STEM PhD graduate who uses OPT and the STEM extension, that is $100,000 per person.

I expect to complete my PhD between late 2027 and spring 2028, and I plan to begin a postdoctoral fellowship in a U.S. neuroscience lab. For many international PhD graduates, post-completion OPT and the STEM extension are the standard bridge into a first postdoctoral position. A $70,000 fee exceeds a full year of a typical NIH-scale postdoctoral salary. Academic labs run on fixed federal and foundation grants that cannot absorb a cost of this size, and the rule expressly allows schools to shift it to students or employers. In practice, universities and principal investigators will simply stop recommending or hiring OPT-dependent scientists. The result would not be stronger program integrity; it would be the loss of trained researchers that U.S. institutions have already invested years in educating.

2. The rule would disrupt ongoing, federally funded research and collaborations

My dissertation project involves long-term work that does not pause neatly at graduation: maintained transgenic mouse colonies, CRISPR-based deletion lines, longitudinal behavioral cohorts, and transcriptomic analyses. It also depends on collaborations across institutions. Postdoctoral research builds on exactly this kind of expertise. If OPT becomes financially inaccessible, researchers like me would be forced to leave the country or abandon research mid-stream, wasting public research dollars and delaying results that matter for understanding psychiatric disease. Labs that train undergraduates, as I do through mentoring students, would also lose the early-career scientists who supervise them.

3. The fraud rationale does not fit university-based research training [8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii)]

DHS justifies the fee as a way to reduce fraud and abuse of OPT. Whatever problems exist at specific institutions or employers, a flat, per-student fee assessed on every SEVP-certified school, including research universities with rigorous oversight, is not targeted at fraud. It penalizes legitimate training at institutions like Yale, where OPT placements are research positions directly related to a student’s field. DHS already has enforcement tools, including SEVIS reporting, employer attestations, and site visits for STEM OPT, that address misuse without pricing out compliant students. DHS should explain why these targeted measures are inadequate before imposing a fee estimated at billions of dollars per year across thousands of schools.

4. The rule would slow scientific progress that benefits all Americans and the world, and cede U.S. leadership in research

Scientific progress is cumulative and collaborative. Discoveries made in U.S. laboratories, from basic insights into brain development to new treatments for psychiatric and neurological disease, benefit patients and families across the country and around the world. Much of that progress depends on international trainees, who make up a substantial share of the graduate students and postdoctoral researchers doing the day-to-day experimental work in American labs. When these researchers are priced out, projects stall, labs shrink, and the pace of discovery slows for everyone.

The United States became the world’s leading destination for scientific training because it welcomed talented researchers and gave them a path to keep contributing after graduation. Other countries are actively competing for this talent by expanding fellowships, streamlining visas, and recruiting scientists trained in the United States. A $70,000 barrier to OPT would send a clear signal that U.S. institutions can no longer reliably retain the scientists they educate. Talented researchers would build their careers, labs, patents, and companies elsewhere, and the scientific prestige, innovation, and economic returns that come with them would follow. Once lost, that leadership is difficult to rebuild.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
​I am writing this comment in regard to Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, specifically the proposed fee structure under 8 CFR § 214.13(i) and the corresponding procedural amendments to 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(11), which would collectively make the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program prohibitively expensive. As a graduate student and now as a postdoctoral researcher at top-tier Ivy League institutions specializing in Biological Physics and Microbiology, I have spent the last 10 years in academic research environments. During this time, I have witnessed firsthand the profound, indispensable contributions of the OPT program to American science, public health, and technological innovation.
​Through the OPT framework, some of the world's most brilliant minds are able to remain in the United States after completing their doctoral degrees at elite research institutions. These individuals fill critical gaps in domestic industry sectors. I personally know remarkable scientists who benefited from OPT and have gone on to work in industry jobs in biomedical research, AI drug discovery, AI for electric grid optimization, quantum computing development, and countless other impactful professions for which there are not enough US nationals to fulfill these roles. Additionally, another large fraction of these students have stayed in academia, driving important research and discoveries in many fields of science. Some of these researchers have now moved on to faculty positions at top programs around the US, training a new generation of scientists.
​In my own research laboratory, multiple colleagues have relied on OPT status. For example, a former post-baccalaureate researcher from Mexico utilized this program to contribute to the discovery of a novel underwater bio-adhesive with vital medical and surgical applications. This practical training provided the necessary foundation for them to transition successfully into a Ph.D. program. Countless international students are fully educated and trained using American institutional resources. Therefore, allowing them to transition into the workforce directly enriches our national capabilities.
​The United States has been at the forefront of scientific and industrial discoveries thanks to aggressive programs to recruit the brightest minds in the world regardless of their place of origin. This allowed our astronauts to be the first on the moon, and our tech companies to achieve worldwide dominance. By effectively eliminating programs such as OPT, we are squandering all the resources that as a country we have invested in recruiting and training these amazingly bright minds and forcing these students to take their advanced skillsets to our direct geopolitical and economic competitors (China, Europe, India, etc). It is in our best interest as a nation to establish programs and incentives that avoid "brain drain" as opposed to limiting opportunities to retain talent.
​I urge DHS to withdraw both the proposed fee structure (8 CFR § 214.13(i)) and the corresponding procedural amendments (8 CFR § 214.2(f)(11)). By shifting the financial burden of OPT authorization to the recommending university and imposing an unprecedented $70,000 fee (compared to the nominal $470 application fee previously paid by the student), the functional outcome is the elimination of the OPT pathway for the early-career researchers who drive our nation's innovation. Enacting these structural barriers will be detrimental to our great nation and will provide immediate advantages to our competitors on the global stage.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sivmey Srin
comments.commentText:
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
RIN 1653-AB01
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Optional Practical Training Fees
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing as an international student currently pursuing my degree in the United States to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees.
The proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and an additional $30,000 for STEM OPT extensions are completely detached from economic reality. They will effectively dismantle the OPT program, decimate America's ability to attract global talent, and inflict severe financial distress on international students and the universities that host us.
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule based on the following critical flaws:
• Unprecedented Financial Barrier for Students: While the rule technically levies this fee on universities, institutions will inevitably be forced to pass these astronomical costs down to students. International students already pay premium tuition rates and are restricted in their ability to work off-campus. Adding a $70,000 to $100,000 financial hurdle just to gain practical experience in our fields of study will price out all but the wealthiest individuals, destroying equity and diversity in higher education.
• Destruction of Practical Learning and Career Pathways: OPT is not a loophole; it is an integral, complementary component of American higher education. Forcing students or their employers to pay up to $100,000 to utilize this benefit makes it completely unviable.
• Severe Harm to the U.S. Economy and STEM Innovation: The U.S. has long been a global leader because it retains the brightest minds educated at its world-class universities. By placing a massive financial penalty on OPT, DHS will drive top international talent to competing nations like Canada, the UK, and Australia, which actively incentivize international graduates to stay and work.
• Flawed Rationale and Benchmarking: DHS’s attempt to benchmark OPT fees against H-1B structures is legally and conceptually flawed. F-1 students are not H-1B visa holders; we are paying customers of the U.S. education system seeking a temporary period of practical application.
As a student funding my education through family savings, a fee of this magnitude would mean I would have to leave the country immediately upon graduation without the chance to apply my skills, rendering my investment in my U.S. education incomplete.
A 30-day comment window is entirely insufficient for the public to analyze and respond to an economically significant rule of this magnitude. This proposal does not protect U.S. workers; it simply punishes students and weakens American universities. I strongly request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule entirely.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition and urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule.

This proposal could also hurt the United States. The opportunity to gain professional experience after graduation is an important reason international students choose American universities. If that pathway becomes prohibitively expensive or uncertain, talented students may choose to study and build their careers in other countries, taking their skills and future contributions with them.

I am especially concerned about students who are already participating in OPT. Many of us made significant educational, financial, and career decisions based on the existing system. If DHS moves forward with these fees, I strongly urge the Department to provide transition protections for students already enrolled in U.S. universities or currently on OPT, including those who will later apply for STEM OPT extensions.

The United States should address fraud without discouraging legitimate, U.S.-educated graduates from contributing their skills here. I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposed fee structure.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Putting a high fee of USD 70,000 for initial OPT and USD 30,000 for subsequent OPT will ultimately be a disadvantage for the United States in the following ways:
• It will discourage international students to choose US universities for their higher education, so they will go to other countries. US universities will experience loss of billions of dollars in tuition and other revenue that international students currently bring.
• US organizations will experience loss of talent that international graduates supply. There may be a serious skills shortage in STEM fields that Americans may not be able to fill, hence it will be a loss for the US economy.

I understand the desire of the US government to protect US jobs for US citizens, but this can be achieved through other ways (e.g., allowing US companies to ask about citizenship in the job application form, and allowing them to reject applicants who are not US citizens or permanent residents, because sponsoring a work visa consumes time, money, and effort, and there is uncertainty in the H1B lottery).

Fraud can be prevented in the following ways:
• Eliminate unpaid or volunteer work for OPT (which some international graduates use to stop the unemployment clock of 90 days in the first year of OPT).
• Eliminate "day 1 CPT" (which some international graduates use to continue working in US jobs if they were not selected in H1B lotteries during OPT).

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (91 FR 64566), Proposed OPT Fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees on SEVP-certified schools. The fees bear no relation to the cost of any service. They rest on contradictory estimates, they are uneconomic for schools by simple arithmetic, and they would push U.S.-trained talent abroad without protecting American workers. DHS should withdraw the proposal.

1. Fee is unrelated to cost
Students now pay about $470 to file for OPT. The school's role is a SEVIS entry by its own staff. The proposed $70,000 is about 149 times that filing fee, and initial OPT plus STEM OPT would rise from $940 to $100,940. DHS projects $8.4-16.5 billion a year in fee payments, far beyond any plausible cost of overseeing OPT. That makes this a penalty, not a user fee, and DHS says one purpose is to discourage OPT use. DHS should identify what authority permits a fee this far above cost, charged to schools that are not the applicants.

2. Revenue estimate contradicts the policy goal
Let N(F) be the number of OPT recommendations at fee F, with N falling as F rises. Revenue is R(F) = F x N(F). DHS's $8.4-16.5 billion projection implies about 120,000-236,000 fee-paying recommendations a year, roughly today's level. So DHS assumes the fee barely changes behavior, while saying its aim is to change behavior. The Economic Innovation Group projects a 35% drop in international graduate applicants under a $100,000 fee, and 80% of surveyed students said they would reconsider staying. Both cannot hold: if the fee deters, revenue is overstated; if revenue is accurate, the fee does not deter. DHS's cost estimate spans $32 million to over $8 billion, a factor of 250, which shows it never estimated N(F).

3. Schools would lose money
A school recommends OPT only if its net margin on the student covers the fee: m x T >= F, where T is total tuition and m is the margin after costs. For an illustrative STEM master's with T = $80,000, initial OPT requires m >= 87.5%. Adding STEM OPT (F = $100,000) requires m >= 125%, which is impossible. For PhD students, tuition is usually waived, so each fee comes directly out of research budgets. DHS itself says over 56% of SEVP-certified schools may be small entities.

4. Pass-through is a confiscatory tax
If schools pass the fee on, the effective tax on the graduate's work is F / (w x t). At an illustrative salary of $85,000, 12 months of OPT is taxed at 82%, and 36 months of OPT plus STEM OPT at 39%. An employer facing this can hire the same graduate in Toronto or London, or offshore the work. The job then leaves the U.S.; it does not go to an American.

5. The displacement premise is weak
The rule treats jobs as a fixed quantity. Economists call this the lump-of-labor fallacy. Peri, Shih and Sparber (2015) link foreign STEM workers to higher wages for college-educated natives. Hunt and Gauthier-Loiselle (2010) find immigrant graduates raise patenting. Immigrants founded or co-founded over half of U.S. billion-dollar startups (NFAP). Studies that find some firm-level substitution, such as Doran, Gelber and Isen (2022), support targeted measures, not dismantling the program. Those measures already exist: STEM OPT requires E-Verify, a Form I-983 training plan, comparable terms of employment, and DHS site visits. DHS should enforce them rather than charge a fee it does not dedicate to fraud detection.

6. Lost investment, stronger competitors
U.S. universities and taxpayers invest heavily in training these graduates. This rule ensures the return is realized elsewhere, in Canada, the U.K., and strategic competitors such as China, weakening long-term U.S. technological strength.

7. Alternatives were not analyzed
DHS calls effects on universities and competitiveness too speculative and does not adequately weigh less burdensome options such as SEVIS data matching, risk-based employer audits, and enforcing existing STEM OPT rules, as regulatory analysis and the Regulatory Flexibility Act require.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees in full.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and argues they should be withdrawn.

I urge you to rescind the changes proposed in ICEB-2026-0100-0001, Optional Practical Training Fees, because of the harm it will cause to higher education, the economy and our standing in global competitiveness.

It also benefits businesses by allowing them to hire talented U.S. trained and educated graduates from other countries. It benefits our global standing, because the graduates use their talents here instead of abroad.
The proposed 140 times increase in fees, from $500 to $70,000 (plus an additional $30,000 for extensions) would dramatically decrease participation in the program. In the 2024-25 academic year, roughly one-quarter of all international students (more than 294,250) participated. Their loss would be felt immediately and become even greater over time.
Please act to keep our higher education high quality, the economy strong and our standing in global competitiveness high, by withdrawing this proposal and keeping the fees the same or lower.
Thank you

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security,

Introduction and background:
I am a PhD student in STEM at an American R1 university, here on an F-1 Visa, writing to oppose the proposed OPT fees ($70k for initial OPT, $30k for subsequent OPT). In my comment, I will focus specifically on the impact of this proposed rule on graduate students.

Analysis:
Research in my field is often funded by Department of Defense and private industry grants, due to its strong applicability in defense and profitable commercial technologies. These are also the fields in which I and students in similar programs are likely to make contributions, if allowed to remain in the United States through OPT. The fees proposed, particularly if passed down to students as the document acknowledges is probable, would make it financially untenable for students to participate in OPT. Thus, students in my position would likely have to leave the US and aim to make these contributions elsewhere.

The majority of graduate students, myself included, are financially self-supported by stipends (paid from a variety of sources including fellowships, scholarships, TA-ships, or research grants) which are significantly below $70k/year. That is, even the initial OPT fee of $70k would significantly exceed a year’s wage for a PhD student. Most students I know budget carefully, often choosing to live with roommates to reduce costs. The $70k fee is not an amount that students can realistically be expected to save up. The alternative—that the university pays the OPT fees instead of the student—seems very unlikely given that this same money could support a student actively working for the university rather than a student who (in the case of post-completion OPT) is most likely leaving the institute. The document states that DSOs “can elect not to pay the fee for a particular F-1 nonimmigrant who is not a strong candidate for OPT.” I would add that universities/colleges can elect not to pay the fee regardless of how strong a candidate is—after all, what incentive do they have to pay for a worker they will not be retaining themselves? Finally, the document suggests that the cost could be passed on to prospective employers instead. I can’t speak to the likelihood of an employer agreeing to this but, from a personal standpoint, it is a hope I would not be prepared to financially rely on.

Conclusion:
If they were to pass, these proposed fees would create at best strong financial uncertainty and at worst an impossibility for PhD students wanting to use OPT to exercise their highly specialized research expertise in the US. DHS proposes this rule to deter adverse actors—I would argue that it will deter all actors, including those for which the OPT program was designed.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Zachary Clifton
comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Optional Practical Training Fees

I write as an American citizen from Kentucky and an undergraduate at Yale College. My family came to this land before it was the United States. In the three centuries since, people have kept coming for the opportunity this country promises. There was nothing morally right in my ancestors’ timing, and there is nothing morally wrong in the timing of those who ask for that promise now. Some of my closest friends and the most remarkable people I know are international students. This rule would treat them as suspects and price them out of the training that their education is meant to include. I oppose it in its entirety. My reasons follow, with references to the sections of the proposal.

1. The fee is not tailored to the fraud it cites (Section IV.A). Nearly every example of abuse in the proposal involves shell employers, staged worksites and fraudulent offer letters. Yet the fee is charged to schools, for every student, before any employer is even identified; the proposal says the fee “would not be tied to a specific employer.” The investigation the Department highlights found about 10,000 students working for suspect employers. More than 190,000 students reported OPT employment in 2024 alone, and more than 165,000 more were in STEM OPT. A $70,000 charge on every student is not a reasonable response to misconduct by a small set of employers.

2. The fee raises serious legal questions. The Department says it set the fee to “closely align” with H-1B fees. On June 8, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 H-1B fee, holding that it was a tax Congress never authorized (State of California v. Mullin, No. 25-cv-13829). This proposal has the same features: a very large charge, revenue sent to the general Treasury, and a stated purpose of reducing participation. INA 214(a) lets the Secretary set the “time and conditions” of admission. It does not give the Secretary the power to tax.

3. It selects for wealth, not merit (Sections IV.C and VI). The Department says the fee will lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students.” A $70,000 price tag does not measure promise. It measures who can pay. The Department admits schools may pass the cost on to international students, to all students, or to employers. That means American students like me could end up paying it through tuition. The Department itself compares the fee to one or two extra years of education. In practice, OPT would become a privilege of the wealthy, and talented students from modest backgrounds would go to countries that welcome them.

4. The Department’s own numbers show severe harm. By its own estimate, the rule would cost about $4.1 billion a year (primary estimate), with lost-participation costs of up to about $8 billion a year, and would transfer about $109 billion over ten years. It also estimates that 116 small institutions would lose more than 20 percent of their annual revenue in the first year, and that 841 small institutions would lose more than 1 percent. It considered exempting small institutions and rejected the idea. It also says it cannot confidently predict how much participation would fall. A rule this large, resting on admitted uncertainty, needs far more justification than this one gives.

5. The structure is arbitrary (Section V.A; Section VII.A.5.d(3)). A student who does a summer internship through pre-completion OPT and then post-completion OPT would cost the school $100,000. The same 12 months taken all after graduation would cost $70,000. The Department expects this to discourage pre-completion OPT, which is the form most closely tied to a student’s ongoing studies. A rule that claims to protect OPT’s educational purpose should not penalize its most educational use.

6. The process is inadequate. The Department admits this is an economically significant rule, yet it allowed only about 30 days for comment. Executive Order 12866 says comment periods should generally be at least 60 days. The Department also says it did not consult state, local or tribal governments, even though about 1,044 public institutions would be affected.

If the Department has evidence of fraud by particular employers or schools, it has tools to go after them: site visits, training-plan requirements, employer verification, SEVP decertification and criminal prosecution. I urge it to withdraw this proposal and use those tools against the wrongdoers, not to charge every international student and every school for the misconduct of a few.

This country made a promise to the people who came before me. I ask the Department not to break it for the people who are asking for it now.

Zachary Clifton 
Yale College, Class of 2028, a native son of Kentucky
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they oppose the proposed rule and argues the fee prices international students out of training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Emily Scott
comments.commentText:
Public comment on the proposed Optional Practical Training fees

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am the F. F. Blicke Collegiate Professor of Pharmacy at the University of Michigan, where I teach and conduct research in medicinal chemistry and pharmacology. My lab studies how human cytochrome P450 enzymes affect the way our bodies process medicines and how these enzymes can be targeted to develop better treatments. I am writing in my personal capacity to urge DHS to withdraw its proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee rule in its entirety. The proposal would require schools to pay $70,000 for a student’s initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I am concerned that fees of this size would put OPT out of reach for many otherwise eligible scientists. Federal Register proposed rule

Keeping research projects moving

Several postdoctoral researchers in my lab have worked under OPT. In experimental research, it takes time to learn a technique well enough to troubleshoot an experiment and interpret the results with confidence. As postdocs gain that experience, they can take on more responsibility and help move projects forward. If the fees lead universities to make fewer OPT recommendations, labs like mine will have fewer opportunities to bring in researchers with the right scientific background. When a position goes unfilled, the experiments that depend on that person’s work can be delayed.

Helping scientists start careers in the United States

The postdocs I have worked with used their time on OPT to learn techniques and gain research experience they went on to use in the pharmaceutical industry. I have seen how a period of practical training can connect university research to the skills employers need. Here in Ann Arbor, that connection matters because our research labs help train the scientists that pharmaceutical and biotechnology employers can hire. Making it harder for graduates to take their first research positions in the United States would weaken that connection and make it harder for U.S. employers to benefit from the scientists we train here.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in full and preserve access to OPT. Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Emily E. Scott, Ph.D.
F. F. Blicke Collegiate Professor of Pharmacy
Professor, Departments of Medicinal Chemistry and Pharmacology
Affiliate faculty, Department of Biological Chemistry, Biophysics Program
University of Michigan
1007 E. Huron St.
Ann Arbor, MI 48104-1628

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong concern about the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. I am concerned that a fee this large could have significant economic consequences for the United States itself.

The economic impact of this proposal is bigger than whether a particular job is ultimately filled by an international student or an American worker. When OPT participation falls, the United States can lose the economic activity that comes with these students staying, working, earning, spending, and contributing to the economy after graduation.

International students already spend substantial amounts of money in the United States while earning their degrees. They pay tuition, rent apartments, buy food and other goods, use transportation, and spend money in the communities where they live. If the cost of OPT makes the United States less attractive as a place to study, some students may choose other countries instead. That means the economic impact begins before graduation, through lost enrollment, tuition revenue, and local spending.

American universities could also be affected. Many universities rely on international enrollment, and the opportunity to gain practical work experience after graduation is an important part of the value of a U.S. degree for international students. If OPT becomes financially difficult to offer, some prospective students may decide that studying in the United States is no longer worth the cost. Over time, that could reduce enrollment and the revenue that supports American educational institutions.

There is also a broader loss of economic value when people who were educated in the United States leave immediately after graduation rather than working here. Their education was partly supported by the U.S. economy, and OPT allows them to continue contributing through their work, income, consumption, and taxes. Reducing that participation means the United States may receive less economic benefit from the investment already made in educating these students.

The proposed fee could also have a disproportionate effect on smaller universities and nonprofit institutions that do not have the financial resources to absorb such a large cost. If these institutions are unable or unwilling to pay the fee, fewer students may be able to participate in OPT, further reducing the economic activity associated with the program.

I believe the economic consequences of this proposal deserve much more consideration. For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees will harm the US economy, universities, and international student enrollment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed fee.

International students often pay higher tuition than domestic students, in addition to housing, transportation, university fees, living expenses etc. They can't access federal financial aid, and many scholarships are restricted to citizens. Even available scholarships may only reduce tuition to the in-state rate rather than cover the cost of education. Beyond tuition, international students support local businesses through everyday spending and provide significant revenue to universities. Reduced international enrollment could therefore affect educational institutions, local businesses, and surrounding communities. The proposed fees could make the US less attractive to international students, resulting in lost tuition revenue for universities.

CPT and OPT authorize eligible students to work under specific conditions, but they do not provide employer-sponsored immigration status. Many employers remain reluctant to hire international candidates, even when they are currently authorized to work, because of anticipated future H-1B sponsorship costs, administrative requirements, and immigration uncertainty. Some exclude international applicants from internships, co-ops, and entry-level positions altogether. Consequently, qualified graduates may be rejected because of their immigration statues rather than their qualifications. Sponsorship is neither automatic nor guaranteed. Employers make selective decisions based on business needs and the value a candidate brings. Many international graduates never receive sponsorship and must leave the country when their work authorization expires. It is therefore an oversimplification to claim that international graduates broadly displace American workers. They often have access to a narrower pool of employers and face barriers that domestic candidates do not. It is also important to recognize the circumstances of international students before characterizing them as competition for American workers. They have a lot of immigration and employment restrictions, pay out of pocket, and pursue an education in a country where English isn't their first language. Their presence does not automatically mean that an American worker has lost an opportunity. In many cases, employers hire international graduates because they possess specialized technical abilities, or qualifications that are difficult to find in the domestic labor market. Those who eventually receive H-1B sponsorship do so through an employer's decision to pursue that process, not through an automatic entitlement. Rather than viewing these graduates as a threat to American workers, they should be recognized as an important part of the skilled workforce that helps meet the needs of the US economy.

Some may say that F-1 students who are nonresident aliens for U.S. tax purposes may be exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes on qualifying authorized employment, potentially saving employers up to 7.65% of wages. However, this exemption does not apply to all international students. F-1 students are generally exempt from the substantial presence test during their first five calendar years in the United States. After that, they may become resident aliens for tax purposes, in which case the FICA exemption generally no longer applies. Resident alien status for tax purposes does not mean U.S. citizenship. This limited tax provision should not be portrayed as a universal employer advantage or used to suggest that international students as a group have an unfair employment advantage.

The proposed fees do not distinguish between legitimate OPT participants and institutions or employers involved in misconduct. A university recommending an eligible student who fully complies with program requirements would face the same fee structure as an institution associated with potential violations. Furthermore, the proposed amounts are not clearly tied to the actual administrative or investigative costs of individual cases. DHS should explain how it calculated these fees and why less burdensome alternatives would not achieve the same objectives. Universities can verify student eligibility and fulfill their compliance responsibilities, but they cannot reasonably be expected to investigate every employer's internal practices or prevent all employment fraud. Instead of imposing extraordinary costs on every institution, DHS should strengthen risk-based audits, verify legitimate employment arrangements, investigate repeat offenders, and impose meaningful penalties on those actually responsible for violations.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees make the US less attractive and harm international students and educational institutions.
